item.title: Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office

It comes a month after opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to Venezuela.

Venezuela will repeal a law that prohibits opposition figures from office, National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodriguez has announced.

The legislation, approved in 2024 and criticised for enabling political persecution, targeted those who promoted or supported sanctions against the country.

“That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through,” Rodriguez said on Thursday.

The law was passed just after fraught elections which the then-incumbent Nicolas Maduro ultimately won amid widespread allegations of fraud.

An interim government headed by Delcy Rodriguez, the parliamentary chief’s sister, has run Venezuela since Maduro’s abduction by US forces in January. Delcy Rodriguez promised in September during a speech at the United Nations that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.

Since then, the US-backed government has been in political transition talks with parts of the opposition selected by Washington. That dialogue had reached an agreement to review several laws, including the one up for repeal now, according to Jorge Rodriguez.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado shook up Venezuelan politics with her surprise return from exile last month. Machado won an opposition primary in 2023 to take on Maduro in the following year’s election, but she was legally barred from running. The Nobel Peace Prize laureate is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election, despite her exclusion from transition talks.

Despite being shut out, on Thursday Machado launched a system of neighbourhood assemblies aiming to gather proposals for a future government programme and democratic transition. The assemblies are expected to bring together over a million people over several months, according to Machado’s team.

“We listened to neighbours who are breaking down barriers that many thought were impossible, debating the issues that will lay the foundations for the Venezuela to come,” Machado said on social media on Thursday after the meetings. “We are designing the transition to democracy, the Venezuelan way.”

Around 2,000 meetings with residents were organised in Venezuela and abroad on the first day of the initiative, her team told the AFP news agency.

Nineteen questions are asked during the assembly, with responses fed into a digital platform. Issues of national interest range from dates for the presidential election to changes in the justice, education, health, wage and pension systems, as well as the role of the public and private sectors.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-27 20:44 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/27/venezuela-to-repeal-law-that-bans-opposition-figures-from-office?traffic_source=rss

OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secrets as AI race heats up

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition.

OpenAI has sued Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.

Apple and OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology.

In July, Apple sued OpenAI and two former employees, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware. OpenAI has denied those allegations.

The litigation sets up a battle over who will control future AI devices that may not use traditional apps or operating systems — devices which, if successful, would direct consumer attention away from Apple’s best-selling iPhone. Analysts believe OpenAI is working on a phone or other device of its own.

Putin unveils new Russian nuclear-powered submarine with hypersonic weapons

The Kremlin plans to expand its naval fleet with five new nuclear submarines by 2030.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has unveiled a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first equipped with Russian Zircon hypersonic missiles.

The Russians say they will add five more nuclear submarines to the country’s fleet by 2030.

Putin attended the flag-raising ceremony aboard the Perm at the Sevmash shipyard in the northwestern city of Severodvinsk on Friday, marking the submarine’s formal transfer to the navy, according to video released by the Kremlin.

“Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building powerful nuclear submarines of this kind, weapons with global reach and significance,” he said.

Nuclear-powered subs are a key part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent because their ability to operate covertly underwater ensures a retaliatory strike capability in the event of an attack.

Putin said the navy will receive five more submarines by 2030, including three Yasen-M class, the same as the Perm. They can operate in “any part of the world’s oceans” while carrying a range of cruise missiles, he added.

Putin also stated that Russia intends to continue modernising its navy and expressed confidence that all plans to build a powerful naval force will be implemented in full and on time.

item.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill

November 27, 2026

Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

What did the Supreme Court say about the law?

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."

Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec from in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections

Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

Source: DW Top Stories | Published: 2026-11-27 20:43 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.dw.com/en/canada-supreme-court-largely-upholds-quebec-secularism-bill/a-80082571?maca=en-rss-en-top-1022-rdf

item.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.

Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.

Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".

"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.

Regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.

Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.

More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

Source: BBC World | Published: 2026-11-27 20:34 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

“His main political platform is to say, I am not Sánchez, I am the opposite of Sánchez.” As Spain heads to the polls, what do Alberto Núñez Feijóo's campaign and political career tell us about the kind of prime minister he might become? Javier Carbonell, Policy Analyst at the European Politics and Institutions Programme and lecturer at Sciences Po in Paris, joins Gavin Lee to break down the Popular Party leader's efforts to avoid the mistakes of 2023 and keep right-wing voters mobilised without galvanising the left.

Carbonell explains the apparent paradox of Spain's strong macroeconomic performance and the difficulties many Spaniards face in their daily lives. “People still feel that their salaries are not enough to cover the cost of living.” Addressing the housing crisis, he acknowledges a problem he knows personally: “As young people, we are really, really struggling to find a house. I include myself in there.” Yet he believes pensions and pensioners will ultimately carry greater electoral weight.

What about Feijóo himself? Carbonell describes a traditional party politician whose lack of charisma is, in his view, part of his appeal. He discusses the controversy surrounding Feijóo's “calladita” remark to Ada Colau, his lack of engagement in international affairs and the significance of his inability to speak English. The conversation also explores the PP's use of AI and social media to reach young voters, many of whom support Vox, and Santiago Abascal's decision to cancel his interview with Jordi Wild, a decision Carbonell describes as “a massive mistake”.

item.title: Melting Barents Sea ice gives Eastern Europe's farmers a spring boost
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

November 27, 2026 report

Melting Barents Sea ice gives Eastern Europe's farmers a spring boost

For decades, sea ice in the Barents Sea, a part of the Arctic Ocean north of Norway and Russia, has been shrinking as the Arctic warms. The loss of so much ice can alter weather patterns well beyond the polar region, including in Europe. But how these changes might affect vegetation growth and agricultural production is less well understood.

Now, scientists led by researchers from Nanjing University in China have analyzed four decades of data and found that sea ice loss could be good news for wheat farmers in Eastern Europe but bad news for those in Western Europe.

Decades of data

The researchers examined satellite records of sea ice cover during each February from 1982 to 2022. They also looked at information about vegetation growth, wheat yields and weather conditions across Europe to see how these were affected by fluctuations in the amount of ice.

More specifically, they focused on year-to-year variations. This was to minimize the influence of long-term trends such as global warming and rising carbon dioxide levels.

The team also used computer simulations to investigate how changes in sea ice cover alone could affect weather patterns across Europe.

In their paper, published in the journal Science Advances, the scientists describe a striking geographical divide. In years with less ice in the Barents Sea, spring temperatures were higher across much of Eastern Europe but lower in Western Europe. And this had a marked effect on how well plants grew in both regions.

In Eastern Europe, this meant an earlier start to the growing season and fewer days of frost once plants began growing. In fact, the researchers estimate that nearly half of the increase in spring photosynthetic activity over the past 40 years is due to the loss of sea ice.

Wheat farmers also benefited. In Belarus, for example, wheat yields were higher in years with unusually little sea ice than in those with extensive ice cover. The difference amounted to around 16.5% of the country's average wheat yield over 20 years.

But the picture wasn't so healthy in Western Europe, where cooler temperatures hampered spring vegetation growth. In Spain, for example, wheat yields were around 5% lower in years with unusually little sea ice.

"The response is heterogeneous: BSIA [Barents Sea ice area] loss significantly enhances spring GPP [gross primary productivity] and wheat yields across EE [Eastern Europe] yet suppresses them in Western Europe," the scientists wrote.

Shifting wind patterns

So how does sea ice loss bring about these changes? According to the study authors, when less ice covers the sea, more heat escapes from the ocean into the atmosphere. This changes wind patterns, drawing warm air from the Mediterranean into Eastern Europe and cooler air from the North Atlantic toward the Iberian Peninsula.

However, plenty of unknowns remain, as the effects of Arctic sea ice loss may change as the region continues to warm.

"Looking ahead, the rapid transition of the Arctic toward a seasonally ice-free state is expected to alter, rather than necessarily intensify, the influence of Arctic forcing on midlatitude climate," the authors conclude.

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-27 20:40 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-barents-sea-ice-eastern-europe.html

item.title: Is AI‑assisted thinking devaluing business degrees?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear prose, real reporting, concrete detail

Is AI‑assisted thinking devaluing business degrees?

As AI models improve, high-quality knowledge is becoming easier to access. A degree therefore has to certify something more durable than the ability to retrieve knowledge or produce a plausible answer. It must show that a student can exercise judgment, make decisions and defend them.

Since mid-September, high school students across France, joined by university students, have blocked schools and taken to the streets to protest the conditions in which they study. Their demands include more staff, shorter school days, smaller classes, better-maintained buildings and the reform or abolition of Parcoursup, the admissions platform they regard as opaque and unfair.

These grievances stand on their own, and they are not about artificial intelligence. But they do raise questions that every school in France, including mine, will have to confront.

What value do business schools add in the age of AI?

What should business school students be able to do after graduating that they could not do before they enrolled? What does a teacher bring to the classroom that teaching material alone cannot? And now that artificial intelligence makes so much of what we teach easier to get for free, what else is there left that only schools can provide? We all owe our students an answer, and at business schools like mine, which charge substantial tuition fees, we owe it first.

A degree is only worth what it can certify that the student, not the machine, has reasoned through, and that depends on judgment, the point where critical thinking has to lead to a decision. Students should know what to do when there is no single right answer and be able to defend it. But judgment is formed in teaching, and our analysis suggests that higher education institutions are changing how they teach more slowly than they are writing rules for AI or building tools with it.

Three AI in higher education tracks moving at different speeds

We organized ESCP's first AI in Higher Education Summit at our Paris campus on March 17–18, 2026, where experts, professors, EdTech providers, university deans, directors and vice presidents from 14 countries presented their work in 12 parallel sessions. I built the ABC Framework to assess the 44 contributions we collected around three things a university has to do at once: governing the AI that it uses, building capability with it and rethinking teaching around human judgment.

The framework takes its name from the school's mission to educate accountable (A), bold (B) and creative leaders (C). Each of the three tracks seems to be moving at different speeds. Accountability is taking shape, as institutions start asking who owns the risk and who is held responsible when an AI-assisted decision goes wrong. But most of this work was still on paper.

The bold track is further ahead: most contributions on capability described tools already being built and used. The creative track lags furthest behind: most contributions on teaching were still asking what should change and how to protect students' capacity to think and judge for themselves when AI can do so much of the thinking.

The paper behind the framework also reviews just over 700 contributions to five other conferences between 2023 and 2025, and finds that in not one single year did more than about one in 13 address all three areas. Conference papers are not classroom practice, but if they are any guide, schools seldom treat all three as one task. The summit contributions suggest that teaching is the part most likely to be left behind.

Keeping up with AI in the classroom and thinking outside the bots

I see that gap every year, because I designed a course that 900 to 1,000 second-year students at ESCP Business School take on its Paris, Madrid and Turin campuses.

Instead of writing essays on AI, they build working systems with it on platforms most of them have never opened, then test those systems until they fail and defend what they would recommend. Last year they built AI agents, such as a customer-support system for a fictional sustainable fashion company, and each team explained in a short memo the trade-off it accepted.

The gain from cheaper knowledge is easy to see. A second-year student halfway through an introductory course in Python can now assemble, within a few sessions, a system that sorts incoming customer emails by topic and flags the urgent ones. But what I teach dates just as quickly: when I finalized my syllabus in June 2024, one assignment taught a particular way of writing instructions for a chatbot. By December it already looked like a relic.

For me, catching up with AI has meant rebuilding the course every year rather than patching it up. In its second year, I rewrote about nine of its 15 hours. I rebuild it often because I teach AI, which keeps changing, but a colleague teaching another subject is likely to face a similar pressure, because the way students use AI keeps changing too.

That is easier to say from a school that can afford the time to redesign a course than from a high school short of staff, which is precisely why a school like mine should be the one to say it.

Updating the content every year is only part of the work. How students learn has to change as well. Whether a student understands the system they built only becomes visible when a teacher or a classmate asks them to explain it, or when their work is compared with everyone else's.

Last year, one team building a support system chose the more accurate option despite its higher energy bill. Another, on a client-risk case, chose to flag too many clients rather than miss a risky one. A third routed ambiguous customer requests to a human. Each team had to decide what an error would cost and who would live with the consequences, because the cases forced them to choose.

What schools must protect…

item.title: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking

Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.

Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.

The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".

This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.

Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (Â£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.

Satellites give a clearer picture

In the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.

But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.

Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days.

"[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".

The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.

The ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.

If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted, external, under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.

Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.

Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively.

Sinking caused by local activities

The man-made drivers of subsidence are usually "extremely local, [which] means that we can combat them by creating local policies", Shirzaei explained.

One major cause is the increased water consumption of rapidly growing cities. Too much water being extracted from the ground can lead to the soil becoming compacted and the surface sinking.

The Aswan Dam on the Nile may also be trapping sediment upstream and preventing the replacement of sinking land in Alexandria, the study suggests.

In Lagos, the reclaiming of land from the ocean to create artificial islands and the construction of buildings on loose ground are other possible causes of subsidence.

Methods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops.

"Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level.

The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring.

The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested.

Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances,, external could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations".

item.title: Once logging stops, recovery of Vietnam's tropical forests isn't guaranteed
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Once logging stops, recovery of Vietnam's tropical forests isn't guaranteed

Deep in the jungle of central Vietnam, the heat is heavy, the mosquitoes are relentless and the terrain offers no easy paths. My colleagues and I don't hike on clear trails; we wade up riverbeds, stepping carefully over slippery rocks to access the thousands of trees we have been measuring for the last decade.

In 2024, I spent nearly two months camping in the forests of Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong, a nature reserve in central Vietnam. I worked with a field team of 12 people in the grueling conditions required to gather long-term ecological data.

Logging was particularly intense in the tropical forests of Vietnam between 1982 and 2007. As a result, the forest cover and the quality of those forest ecosystems have declined substantially. While forest cover in Vietnam has increased since the 1990s due to plantations and natural regeneration, the quality of forest recovery is less clear.

We visited every tree in our 24 study plots to measure them by hand in a meticulous, physically exhausting process that has been carried out four times since 2016. By identifying the species of each tree, measuring its diameter with a tape measure and noting any trees that have died, we tracked how these once-logged forests were recovering. Our findings challenge a key assumption about tropical forest regrowth.

Both governments and global carbon markets (trading systems that incentivize cuts in greenhouse gas emissions) invest in natural climate solutions. This often involves investing in schemes to plant new trees that absorb atmospheric carbon during photosynthesis in order to offset other carbon emissions. But these schemes rely heavily on an assumption: that once logging stops, tropical forests will naturally bounce back and recover, rapidly taking up carbon dioxide and storing it in growing trees.

In our latest study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, we show that rapid and predictable recovery may be overly optimistic.

Since 2007, when selective logging in the region ended, these forests have not recovered as expected. Between 2016 and 2024, the forests showed no net increase in the carbon stored in their trunks and branches. The trees are still growing, but carbon gains from growth were almost entirely offset by tree deaths. Recovery rates were far below what the U.N."s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates for the region and rates reported for comparable logged forests in Southeast Asia.

Heat restricts growth

Part of the explanation lies in the very conditions that made our fieldwork so challenging—rising temperatures. Since we have been monitoring these forests, temperatures have risen sharply, and we linked rising maximum temperatures to lower carbon gains. In 2024, the region where our forest plots are located endured severe, prolonged heat waves in April and four in a row in August. Heat is already limiting tree growth here.

These ecological constraints have financial and policy implications. Southeast Asia is central to carbon markets and the ecosystem restoration industry, hosting the majority of profitable forest restoration projects. Protecting young, regrowing forests from being cleared again helps limit greenhouse gas emissions by keeping the carbon already stored in the trees safe, as recovering forests are particularly vulnerable to repeated logging and clearing.

Yet, when calculating the value of protecting or restoring these forests, projects tend to assume steady, rapid tree growth, rather than measuring true forest function under the stress of extreme heat. Without long-term ground monitoring, schemes risk both underfunding necessary protection and overestimating carbon removal that may not be happening.

Despite harsh conditions and past disturbance, the forests managed to keep almost all the carbon stored in their trunks and branches intact. Long-term monitoring by our team and partners provided the evidence base that helped designate Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong as a nature reserve in 2020. Protection as a nature reserve has helped prevent further degradation through logging, securing these forests and the carbon they store.

Easy to overestimate

However, mechanisms allowing countries to work together toward their climate pledges under Article 6 of the Paris climate agreement tend to rely on generalized estimates of recovery. Those mechanisms also risk overestimating how much carbon recovering tropical forests can actually absorb.

To achieve realistic climate solutions in a warming world, policies must remain grounded in committed, local field surveys, no matter how hard those data are to collect.

Sleeping in hammocks in humid jungles, enduring insect swarms and battling steep terrain isn't just about collecting data; this research offers a true insight into how forests are functioning in a changing world.

Journal information: Environmental Research Letters

Provided by The Conversation

item.title: Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea

"Orbital transportation and return form a new layer of strategic infrastructure."

A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit.

Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle, will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project.

"We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18.

The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.

Atmos and MBDA also said this work could lead to demonstrations, but the companies' announcement makes it clear that any deployment or use would be subject to the approval of governmental and military authorities.

"The initiative also directly supports MBDA's broader strategic vision in the space domain, reinforcing both space for defense and the defense of space," Thomas Gottschild, MBDA Deutschland managing director, said in the same statement.

This news comes a few months after Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said that the U.S. Space Force operates orbital weapons.

"Let me be crystal clear: Today, Guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks," Schiess said during a conferenace presentation on Sept. 15 ("Guardians" refers to Space Force personnel.)

Last year, Atmos' Phoenix capsule got its first test run in space. The cargo-return technology launched aboard a Space X Falcon 9 rocket during a rideshare mission in February 2025.

Atmos tested out the inflatable heat shields it has been working on to help future space-manufactured cargo make it through Earth's atmosphere in one piece.

"Orbital transportation and return form a new layer of strategic infrastructure, and infrastructure determines what Europe can achieve on its own terms," Klaus said in the Nov 18 statement.

Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

item.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving

- Published

Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.

Conditions are now expected to improve, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.

Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.

More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.

One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.

Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.

On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.

Parts of some states are under states of emergency, including New York.

Nearly 2in (5cm) of rain fell on New York City's iconic Central Park, making it the wettest Thanksgiving on record at that site as well, according to preliminary data, external from the NWS.

Organisers of the city's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also pushed back the event to Saturday - marking the event's first postponement in its 100-year history.

In neighbouring New Jersey, there were multiple reports of closed roads and bridges, and images of floodwater blanketing city streets.

"This is wild," an Ocean City, New Jersey-based blogger said in a video, external posted on social media, as he waded through water splashing above his waist.

- Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather

- Published1 day ago

The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".

The storm is expected to ease on Friday and move into the Canadian provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland on Saturday, leaving a much drier weekend for the north-eastern United States, according to the Met Office.

However, another deep area of low pressure will likely arrive on Monday - bringing another spell of heavy rain and strong winds, and some further travel disruption.

On the West Coast, the concern was for exceptionally high tides and the associated risk of flooding.

Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft (2.4m) earlier this week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.

Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.

Dramatic footage from Oregon showed a man and a dog being swept into the sea by a fierce, so-called king tide - but both escaped unharmed, police said.

Coastal flood advisories remained in effect on Friday in parts of northern California and Oregon, until the afternoon.

In San Francisco and surrounding areas, the advisory remains in place until Sunday.

NWS officials told Bay Area residents that its beach hazards advisory remained in place through Saturday.

"Continue practicing beach safety by maintaining a safe distance from the water and never turning your back on the ocean," the NWS said on X.

In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.

A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing". No injuries were reported, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is investigating what happened.

An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

item.title: Pregnancy is the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders, but doctors keep missing them
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Reporting for this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

— Katye Jorgensen had been fighting anorexia and bulimia for years when she got pregnant at 25. Weigh-ins at prenatal appointments filled her with dread and certain foods terrified her, but she powered through for her baby’s sake. Then she struggled to breastfeed her son and lose weight after giving birth, and her mental health deteriorated.

After her second pregnancy two years later, Jorgensen became obsessive about exercise and fixated on comments about how well she was “bouncing back.” At her husband’s urging, she started seeing a therapist and a dietitian. Eventually, they staged an intervention and she agreed to enter intensive treatment, which she said saved her life.

“I went to my postpartum appointment, I mentioned a lot of this, and even though I really liked those doctors, it still didn’t set off any red alarms for anybody,” said Jorgensen, who is now 37.

Jorgensen is one of many women who struggle with eating disorders before and after childbirth but slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system. Research suggests about 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or binge eating disorder, though research is limited and no one knows their exact toll.

Those rates are on par with national averages: an estimated 2.6% to 8.4% of women will experience an eating disorder over their lifetimes — that’s up to 14.6 million women and girls in the United States.

Eating disorders have been linked to health issues for pregnant women — including miscarriage, high blood pressure, anemia, and bleeding — and complications for their developing babies, including small head circumference, low birthweight, autism, and asthma. After birth, women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns.

The risks vary by eating disorder. Studies don’t prove that eating disorders directly cause these issues and not everyone with a perinatal eating disorder will experience them. Still, the evidence is enough to worry clinicians.

“If we don’t treat these disorders … there are risks involved there. This isn’t a neutral situation,” said Leah Graves, a registered dietitian and a clinical adviser at the National Eating Disorders Association.

Few screening tools have been validated for eating disorders in pregnancy, and none are widely used. Obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions, leaving them unequipped to identify or manage eating disorders. And even with a diagnosis, many pregnant women and new mothers don’t receive timely treatment due to spotty insurance coverage and a shortage of local specialists, according to research and interviews with more than a dozen eating disorder researchers, doctors, dietitians, therapists, policy advocates, and mothers.

“It’s been a huge gap,” said Elizabeth Claydon, an associate professor at West Virginia University who researches eating disorders. “People have had this; they’ve lived with eating disorders during pregnancy. We just haven’t caught them and been able to help.”

Why is this a high-risk period?

Eating disorders usually develop in adolescence or young adulthood, but they can also emerge around pregnancy, menopause, or other periods of profound physical and life change.

Several factors can raise the risks in pregnancy: the feeling of a lack of control, rapid physical and hormonal changes, negative body image, scrutiny of the pregnant person’s diet and weight for medical reasons, the need to consume extra calories to breastfeed, a new identity and family role, and societal pressure to return to pre-pregnancy weight and succeed at motherhood.

Many women struggle with body image issues or unhealthy thoughts or behaviors around food, weight, or exercise that don’t meet the criteria for a clinical diagnosis. Pregnancy can tip the scales into an active eating disorder.

Pregnancy can also hide symptoms that overlap with eating disorders, such as nausea, vomiting, appetite changes or pumping breast milk specifically to burn calories, said Christine Call, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the University of Pittsburgh.

But many women hide their symptoms, making it difficult for doctors, or even family members, to know when someone needs help.

There’s no single trajectory in the perinatal period. Some women with eating disorders fare better during pregnancy and sustain that recovery, while others relapse once their child is born. Other women, years into recovery, see their eating disorders come roaring back in pregnancy or postpartum. Some struggle throughout pregnancy, with no respite. And others develop an eating disorder for the first time in the perinatal period.

“There’s so much shame and guilt about eating and doing things right, taking care of yourself for your baby during this period,” Call said.

Jennifer Kreatsoulas was diagnosed with anorexia 15 years before her first pregnancy, but her eating disorder “came back with a vengeance” after her second child was born, alongside postpartum depression. She decided to seek treatment when she realized she was too weak to push a stroller while out on a Mother’s Day walk with her husband and 1-year-old daughter.

“It’s destructive, but I was really trying to cope, and my brain just switched back to what it knew how to do from all those years previous,” said Kreatsoulas, now 50 and living in Pennsylvania. She attributes her relapse to “hormones, lack of sleep, complete overwhelm, your identity becoming something that you don’t know — you lose yourself in it, just because that’s what’s demanded as a mother.”

Screening and identification gaps…

item.title: mRNA Ebola vaccine trial starts in Uganda: Institute
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

mRNA Ebola vaccine trial starts in Uganda: Institute

Trials of an experimental Ebola vaccine aimed at the strain behind the current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo have begun in neighboring Uganda, its virus research institute said Friday.

There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo strain of Ebola behind the outbreak in DRC, which has led to more than 5,700 confirmed deaths out of more than 11,000 cases since being declared in May, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Two experimental vaccines are due to start testing on Monday in the outbreak's epicenter in eastern DRC, focusing on contacts of cases and people deemed at high risk of infection.

But neighboring Uganda announced it had also launched a trial of one of the vaccines, developed by the U.S.-based Moderna group using the mRNA technology made famous during the COVID pandemic.

The Uganda Virus Research Institute said in a statement it had "launched Africa's first mRNA phase 1 clinical trial ... in collaboration with Moderna of an investigational vaccine against Bundibugyo ebolavirus."

The trial is aimed at testing the vaccine in a group of 224 healthy volunteers aged between 1 and 65 to measure its safety and immunity potential.

Despite a long and porous border with eastern DRC, Uganda has successfully contained the virus after receiving some imported cases earlier this year.

It was declared Ebola-free in August after registering 20 cases, including two deaths.

item.title: In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D

For the first time, a research team at the Inserm Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) in Paris has succeeded in visualizing the entire vascular network and blood flow in a human kidney. This breakthrough opens up promising clinical prospects: improving our understanding and diagnosis of kidney diseases linked to vascular defects. To achieve this, the researchers used a new ultrasound technique developed in their laboratory and previously tested in animals, which could eventually be extended to other organs. The results are published in The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics.

The proper functioning of an organ depends closely on its vascular network. When arteries or veins are abnormal, the cells' needs for oxygen and nutrients are not met as effectively, and cellular waste is not eliminated as efficiently. The organs then suffer.

The kidney is particularly affected: changes in its microvasculature play a major role in many kidney diseases. This is particularly true of hypertensive nephrosclerosis and diabetic nephropathy, which are characterized by progressive damage to the small arteries and arterioles of the kidney, contributing to the loss of its filtration function.

"Currently, there is no specific biomarker that can directly detect these vascular abnormalities and monitor their progression. And the imaging techniques currently used cannot visualize the affected arterioles, whether it be conventional ultrasound—which lacks sufficient resolution—or MRI and CT scans," explains Clément Papadacci, an Inserm research fellow and team leader at the Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS).

Consequently, in the absence of early diagnosis and intervention, the disease is a major contributor to the development of kidney failure, requiring patients to undergo dialysis.

Directly observing the small blood vessels involved in kidney diseases is therefore a major challenge for clinicians. It is for this purpose, among others, that the team has developed a new ultrasound technique in recent years. By combining several innovations, they have developed an ultrasound probe that makes it possible to visualize the entire vascular system of an organ in three dimensions—down to the smallest capillaries—and to track blood flow in real time.

This is a remarkable achievement, given that some vessels are 50 micrometers in diameter—the size of a fine hair—and that conventional ultrasound can only visualize vessels 1 to 2 millimeters in diameter, or the size of the head of a pin.

The team has already demonstrated the effectiveness of this tool in animals for visualizing the vascular system of kidneys—and even entire hearts and livers. Now, they have demonstrated its feasibility in humans.

For the first time, the team is providing images of entire kidneys along with quantitative data on the organ's complete vascular architecture—from the largest arteries down to the microvessels—and the blood flow within each vessel. The system also allows the organ to be segmented to focus on areas of interest, or to separate venous and arterial blood flow for separate study.

"Beyond its technological capabilities, this new generation of ultrasound technology could lead to significant advances in research and medicine. In the case of hypertensive nephrosclerosis in particular, our device could help us not only better understand the condition but also, likely, identify early biomarkers to improve diagnosis," explains Hannah Plath, a doctoral student at the Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) and the study's first author.

This new generation of ultrasound could well contribute to our understanding of other types of diseases, since, in principle, all organs can be observed in their entirety and with their full vascular complexity.

In a clinical trial, the team will monitor blood flow in the kidneys, as well as in the brain and heart, of patients with atherosclerosis who are candidates for complex surgery.

"This surgical procedure alters blood flow and can compromise these organs. The clinical study aims to predict potential risks for patients," explains Papadacci, who led the research.

How does ultra-high-definition ultrasound imaging of an entire organ work?

To visualize an entire organ with high precision, researchers have developed an ultrasound probe that is much larger than a conventional probe and incorporates numerous components. Acoustic lenses, in particular, are responsible for focusing sound waves with great precision. This probe makes it possible to explore a large volume in three dimensions with high resolution thanks to very high-speed image acquisition.

Finally, microbubbles injected into the bloodstream and carried along by blood flow reveal even the smallest vessels. The combination of these innovations thus makes it possible to achieve two capabilities that were previously difficult to combine: viewing an entire organ and distinguishing its microvasculature.

More information

Hannah Plath et al., Whole-organ mapping of renal microcirculatory haemodynamics in vivo using three-dimensional ultrasound localisation microscopy: a first-in-human feasibility study, The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.lanmit.2026.100039

item.title: A new map reveals how individual brain cells use different RNA versions of the same genes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

A new map reveals how individual brain cells use different RNA versions of the same genes

In complex organisms such as humans, the same gene can produce different RNA molecules. This is known as alternative splicing. The differently spliced RNA molecules, called isoforms, may in turn result in different proteins.

Not all changes in isoforms have a visible effect. Sometimes, however, the wrong version can have drastic consequences. Incorrect isoforms have been associated with several brain diseases, including ALS, frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

"In these diseases, a protein named TDP-43 leaves its normal place in the cell and forms clumps, so it can no longer do its job," says Andrey Prjibelski, a university researcher at the Department of Computer Science, University of Helsinki.

"As a result, certain RNAs are spliced incorrectly, and neuronal cells lose proteins they need."

Detecting faulty splicing in the brain is not easy. Researchers at the University of Helsinki have now developed a method that maps which gene isoforms the cells in brain tissue use. In the future, it can also be used to identify faulty splicing.

For this work, the team engineered new laboratory techniques as well as algorithms, software and statistical tools for analyzing the data.

Resolution down to single cells

The main goal of the study was to show that spatial isoform mapping at single-cell resolution is possible. This was achieved: the method works at a resolution of 500 nanometers, which is clearly smaller than a single cell. The method was applied to brain samples from mice. The research is published in the journal Nature Methods.

Once the method is applied to samples from people with brain disorders, it may reveal new cases of malfunctioning splicing in specific cells or brain regions. It can also help in studying processes in the healthy brain, such as development, many of which remain understudied.

Toward new drugs that correct splicing

In the long run, these findings may help in designing new drugs for splicing therapy.

For example, since 2016, patients with spinal muscular atrophy, a disease of nerve cells, have been treated with a drug called nusinersen. It works by correcting how the RNA of a gene is processed inside cells. Drugs based on similar principles are now being tested in clinical trials for ALS and dementia.

"Although it's a pretty long way from discovering irregular splicing patterns to new drug candidates for disease treatment, all big things start with smaller steps," Prjibelski says.

Next project: Alzheimer's disease

The next step is to launch projects that analyze human data to study neurological diseases, in particular Alzheimer's disease. The researchers also plan to reanalyze public sequencing archives, which contain large amounts of data that have not been used to their full potential.

"Reanalyzing public data may also yield interesting results without requiring additional resources for sequencing," he says.

Publication details

Lieke Michielsen et al., Spatial isoform sequencing at single-cell resolution reveals cell-type-specific spatial isoform variability in multiple brain cell types, Nature Methods (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41592-026-03211-w

Journal information: Nature Methods

item.title: Scientists identify brain circuit behind sensory hypersensitivity in autism
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Scientists identify brain circuit behind sensory hypersensitivity in autism

For many people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ordinary sensory experiences can be unusually intense or overwhelming. A light touch or a mildly uncomfortable sensation may provoke a disproportionately strong response, making everyday activities difficult.

Sensory abnormalities affect more than 90% of individuals with autism, yet the neural mechanisms underlying these heightened responses remain poorly understood. Scientists have now identified a brain circuit involved in sensory hypersensitivity associated with an autism-related genetic mutation, demonstrating that selectively suppressing specific neurons can alleviate abnormal sensory responses in mice.

A joint research team led by Director Kim Eunjoon of the Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions within the Institute for Basic Science (IBS) and Professor Chung Changuk of KAIST's Graduate School of Medical Science and Engineering has identified excessive neuronal activity in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) as an important contributor to sensory hypersensitivity in a mouse model of an autism-related disorder. The study is published in the journal Molecular Psychiatry.

The researchers also demonstrate that selectively suppressing certain neurons within this region could alleviate heightened sensory responses, suggesting a potential direction for developing more targeted treatments.

Tracing hypersensitivity to brain circuits

The researchers focused on ADNP (activity-dependent neuroprotective protein), a protein involved in brain development and the regulation of gene expression. Mutations in the ADNP gene cause ADNP syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder associated with autism and heightened sensitivity to touch and pain. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, the team studied mice lacking one of their two functional copies of the Adnp gene. These mice reacted more strongly to mechanical stimuli, heat and electric shocks than normal mice.

However, mice in which Adnp was deleted in the spinal cord and peripheral tissues, but not the forebrain, did not develop the same abnormalities, suggesting that brain circuits play a major role in the hypersensitivity.

Using neuronal activity mapping and ultrahigh-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the researchers identified excessive activity across several brain regions, particularly the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is involved in processing the emotional aspects of pain.

Further experiments revealed that excitatory neurons in specific layers of the ACC were unusually easy to activate and exhibited altered communication with neighboring cells. These findings suggest that excessive neuronal activity in the ACC could contribute to the heightened sensory responses.

Selective suppression produces different results

To test this possibility, the team used chemogenetics, a technique that allows researchers to control neuronal activity using chemical compounds. Broadly suppressing excitatory neurons in the ACC reduced hypersensitivity to touch and heat but unexpectedly increased freezing behavior during electric shocks.

The researchers then took a more selective approach, inhibiting only ACC neurons that had previously been activated by electric shocks. This intervention normalized the mice's heightened responses to mechanical stimulation and paw heat while also reducing certain shock-related defensive responses.

The contrasting outcomes suggest that targeting specific neuronal populations may be more effective than broadly suppressing activity across an entire brain region, although further studies are needed to determine precisely why the two approaches produced different effects.

Molecular clues point toward targeted treatments

The team also investigated the molecular changes underlying the abnormal neuronal activity. By analyzing gene expression and protein regulation, they identified alterations in pathways associated with synapses and ion channels, which control communication and electrical signaling between neurons.

These changes were particularly prominent in excitatory neurons in specific layers of the ACC, providing additional clues to how reduced ADNP function may contribute to excessive neuronal activity and sensory hypersensitivity.

Kim stated, "Our study demonstrates, at the behavioral, cellular, synaptic and molecular levels, that the hypersensitivity to touch and pain commonly observed in people with autism is closely associated with excessive activity in specific populations of brain neurons, particularly in the anterior cingulate cortex."

He added, "Rather than suppressing activity across an entire brain region, precisely targeting the neuronal populations responsible for these abnormalities may provide an important direction for developing future treatments for sensory hypersensitivity associated with autism."

The findings highlight the importance of higher brain circuits in autism-related sensory abnormalities, extending previous research that has largely emphasized peripheral sensory pathways.

Publication details

Heera Moon et al., ACC hyperactivity and synaptic remodeling underlie sensory hypersensitivity in Adnp-haploinsufficient mice, Molecular Psychiatry (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41380-026-03972-y

Journal information: Molecular Psychiatry

item.title: PROLIFIC risk score made publicly available to pulmonary fibrosis researchers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

PROLIFIC risk score made publicly available to pulmonary fibrosis researchers

The Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation and Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium (PROLIFIC) have published a paper in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine detailing the development and validation of the PROLIFIC Risk Score, a novel blood biomarker-based tool designed to predict disease progression in people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

For the first time, the publication makes the methodology and formula behind the PROLIFIC Risk Score publicly available, giving researchers the tools to apply and evaluate the score in their own IPF research. IPF is a life-threatening, progressive disease that causes scarring of the lungs and makes it increasingly difficult to breathe. More than 250,000 Americans are living with IPF and other interstitial lung diseases (ILD), underscoring the urgent need for better treatments.

"Publication of this study in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine is a major milestone for PROLIFIC and for the broader ILD research community," said Peter Schafer, Ph.D., lead author of the study and chair of PROLIFIC. "By publishing the full methodology and formula, researchers can begin evaluating and using the score in their own work while we continue advancing it through the FDA qualification pathway."

Researchers evaluated 12 blood biomarkers reflecting three key processes involved in IPF: lung cell injury, scarring and inflammation. The resulting PROLIFIC Risk Score is designed to estimate the likelihood of disease progression, including lung function decline, lung transplantation or death within one year.

The score was derived and validated in two independent IPF cohorts totaling 886 participants, including 657 participants from the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry and 229 participants from the ISABELA Phase III clinical trials.

Addressing a major challenge in IPF research

The clinical course of IPF can vary considerably from one patient to another, making it difficult to predict who will progress quickly and who may experience a slower course of disease. That uncertainty also presents challenges in clinical trials, where differences among participants can make it more difficult to evaluate the effects of an investigational treatment.

The PROLIFIC Risk Score was developed primarily as a drug development tool that could help researchers better characterize the prognosis of clinical trial participants and potentially improve the design and efficiency of IPF studies.

The score is currently progressing through the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research Biomarker Qualification Program. In 2025, it became the first IPF biomarker accepted into the program, an early step toward potential qualification for use in drug development.

"The PFF Patient Registry was created so that the experiences and contributions of people living with pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung disease could accelerate research," said Scott Staszak, president and CEO of the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation. "Seeing registry data contribute directly to the development of the PROLIFIC Risk Score demonstrates exactly why participation in research matters."

Expanding beyond IPF

PROLIFIC is also evaluating whether similar biomarker approaches could have value in other forms of interstitial lung disease.

The consortium has analyzed additional samples, including those from the PROFILE study led by investigators at Imperial College London, as it explores the potential application of prognostic biomarkers beyond IPF.

"Our goal is to understand how these biomarkers can be used most effectively to advance research and drug development across pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases," Schafer said.

Publication details

Multi-biomarker risk score for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis based on serum proteins by the Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium (PROLIFIC): a risk score development and validation study, The Lancet Respiratory Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1016/S2213-2600(26)00297-3

item.title: Plant‑based 'tuna' or pea chips? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Plant‑based 'tuna' or pea chips? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives

People prefer plant-based products to be local and sustainable, minimally processed and familiar, according to our latest research. This is alongside typical consumer expectations for food products such as taste and value.

Understanding consumer needs for plant-based food is vital for their success, and that's an essential part of building a more sustainable food system that moves away from carbon-intensive meat products.

Introducing new and exciting plant-based alternatives might encourage meat and dairy lovers to substitute some of their animal-based intake. However, many of those alternatives are ultraprocessed, so there are still potential health concerns surrounding such products.

Our project involved working with consumers to create ideas for plant-based food and drink products. As part of Protein-I, a project investigating how to diversify plant protein production and consumption around Ireland and Northern Ireland, we ran five workshops with consumers.

These workshops focused on plant proteins that could be grown for human consumption locally (such as barley, oats, peas, rye and wheat), rather than ones that are typically imported such as soy. Crop trials across research sites and farms had found that varieties of these crops can be grown in sufficient quantities in countries such as Ireland at a quality suitable for human consumption (rather than animal feed).

Following guided group discussions, interesting ideas from our 38 participants included a plant-based tuna alternative called "toona," made from wheat and pea protein, pea and onion chips plus wheat and barley pasta.

Many ideas focused on peas. However, some of the industry and academic experts we interviewed had reservations about peas, as they have a strong taste and color, which can be off-putting to some people. To make them appealing as an ingredient in products, processing would be needed to refine the taste and color, which may lead to products classed as ultraprocessed and concerns associated with this.

After the 38 participants voted for their favorite products and following input from experts, a vegetarian bolognese and flavored protein oat milk came out as favorites.

A follow-on project from our work (Protein-I-2), which has just started, will explore the development of minimally processed products, using local and sustainable crops.

Research shows that familiarity is an important factor in helping uptake of alternative proteins. Unsurprisingly, many of the food product ideas that originated during our research had similarities to existing products. Our participants weren't given limits on the ideas that they could come up with, yet many of them suggested products based on existing foods such as porridge and pasta.

In our research, when asked what sustainability meant to them, participants often mentioned where a product comes from and locality. One said: "How it's like made … what it is or where it comes from, ye know?" Another commented: "If I'm shopping and I see something that's been flown in from Kenya, beans or something, no, I wouldn't buy. I always go for something that's local."

Plant-based provenance

Highlighting the source or origin of plant-based products on labeling may encourage consumer uptake. As part of the Protein-I project, a digital track-and-trace platform was developed to improve food supply chain transparency. This enables consumers to access information on a product's origin, production journey and environmental footprint through a QR code on the product label.

To explore the connection with local familiar foods, Protein-I ran a hands-on bread-making workshop using Irish-grown cereals. Feedback from participants was positive. Many reported feeling a stronger appreciation of Irish-grown cereals and left with an intention to purchase Irish cereal products in the future.

The workshop helped strengthen participants' connection with where their food comes from and raised awareness of the role Irish-grown cereals can play in a more sustainable food system. By tailoring new product launches to consumers' wants, there is a greater chance of acceptance, which should ultimately be better for sustainability and our environment.

item.title: No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories

Back in my early days as a dietitian, I used to hear about the miracle properties of celery.

The idea was that you used more energy chomping and digesting celery than you got from the calories in celery.

So the very act of eating celery made you lose weight.

It probably sounded plausible as celery is a low-calorie food. One stalk of celery only contains about 4.3 calories (18 kilojoules).

Celery also takes a lot of chewing, which added to its reputation as a "negative-calorie" food.

So is there any truth to all this? And what do bearded dragon lizards have to do with it?

Can some foods really make you lose weight?

Calories (or kilojoules) refer to the amount of energy a certain food provides. Celery is an example of a nonstarchy vegetable. Like other nonstarchy vegetables, such as cucumber and bell pepper, celery contains virtually no fat or protein and very small amounts of carbohydrates.

Losing weight begins to occur when you are in a negative calorie balance—that is, you use more energy during exercise or everyday activity than you eat.

Because eating fewer calories is a way to manage your weight, it is easy to see how low-calorie celery led to the negative-calorie theory.

How much does it cost to chew and digest food?

The total amount of energy your body burns every day is called the total energy expenditure.

That's made up of the:

- resting metabolic rate, or the calories your body uses to keep you alive at rest, while fasting (that is, whenever you're not moving or eating)

- thermic effect of food, or the "cost" of digesting and absorbing nutrients

- cost of physical activity.

Let's focus on one of those that often confuses people—the thermic effect of food. This is not a "fixed calorie cost." So we cannot say eating a stick of celery uses a certain number of calories. Rather, this thermic effect of food is a percentage of the total energy the food provides.

So a higher-calorie meal will cost more to process than a lower-calorie meal. As the thermic effect of food is expressed as a percentage of the total energy the food provides, you never burn more calories than you eat.

The thermic effect of food also accounts for a small part (about 10%) of your total energy expenditure.

Physical activity can account for 15%–50% of the total, depending on how active you are.

But the resting metabolic rate accounts for about 60%–70%. In other words, the very act of keeping you alive—your brain working, your heart pumping, your core temperature stable, for example—is what uses the highest proportion of calories.

What's the evidence?

One group of researchers tested the concept of "negative-calorie" food on the bearded dragon lizard. This isn't as strange as it sounds. This lizard has been used to study digestion as it processes foods in similar ways to mammals.

This research is posted online as a preprint. As far as I can tell, it has yet to be independently verified by other researchers and published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The lizards ate celery meals equal to 5% of their body weight. The researchers then measured the energy used for chewing and digestion as well as the energy lost in their feces and urine.

As expected, the lizards used energy to digest the celery. But they still gained at least 24% of the meals' energy overall.

I have only found one relevant study in humans, based on research presented to a conference in 2012. Researchers measured how many calories women used after eating 100 grams (3.5 ounces) of celery. A large amount of the calories (86%) in celery was used to chew and digest it. But the women did not burn more calories than what was in the celery.

Together, these studies show celery is not a negative-calorie food.

This myth is an example of the illusory truth effect. This is when repeated exposure to claims makes them seem more believable, even when scientific evidence proves otherwise.

Is celery a con, then?

Celery contains vitamins and minerals. Like all vegetables, it contains other nutrients with antioxidant, anticancer, antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity. Celery also contains fiber.

An analysis of all trials looking at celery as a food or as a supplement found it may provide some benefits for high blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol levels. However, more studies are needed to confirm this.

So, by all means, eat celery (and other low-calorie, nonstarchy vegetables) in place of energy-dense, nonnutritious foods (such as ultraprocessed snacks and drinks) to support a healthy weight.

But eating celery to give you "negative calories" won't help you magically lose weight.
