item.title: RightClick Unchained is on the Chrome Web Store
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Some websites turn off the context menu, stop you from selecting text, or intercept Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V. RightClick Unchained turns those browser basics back on, and you choose where it runs.

It is now live on the Chrome Web Store as v1.0.2 (the public listing was updated 23 November 2026). The source is MIT: JehadurRE/rightclick-unchained.

What it unblocks

- Right-click: the normal browser context menu comes back

- Text selection and drag, including pages that set user-select: none

- Copy and cut (Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X)

- Paste into form and password fields that block Ctrl+V

Each of the four can be switched on or off on its own. The store listing and the source agree on this; I am not adding claims beyond that.

Two modes, per site

Smart (the default) lets the site's own scripts keep running, but they can no longer cancel right-click, select, copy, or paste. Menus and widgets on the page should keep working.

Absolute is for stubborn pages: blocking listeners for those actions are never attached, and stronger selection CSS is applied.

The popup has one switch for the current site, and you can pick Smart or Absolute per domain. There is also a settings page to add, change, pause, or delete site rules.

Tools and shortcuts

- Text Lasso: click a block of text, or drag a box over part of the page, and the text is copied

- Force Copy: copies the current selection even when the site blocks copying

- Keyboard shortcuts (changeable at chrome://extensions/shortcuts): Alt+Shift+U opens the popup, Alt+Shift+R toggles the current site, Alt+Shift+C force-copies the selection

Why it is Manifest V3

Older "enable right-click" extensions were written for Manifest V2. This one is built as Manifest V3, with a content script in the page's own world (world: "MAIN") at document_start, plus a separate isolated script for UI, CSS, and settings. The idea is to be in place before the site's own listeners attach, without violating the page's Content Security Policy.

Privacy

No analytics, no ads, no tracking, no remote code, and no network requests from the extension itself. Site rules stay in chrome.storage.local. You can export or import settings as JSON.

It has to run on the pages you visit, because copy and right-click blocking can happen on any site. It only changes how those pages handle right-click, select, copy, cut, paste, and drag. It does not send page content anywhere. Please respect copyright and each site's terms when you copy content.

Install

Or load the repo as an unpacked extension from GitHub.

I am JehadurRE. If a specific site still blocks selection after you try Absolute mode and Text Lasso, open an issue with the URL and I will take a look.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-27 20:51 UTC

Original link: https://dev.to/jehadurre/rightclick-unchained-is-on-the-chrome-web-store-55dg

item.title: Patches Welcome #7: Your Scheduled Notification Disappears If the User's Calendar Isn't Gregorian
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

zonedSchedule notifications on iOS and macOS fire correctly on most devices. Set the device calendar to Islamic, Buddhist, or Japanese, and the notification is silently dropped. No error, no callback, nothing in the console. It just doesn't fire.

How I found it

I was wiring up shift-end reminders in a workforce app. QA passed on every device we had. A field tester in the Middle East reported that reminders never arrived. Their iPhone was set to the Hijri calendar. That was the only difference.

The mechanism

flutter_local_notifications builds an NSDateComponents from the target date to create a UNCalendarNotificationTrigger. On iOS, FlutterLocalNotificationsPlugin.m:878 uses [NSCalendar currentCalendar] for the decomposition. On macOS, the Swift equivalent uses Calendar.current.

When the device calendar is Islamic, currentCalendar returns a Hijri calendar. Decomposing a 2026 Gregorian date into Hijri components gives you year 1448, month values in a different range, day counts that don't map. UNCalendarNotificationTrigger reads those components as Gregorian (it always does), sees a date in the past by roughly 578 years, and discards the trigger.

The input date is an ISO 8601 string parsed via ISO8601DateFormatter, which always produces a Gregorian date. The decomposition has to match.

The fix

Two lines. One per platform.

iOS (Objective-C):

NSCalendar *calendar = [[NSCalendar alloc]

initWithCalendarIdentifier:NSCalendarIdentifierGregorian];

macOS (Swift):

var calendar = Calendar(identifier: .gregorian)

2 additions, 2 deletions. The diff is symmetrical because the bug is symmetrical.

Why it went unnoticed

Most developers and most CI runners use Gregorian calendars. The plugin's own test suite doesn't mock a non-Gregorian calendar context. And the failure is silent: UNCalendarNotificationTrigger doesn't throw or log when the date components resolve to the past. It just never fires. You'd only catch this with a physical device (or simulator) set to a non-Gregorian locale and a notification you're actually waiting for.

I verified the fix on an iOS Simulator set to ar_SA (Islamic calendar). I haven't tested Buddhist (th_TH) or Japanese imperial, but the code path is identical: currentCalendar returns whatever the user has, and the fix bypasses it entirely.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-27 20:49 UTC

item.title: Supabase Backup and Restore: Dumps, Gaps and a Test Plan
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

A Supabase backup comes from two places: the daily backup Supabase takes on paid plans, which restores inside the dashboard, and a dump you take with the CLI, which restores into any project. Most teams rely on the first and skip the second. Own both, and run the second one at least once.

This guide is for founders and developers running a live product on Supabase, including Lovable apps that use their own Supabase project. It covers where the backups live, the CLI commands from Supabase's own guide, what a restore leaves out and a drill you can run in an afternoon. It adds to our general guide to database backups for startups, which covers how much data you can afford to lose. This one stays on Supabase.

Key takeaways

- Pro projects keep 7 days of daily backups and Team projects keep 14. Free projects have no backup retention, and Supabase recommends regular exports with supabase db dump.

- Supabase's documentation says physical backups are not available for download, so a dump you take yourself is the only copy that leaves the platform.

- Three dump files (roles, schema and data) and one psql command restore a database into a new project.

- A database backup leaves out Storage files, Edge Functions, auth settings, API keys and custom role passwords. Each needs its own copy.

- Lovable Cloud keeps its own backups outside your Supabase dashboard, so check which backend your Lovable app uses before you trust either set.

Where do Supabase backups live, and what do they cover?

They live in the dashboard under Database, then Backups, for Pro, Team and Enterprise projects. Free projects get none. Each plan keeps a different number of daily backups, and point-in-time recovery is a separate add-on.

Supabase's pricing page lists Pro from $25 a month and Team from $599 a month. Our guide to Supabase pricing works through what a real app costs on each plan.

Can you download a daily backup?

On a current project, the documentation says no. Projects on Postgres 15.8.1.079 and newer use physical backups, and Supabase's backups documentation says physical backups are not available for direct download. The dashboard restore guide covers older projects that still use logical backups. If your project is newer, the daily backup is a restore point inside Supabase and the dump in the next section is the copy you can hold yourself.

What does point-in-time recovery change?

It replaces daily backups with a restore to a moment you choose. Supabase archives write-ahead log files every two minutes by default, which gives a worst-case recovery point of two minutes. The add-on costs about $100 a month for each 7 days of retention, so 14 days costs about $200 and 28 days about $400. Enabling it stops the daily backups. A point-in-time restore replaces the current database, so Supabase advises that you restore to a new project first if you want to keep the current state.

How do you back up a Supabase database with the CLI?

Run three supabase db dump commands against your project's connection string, one each for roles, schema and data. The machine that runs them needs the Supabase CLI, Docker Desktop and the Postgres client tools that include psql.

Copy the connection string from Connect in the dashboard. Reset the database password in Database Settings if you do not have it. Use the direct connection string. If your network has no IPv6 and the project has no IPv4 add-on, use the session pooler string instead. The direct string looks like this:

postgresql://postgres:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@db.[PROJECT-REF].supabase.co:5432/postgres

Supabase's backup and restore guide gives these commands:

supabase db dump --remote=[CONNECTION_STRING] -f roles.sql --role-only

supabase db dump --remote=[CONNECTION_STRING] -f schema.sql

supabase db dump --remote=[CONNECTION_STRING] -f data.sql --use-copy --data-only -x "storage.buckets_vectors" -x "storage.vector_indexes"

The roles file holds cluster roles. The schema file holds your tables, functions and policies. The data file holds the rows as COPY statements. The CLI reference says a default dump leaves out the schemas Supabase manages, such as auth and storage.

These commands use the --remote flag from the current CLI reference. Version 2 of the CLI, still common on laptops, takes --db-url in its place. The reference says --db-url still works in version 3 and goes away in version 4. Run supabase --version before you paste a command from any guide.

How often should the dump run?

Daily matches the platform's own schedule. Run the three commands from a scheduled job on a small server or a CI schedule, then copy the files to storage in a different account from the one that holds your Supabase organization. A dump that lands in the same account protects you from a bad query and leaves you exposed to a suspended account. Supabase removes a project's backups when you delete the project, so the second copy carries the most value in that case.

The Management API lists the backups the platform holds:

export SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN="your-access-token"

export PROJECT_REF="your-project-ref"

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" \

"https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/database/backups"

Call it from the same scheduled job and raise an alert when the newest backup is more than a day old.

How do you restore a Supabase backup into a new project?

Create a new project, enable the extensions and webhooks the old one used, and run one psql command that loads the three files in a single transaction. A new project leaves the original untouched, which makes it the safer default for every restore.

- Create the new project in the dashboard.

- Enable Database Webhooks if the old database used them, and enable any non-default extensions it used.

- Copy the new project's connection string and database password.…

item.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall

Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.

Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.

The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.

As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.

The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.

As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.

Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."

A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

Source: Hacker News | Published: 2026-11-27 20:38 UTC

Samsung is reportedly giving its camera app an AI mode

The feature could mirror the Siri mode Apple added in iOS 27.

Samsung's Galaxy S26 phones already ship with Google's Android AI features and Perplexity, and the phone maker is reportedly layering in even more AI for next year's Galaxy S27 devices. Based on code strings in One UI 9.5 Beta 1, Android Authority writes that Samsung is adding a new "Vision" mode to Galaxy phones' camera app that could duplicate some of the use cases for Siri mode in iOS 27.

Vision will apparently be offered alongside the app's other modes, and primarily acts as a way to point your camera at something and ask AI about it. According to Android Authority, the camera mode will display an AI-written summary of whatever you're looking at, along with tappable keywords, suggested actions, a text extraction tool, an "Ask" button that sends the scene to Gemini and a "Translate" button that hands it off to Samsung's AI Vision app.

Samsung's phones already offer a way to open Google's Gemini Live feature to have a live conversation about whatever you're looking at, and even before that, Samsung experimented with multimodal AI features through Bixby. Funnily enough, Android Authority writes that the AI Vision app this new camera feature connects to is actually built on the bones of Bixby Vision, the camera capabilities of Samsung's in-house AI assistant.

Vision also sounds similar to the Siri mode Apple added to the Camera app in iOS 27. Siri mode basically freed the iPhone's Visual Intelligence features from its Camera Control button and brought them into an app people spend a lot more time in. Samsung's Vision feature doesn't sound like it's adding anything new to the concept, but if it makes it even easier to ask AI about the world around you, maybe that will be worth it to some users.

Samsung hasn't announced this feature, and sometimes software appears in betas that never make it to the final release. If Samsung does launch this new Vision feature, it will likely be alongside the Galaxy S27 lineup early next year.

item.title: Inflation is squeezing Americans so hard that rising grocery bills are now a top reason Black Friday shoppers are cutting back
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on inflation's impact on consumer spending, with useful data and context.

Black Friday has arrived, and the National Retail Federation expects about 126 million Americans to shop today, part of an estimated 182.7 million who plan to shop over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

But many of those shoppers are heading out with less to spend, with the cost of groceries being a main reason why. Among Black Friday shoppers who are cutting back this year, 68% point to rising grocery costs, up from 57% in 2025, according to a new survey from market research firm Drive Research. Rising living costs are still the top reason, cited by 76%, up from 70%, while 61% blame inflation, up from 54%.

Black Friday budgets are shrinking as a result. Some 41% of Black Friday shoppers expect to spend less on holiday shopping than they did last year, up from 31% in 2025. The share who typically spend $1,000 or more fell to 18% from 24%, and 34% said they feel pressured to spend more on gifts than they can comfortably afford.

Everyday essentials are also on shopping lists. Household necessities like groceries and cleaning supplies are among the planned purchases for 38% of in-person Black Friday shoppers and 31% of those shopping online. Drive Research surveyed 1,405 U.S. adults from Oct. 6 to Oct. 9, and its Black Friday findings are based on the 1,025 respondents who plan to shop over the weekend.

Grocery prices rose 0.4% in October, the biggest monthly increase since April, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, with beef up 0.9%. Over the 12 months through September, food-at-home prices climbed 1.8%, while overall consumer prices rose 3.7%. Gas has driven much of that broader increase: gasoline prices were up 37.4% from a year earlier in October, before seasonal adjustment. The BLS couldn’t publish most year-over-year comparisons for October because it didn’t collect price data in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

Federal Reserve officials have taken notice. Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said in a Nov. 10 speech the labor market had improved more than she expected this year, but that “our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed.” The Fed held its benchmark rate in a range of 3.75% to 4% at its October meeting.

Walmart remains the top in-store Black Friday destination, with 71% of in-person shoppers planning a visit—the same share for the third straight year—according to Drive Research. Emily Rodgers, the company’s director of marketing, said when budgets are tight, “shoppers stick with the stores they already trust to have low prices.”

Walmart CEO John Furner said last week rising diesel and transportation costs have added about $2 billion in expenses this year, which could make it harder to keep prices low through the holidays.

“We will do everything we can in terms of efficiency,” Furner said on the company’s post-earnings call.

Shoppers also aren’t sure the deals are real. Some 64% of Black Friday shoppers believe retailers raise prices ahead of the sales so the discounts aren’t genuine, and 72% said the deals aren’t nearly as good as they used to be, Drive Research found.

“Black Friday used to sell itself on the date alone. Now shoppers show up with a price tracker in one hand and a healthy dose of doubt in the other,” Rodgers said. “The retailers who win will be the ones who show their math: what the item sold for last month and what the customer actually saves today.”

Most consumers are trying to hold the line. Some 82% are taking steps to manage holiday costs, including buying less expensive gifts (25%), cutting back in other areas (24%) and buying for fewer people (20%), according to NRF’s survey of 7,956 adults.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Nov. 5, 2025.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-27 19:37 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Hackers breach Air Force cloud: 7 things 2026's government hacks exposed, and what to do
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed analysis of government hacks with implications for national security, suitable for an advanced reader.

From Social Security numbers to FBI agents' home addresses, here's what 2026's government hacks exposed and how to protect yourself

Updated November 27, 2026

Kevin Carter / Getty Images

In September, a criminal hacking group called ShinyHunters claimed it had taken data on nearly every FBI agent and job applicant, and knocked the bureau's jobs portal offline. "We have compromised the FBI. We hold very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job," the group's message said, according to PBS News. The FBI said it was investigating the claim, but that it hadn't yet determined the "point of breach."

The stakes go beyond identity theft. A New York Times analysis found that the stolen data may include home addresses, Social Security numbers and job assignments. Reuters reported that the hackers claimed to have 2 to 3 terabytes of data, and some of what it reviewed showed which agents work in specific field offices and in units handling intelligence and counterespionage.

Credit: Joshua Hoehne / Unsplash

In November, the FBI began investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. Local, state and federal police use the database to look up fugitives, missing persons, criminal histories and stolen property. The FBI declined to comment, and the scope of the problem wasn't immediately clear.

This exposure reaches people who never worked for the government: anyone named in a police record. "We just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good," President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview. Administration officials have blamed a separate run of recent outages on routine system upgrades, and there was no immediate sign the two were linked.

Yassine Khalfalli / Unsplash

The exposures this year haven't been limited to federal agencies. Before the FBI's jobs portal was hit, a separate breach may have exposed more than 153 million driver's licenses across the U.S. and Canada, TIME reports. Sherman's warning about not dismissing "just another data breach" was written about that leak.

Combined with Social Security numbers and job details from other breaches, a license record helps a scammer build a fuller profile of one person.

Each breach adds a piece; together they can complete the picture.

Illustration: Quartz

Government hacks tend to be covered as stories about secrets and spies. The breaches that have piled up through 2026 are mostly about something closer to home: the personal records of the people who serve, work for or deal with federal agencies. Social Security numbers, home addresses, job assignments and criminal records have all been in the path of intruders this year.

"It can be tempting to dismiss the next hack of a database as 'just another data breach.'... But breaches do not exist in a vacuum," Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote, as TIME reported. Each exposed record can make the next scam or intrusion easier. Here's what has been exposed so far, and what people caught up in it can do.

When the targets are investigators, a leaked home address can be a safety risk, not just a privacy one.

Credit: Jakub Żerdzicki / Unsplash

ShinyHunters says this attack wasn't about money. It gave the FBI one week to retract a May public advisory that called the group a "cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion," and said it was "offended" by the description. "This is not a ransom, coercion, or extortion. Your federal policies do not apply here. This PSA is NOT financially motivated," the message said.

The FBI's own advisory had warned that the group often uses "real or exaggerated claims of access" to pressure victims. That means its claims about how much it took can't be taken at face value. The group didn't say what it would do if the deadline passed.

Whether the motive is money or pride, the data is the same once it's out.

A breach here would put ordinary Americans' records at risk, not just federal staff's.

Credit: Michał Jakubowski / Unsplash

The FBI's troubles started earlier in the year. In March, the bureau said it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system holding sensitive information about surveillance operations and investigations. That same month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account belonging to FBI Director Kash Patel and posted what appeared to be old photos, a resume and personal documents more than a decade old.

The FBI said the Patel material was "historical in nature" and involved "no government information." Together, the incidents show how often the bureau itself has become a target this year.

Even old personal documents give attackers something to work with.

Credit: Avery Evans / Unsplash

The Pentagon is offering a year of free credit monitoring and identity-restoration services through IDX, a private firm it hired. People with questions can contact IDX at response.idx.us/DMDC or 1-855-744-4556, a defense official told TIME.

Anyone can also place a free credit freeze with each of the three major credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian and TransUnion), according to the Federal Trade Commission. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in a person's name. Active-duty troops and National Guard members can also get free electronic credit monitoring. Experts also warn that exposed records make phishing easier, so unexpected messages that cite personal details deserve extra suspicion.

A credit freeze costs nothing and takes minutes, and it's the simplest protection after a breach.

Source: Quartz | Published: 2026-11-27 19:20 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://qz.com/hackers-breach-air-force-cloud-7-things-government-hacks-exposed

item.title: Hackers breach Air Force cloud: 5 things routine military data could reveal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains the risks of a military data breach, with technical detail but accessible language.

Hackers breach Air Force cloud: 5 things routine military data could reveal

Hackers breached the Air Force's Cloud One platform. Five risks, from the control plane to stalled fixes, show what could be exposed.

When a military network is hacked, the first question is usually whether anything secret was taken. The breach of the Air Force's Cloud One platform shows why that question may be too narrow. Three people familiar with the matter told Reuters that hackers got inside the platform, an intrusion discovered within roughly the past month during upgrade work. Who did it, how far they went and whether they stole data are still unknown.

Security experts who spoke to Newsweek say the bigger risk may sit in ordinary files. "Military readiness depends on much more than weapons and fighter jets," said Dr. Daniel Schatz, a political scientist who studies international security. "It also depends on the digital systems that support logistics, maintenance and personnel."

Cloud One: The Air Force's everything platform

Illustration: Quartz

The Air Force launched Cloud One in 2017 to handle all of its IT needs in one place, pooling computing from Microsoft $MSFT, Amazon $AMZN, Oracle $ORCL and Alphabet $GOOGL. It runs scores of applications, from pay and personnel files to logistics and aircraft maintenance, and two sources describe it as one of the U.S. military's largest cloud platforms. One source said the hackers reached its control plane, the management layer above every application.

That reach is why the platform's most ordinary records matter.

1. Which aircraft are grounded

Sebastian Schuster / Unsplash

Maintenance logs track every repair, so a large enough set of them shows which jets are out of service. Access to the control plane could in theory let intruders check the operational status of military aircraft, though it's unclear whether they did. "Put enough of them together and you can work out which aircraft are grounded, where supplies are headed and how ready a unit really is," said Ryan Reck, founder of security and intelligence firm Reck Advisory.

A grounded fleet is something no military wants a rival to see.

2. Where parts and supplies are headed

Credit: Edoardo Bortoli / Unsplash

Shipment records show where spare parts are going and how fast. In theory, intruders with control-plane access could follow the movement of those parts. Pieced together, Reck says, that data shows where supplies are being sent across the force.

Following the parts can show a rival where the Air Force's needs are greatest.

3. How ready a unit really is

Credit: Edoardo Bortoli / Unsplash

Readiness comes from adding grounded aircraft and missing parts together, and Reck says routine records can reveal it without touching anything classified. "That picture is valuable to a foreign military even if nothing marked secret is touched," he said.

A unit's real readiness can sit in files no one thought to protect as secrets.

4. Weak spots in the supply chain

Illustration: Quartz

The same logistics data can show a rival where the Air Force's supply lines are thin. "If an adversary gains insight into those systems, information that looks routine in isolation could help reveal patterns of military activity or vulnerabilities in the supply chain," Schatz said.

Knowing where supplies bottleneck tells an adversary where pressure would hurt most.

5. Patterns of military activity

Credit: Jeff / Unsplash

Over time, routine records can sketch how the Air Force moves and operates, Schatz says, even when no single file stands out. Reaching the control plane "is potentially more consequential than breaking into a single application," he said, though no one yet knows what the attackers accessed or whether they took any data.

Patterns, not any one file, may be the real prize in this breach.

Source: Quartz | Published: 2026-11-27 19:00 UTC | Difficulty: 65/100

Original link: https://qz.com/hackers-breach-air-force-cloud-routine-military-data

item.title: Hackers breach Air Force's Cloud One: What's at risk and what's still unknown
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Comprehensive overview of the Air Force cloud breach, balancing detail with readability.

Hackers breach Air Force's Cloud One: What's at risk and what's still unknown

Anonymous sources say hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship cloud. Six slides separate what is confirmed from what is still unknown.

For years, the U.S. military has moved software off scattered computer systems and onto shared cloud platforms that are easier to manage but give attackers one larger target. The Air Force's flagship version is Cloud One, and hackers have now reportedly gotten inside it, Reuters reports. Cloud One's leaders had claimed a 100% success rate at repelling penetration attempts in a 2023 FedScoop commentary, according to the same report.

The breach's investigators have asked Cyber Command to help measure the harm. No one has established who the hackers are, how far they went or whether they took any data.

What Cloud One is

Cloud One brings Microsoft $MSFT, Amazon $AMZN, Oracle $ORCL and Alphabet $GOOGL under a single Air Force platform, so users reach all four companies' computing through one system. The Air Force started it in 2017, and Leidos has held the main contract to run it since 2025, replacing SAIC. Nothing on the record connects that change of contractor to the intrusion.

One platform means one place to manage, and one place to break into.

The sensitive systems that run on it

The Air Force's munitions-tracking software, the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, runs on Cloud One and keeps count of weapons at more than 200 sites around the world. So does Cloud-Based Command and Control, which pulls radar and other feeds into a single air-defense picture of North America. Nothing reported so far places the intruders inside either system.

These systems mark the outer limit of what the breach could cost.

How the intruders got in and the control plane risk

One of five unnamed sources said the intruders used a software flaw to reach Cloud One's control plane, the layer that runs the whole platform. Access at that level could let an intruder check which aircraft are ready to fly and follow where spare parts are being shipped. No specific flaw has been identified, so no one outside the investigation can confirm it has been fixed.

The control-plane claim is the gravest risk in the breach, and it rests on a single source.

The disruption to operations

The Air Force has paused plans to move back-office software onto Cloud One and frozen updates to the applications already there, so teams can't patch them even as major new software flaws surface across the industry. Some users have also lost administrator access. The Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems."

The clearest damage so far is a platform the Air Force can't fully use.

item.title: Crate & Barrel CEO plans a 50-store expansion to win customers from rivals: ‘It’s absolutely a market steal play.’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth look at Crate & Barrel's strategic expansion, with insights into retail business practices.

Few retail CEOs have had a more turbulent run than Janet Hayes. Since taking over Crate & Barrel in 2020, she has steered the furniture retailer through a pandemic and repeated tariff shocks. Now she’s betting the company can come out of it on the offensive.

Hayes hews to the old adage, “Don’t let a good crisis go to waste.” She says she took the tariffs as an opportunity to really understand Crate & Barrel’s supply chain weaknesses and to fix them. On her watch, Crate & Barrel has diversified its supplier base, notably sending more sourcing to Vietnam, and invested in infrastructure and technology to position inventory where it is most likely to sell and better forecast demand. She also moved more upholstery sourcing to the U.S. Crate & Barrel has overhauled everything from its warehouse management software to its e-commerce site. And it now accepts buy-now, pay-later services in an appeal to inflation-pinched consumers.

“You don’t feel it until you’re being tested, but the global supply chain is fragile,” Hayes told Fortune in an interview at the new location of CB2, Crate & Barrel’s sister brand, in New York’s Chelsea district. “You can have the best-laid plans, you can map your ocean liners, you can decide what vendors you’re going to work with, but culture is everything to get through it.”

In her time as CEO, she has worked to flatten decision making at the retailer, to make it more flexible in a furniture market that is, in fact, not growing. “You can get into a command room, but you have to have the people to make it happen,” Hayes says.

Crate & Barrel is part of privately held German retail group Otto Group, which does not publish financial results but did report earlier this year that Crate & Barrel revenue rose 1.6% last year. Given that the furniture market is stagnant in the U.S., Hayes says growth has to come at the expense of the competition. “It’s absolutely a market steal play,” says Hayes, who earlier in her career was a senior executive at Williams-Sonoma and at Nike. Hayes plans on adding 30 new Crate & Barrel and CB2 stores to its current count of 100 in the next three years, as well as 20 more in the two years after that.

As she shows Fortune around the CB2 store, she points to touches that she thinks will help it achieve a more elevated look she sees as key for winning customers from rivals. Things like much bigger rug displays with more swatches and new woods in warmer tones that feel homier. “We are building better quality products,” she says. “You have to bring good quality to the market to be able to do that.”

item.title: AI boom or bust? 10 under-the-radar stock picks and investing ideas for either scenario
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Balances investment advice with an analysis of AI's impact on the market, suitable for an advanced reader.

Investors don’t have to decide whether AI will change the world. They do, however, have to determine how much of their portfolio should depend on it. After all, AI bets now extend far beyond the obvious megacap tech stocks. Utilities and power-equipment makers have been swept up in the data center build-out. Even parts of the energy sector now trade on the promise that AI will consume an enormous amount of electricity.

The same goes if the bubble bursts—a risk that Nvidia’s recent troubles heighten. Because classic AI stocks are weighted so heavily in indexes like the S&P 500, even a standard 60/40 portfolio can mean betting big on this nascent technology. Investors looking to hedge must find something that doesn’t depend on the very boom they’re worried about.

To help navigate both sides of the trade, Fortune has identified six investment strategies for 2027. Three are built to ride the boom—and three will help you survive a bust.

Boom

The bet: Picks and shovels

Ticker: RACK

The VanEck Data Center Supply Chain ETF allocates to companies that help power, operate, and equip data centers. It’s a bet on the physical infrastructure of the AI boom rather than solely the hyperscalers and software developers themselves.

That’s because the fund gives investors exposure to several layers of the data center supply chain. Think chipmakers, along with companies that make important computing components, like Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, and Micron. Industrial companies like Eaton, Vertiv, and Johnson Controls that provide the electrical equipment and cooling solutions for these energy-intensive facilities are included as well. Meanwhile, Quanta Services and Amphenol add exposure to the construction and connectivity themes.

Tom Essaye, founder of Sevens Report Research, likened the broadening AI trade to “water sweeping across a floor,” reaching “places that people would not think had anything to do with AI.”

Bryan Armour, director of ETF and passive strategies research for North America at Morningstar, points to RACK as a way to look beyond traditional tech funds and growth stocks to capitalize on the AI trade. “You need to build the data centers, you need to build the chips and the GPUs and memory and all the different components,” Armour said.

The bet: Landlords

Ticker: NCLD

The Roundhill Neocloud ETF bets on the landlords of AI computing: businesses that build specialized data centers packed with GPUs and rent out the processing power AI companies need to train and run their models.

Two neocloud providers, Nebius and CoreWeave, make up more than half of the fund; many of the rest have been in Bitcoin mining and are retooling for AI. The bet is that rising demand for computing will fill up these facilities and lead to new contracts.

The bet: Connectivity

Tickers: LYTE, LUMA

The Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF (LYTE) and the KraneShares Photonic and Optical ETF (LUMA) both target a key bottleneck in the AI build-out: moving enormous amounts of data quickly and efficiently. Both funds offer exposure to companies developing optical technologies that increase bandwidth and reduce the energy needed to move information between chips and across data centers as AI computing demands grow.

These ETFs invest in the suppliers behind those connections. LYTE holds stocks such as Ciena and Eoptolink, while KraneShares’ LUMA counts LandMark Optoelectronics, Soitec, and Marvell among its major holdings.

“AI will still have legs next year,” said Todd Rosenbluth, head of research at VettaFi. “There will still be demand for companies that offer [this] exposure.”

Still, investors allocating to these more specialized funds must be prepared: All the names here launched in 2026, so they don’t have long track records and tend to swoon when the AI trade comes under pressure. “The narrower you invest in the market,” Rosenbluth said, “the greater the volatility.”

Doom

Think the AI boom is overheated? These strategies can help hedge your portfolio if the AI trade falls back to earth.

The bet: Reweighting

Ticker: RSP

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF offers a straightforward way to loosen AI’s grip on your portfolio. Unlike the traditional S&P 500 index, which gives the biggest companies the largest weighting, RSP resets its holdings to equal weighting each quarter. That puts chipmaking giant Nvidia on par with any other company at each quarterly rebalance. If megacap tech underperforms while the rest of the market holds up, RSP could lose less than the traditional S&P 500 index. That said, for the first nine months of 2026, RSP returned roughly 9.9%, including reinvested dividends, lagging the broad-market index’s 12.7% total return.

The bet: Low drama

Tickers: SPLV, HDV, VTV

The Invesco S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) buys the 100 S&P 500 stocks with the smallest price swings over the previous 12 months. SPLV can offset some AI risk because the fund allocates to seemingly steadier businesses, rather than companies with exceptionally high growth expectations. The fund has little exposure to Big Tech and much larger allocations to utilities, financials, and real estate. Because SPLV counts utilities among its holdings, however, it’s not completely AI-free.

Although SPLV lagged the S&P 500 during the first nine months of 2026, it remained positive for the year through Sept. 30. The fund provided some downside cushioning in 2022, when the Federal Reserve started aggressively hiking interest rates. That year, in total returns, the S&P 500 dropped 18.1%, while SPLV fell only 4.9%.…

MARTIN MARECHAL: We probably pitched it earlier this year - like, January or February.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.2%, to close at 50,774.94 on Friday.

The S&P 500 gained more than 5% and the Nasdaq more than 6% for the week, which ended with an early close

The S&P 500 climbed 1.6%, settling at 7,297.49, and a 2.3% rise lifted the Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite to 24,129.50. U.S. markets were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and shut at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.

Technology stocks led the rebound. Meta $META Platforms stock rose more than 3%, Amazon $AMZN stock gained about 4% and Broadcom $AVGO stock climbed close to 4%.

For the week, the Dow and the S&P 500 each gained more than 5%, and the Nasdaq gained more than 6%. The S&P 500 turned in its strongest week since April 2025, and the Nasdaq posted its largest weekly gain since April, according to CNBC.

The week began with Nvidia $NVDA reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Nvidia stock jumped 31% on Monday, and the Dow gained over 1,400 points, or 3%. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each logged their strongest one-day performance since April 2025 on Monday, according to CNBC.

Nvidia and other artificial-intelligence names have since surrendered a portion of that advance, dragging on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, according to CNBC.

Huang left the company earlier this month. Before his departure, sentiment on AI stocks had already soured, according to CNBC, because investors were uneasy about how the buildout is funded with debt, indications that companies were trimming capital spending, and an expected slowing of data center construction following Democratic victories in the midterm elections.

Some market participants attribute the recent weakness more to the prospect of Federal Reserve interest rate increases, according to CNBC. Traders' expectations of several rate increases in the months ahead were strengthened by this week's newest personal consumption expenditures price index data.

item.title: The Scientist Who Kickstarted Pennsylvania’s Fracking Boom Thought Gas Would Be a ‘Bridge Fuel’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of a significant environmental issue with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Almost 20 years ago, a Penn State University geoscientist named Terry Engelder published an eye-popping estimate of the volume of gas sitting beneath Pennsylvania. It’s now the second-biggest producer of gas in the U.S., behind only Texas.

At the time, Engelder says now, he hoped that his assessment would help to curb greenhouse gas emissions because it would encourage the transition away from coal. But he now fears that natural gas has become a long-term occupant of the energy landscape rather than the “bridge fuel” that he and others thought they were promoting.

Engelder, now an emeritus professor of geology at Penn State, is writing a book describing his work in estimating that the Marcellus Shale deposit—which also underlies parts of West Virginia, New York and Ohio—had enough gas to meet total U.S. needs for about 20 years under consumption rates at the time.

Engelder’s estimate of 489 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of technically recoverable gas—published in 2009, and still, he says, underlying industry assumptions today—first persuaded bankers to lend the energy industry billions of dollars to extract the gas using hydraulic fracturing of mile-deep shale beds. Critics say the process causes environmental and public health harms, adds to global emissions and that its entrenchment in Pennsylvania has stunted the growth of renewables.

His estimate was broadly confirmed by the U.S. Energy Information Administration, which in 2011 estimated the Marcellus contained 410 tcf of gas. In 2018, it was revised upward by the University of Texas, which calculated the field had about 560 tcf of technically recoverable gas.

Engelder hoped natural gas, which creates about 55 percent of the carbon emissions of coal, would act as a transition on the way to a renewable-dominated future. But with its increasing use since the start of the fracking revolution in Pennsylvania, its status is now at odds with Engelder’s original vision. Almost 60 percent of Pennsylvania’s electricity now comes from gas.

Demand for natural gas is expected to increase further, driven by energy-hungry data centers, dozens of which are planned for Pennsylvania.

“I really was optimistic that wind and solar were going to become American industries, and America was going to have the best solar cells, and that gas was going to serve as a bridge fuel,” Engelder said, in an interview with Inside Climate News. “It turns out that it’s become more of a permanent feature than a bridge fuel.”

Engelder described how he calculated the size of the Marcellus reserve, and how he hoped its exploitation would help slow climate change by encouraging the use of natural gas rather than coal. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. .

JON HURDLE: In making your estimate of the huge amount of natural gas in the Marcellus, were you motivated by the idea that increased use of natural gas rather than coal would help to reduce carbon emissions?

TERRY ENGELDER: Absolutely. The most low-hanging fruit in terms of slowing the American rate of injection to the atmosphere was that conversion of coal to natural gas. That conversion, particularly in places like Pennsylvania, had a huge impact. Probably the most important thing my calculation did was it rapidly made the rate of CO2 being added to the atmosphere go down.

HURDLE: Do you have any qualms about providing the information that the industry needed to exploit the vast reserves that it has done so far?

ENGELDER: Evidence of my concern about climate change is shown in a TED Talk I gave in 2013 in which I said I had to make the judgment between furthering the era of fossil fuels, and trying to get into a position where climate change could be dealt with.

HURDLE: Did you try to reconcile those positions described in the TED Talk?

ENGELDER: These two positions just can’t be reconciled. This was always a scientific Sophie’s choice. It still is the type of choice for most, if not all, geologists who work in industry. They all know the terrible choice they are making.

HURDLE: What prompted you to do the estimate?

ENGELDER: These [fracking] companies were asking for billions of dollars; it was non-trivial money. Banks weren’t going to give these companies billions of dollars without some sort of outside confirmation that these companies were actually on the right track. I gave a webinar in 2007 to a bunch of the banks that included Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank. One of the bankers asked, “How much gas is there in the Marcellus? How much can be recovered for our billions of dollars?” That led to my calculation.

Suddenly, the banks freed up a lot of money for companies like Chesapeake and Range and Anadarko.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

HURDLE: How did you calculate the 489 tcf number?

ENGELDER: By using production data from Pennsylvania, Ohio and West Virginia from the end of 2008. That number has held up for a decade and a half now.

HURDLE: Did you make earlier estimates?

ENGELDER: Yes, I came up with a number which was, I thought, incredibly large. At the time, it was 363 trillion cubic feet. I said: “This is too large; I don’t need to tell anyone it’s that large. They might not believe me.” So the first number was 50 tcf, published on Jan. 17, 2008, but it was not based on production data because there weren’t any yet. The 50 tcf estimate was arbitrary. It could have been 100 tcf.

HURDLE: How much public interest was there in your estimate at the time?…

item.title: ‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important research on a critical environmental issue with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050

Sinking land and rising seas could expose more than seven million people living in Africa’s coastal “megacities” to flooding by the middle of the century, according to new research.

The analysis, published in Science Advances, combines satellite data with projections of sea level rise to assess the risk of flooding in 20 of Africa’s most populous coastal cities.

The study finds that, under a moderate warming scenario, an “extreme sea level event” – when sea levels are unusually high due to short-term changes in weather and ocean conditions – could expose a million buildings and $180bn of assets to flooding.

Lagos, the capital of Nigeria, and Alexandria in Egypt are the most vulnerable cities in the analysis.

In these two cities alone, five million people and $150bn in assets could be exposed to flooding and the cities by mid-century.

Human activity, such as pumping groundwater or drilling for fossil fuels, can cause the ground to sink, in a process called “subsidence”.

Seismic or volcanic activity can also drive changes in the height of the land, causing it to either rise or fall. This “vertical land movement” can either alleviate or exacerbate the effects of sea level rise.

The researchers combined more than 4,000 satellite images of Africa’s coastline to determine how quickly different regions are rising or sinking.

They identified Lagos and Alexandria as “subsidence hotspots”, finding that the two cities are sinking at rates of 5.2mm and 6.3mm per year, respectively.

This is “comparable to rates reported for south-east Asian megacities such as Jakarta, Manila and Ho Chi Minh City”, which have recorded “some of the highest subsidence rates yet observed”, according to the study.

The authors combined these estimates with sea level rise projections from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s sixth assessment report under three different emissions scenarios, to assess the regional sea level rise across the African coastline.

They used 2020 population data, building footprints and GDP per capita to estimate how much of each city would be exposed to these flooding events over the 21st century, if the city itself stays the same.

While Lagos and Alexandria are the most vulnerable cities, the research finds that Djibouti City in Djibouti, Mogadishu in Somalia and Tripoli in Libya will face “minimal economic exposure due to their smaller populations and infrastructure bases”.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho, a PhD student at Virginia Tech, tells Carbon Brief that the analysis holds population and city data constant at 2020 levels, so that the authors can isolate the effects of sea level rise and vertical land movement on changing flood exposure.

He notes that if people move away from “threatened areas” over the coming decades, then estimates could be too high. However, if “continued urban growth” causes city populations to increase, the estimates could be too low.

Africa is the world’s fastest-urbanising region, with cities growing at an average rate of 3.5% every year. By 2050, Africa’s urban population is expected to double from 7m to 1.4bn.

He also notes that “the flood model assumes no coastal defenses, so the estimates are a worst-case physical picture”.

Subsidence in African coastal cities has not been consistently monitored in the past, largely due to a lack of local data, the study explains.

The authors say their method of using satellites to assess subsidence and uplift could be used in other “data-scarce coastal regions across the global south”.

Dasho, O., et al (2026), Sinking cities: Latent flood risk in Africa’s coastal megacities, Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh6538

Source: Carbon Brief | Published: 2026-11-27 19:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Refugee families use agroforestry to restore degraded landscape in Bangladesh camp
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging story with clear reporting and useful vocabulary on environmental restoration efforts.

- After the 2017 influx, over 1,500 hectares of protected forest in Cox’s Bazar were cleared to build refugee shelters, stripping the hillsides of vegetation and triggering a crisis of deadly landslides and soil erosion.

- Rohingya refugees are using traditional agroecology techniques on agroforestry plots, such as multi-layered intercropping, organic composting, and seed saving, to heal the degraded landscape and grow food amid deep cuts to international food aid.

- Supported by NGOs like UNHCR and FAO, large-scale reforestation projects have planted nearly one million tree seedlings and restored 200 hectares of camp land, using a mix of fast-growing species and deep-rooted native trees, including fruit trees, to stabilize the sandy slopes and prevent landslides.

- While reforestation efforts in the camp are showing measurable success, the long-term survival of forests is impacted by funding shortages and a lack of secure land rights for refugees.

KUTUPALONG REFUGEE CAMP, Bangladesh —”It is like a jail, but it isn’t a jail,” says Roshid Ahamed Bin, a 47-year-old Rohingya farmer, living in what is now a refugee camp in Bangladesh. It is far from the farmland where he used to live in Myanmar, before he and thousands of Rohingya people like him fled persecution eight years ago.

Here, amid the world’s largest refugee settlement with over 1.1 million refugees, space is tight and evergreen forests have paid the price. But families are combining NGO-funded farming projects with traditional Rohingya agroecology techniques to create agroforestry plots that are restoring land while helping refugees become self-sufficient in response to deep cuts in international food aid.

“I feel so bad here as I have no land, but I am keeping my ancestors’ heritage alive. Growing these crops reminds me of the life we had in Myanmar. Here, life is difficult,” said Amina Khatun, a 58-year-old refugee living in Camp 1W, a sector of the sprawling settlement.

Before the 2017 influx, Kutupalong refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar was a tropical evergreen forest, dominated by Dipterocarpus species, and sanctuary for endangered Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). To make way for the massive refugee settlements, the Bangladeshi government allocated roughly 2,500 hectares (6,100 acres) of protected forest land, and refugees and aid agencies cleared the vegetation to build shelters and provide firewood. Over 1,500 hectares of forest were cleared in total.

The rain, with nowhere to soak in, ran straight down the slopes. Landslides became a seasonal terror, sources told Mongabay.

But in the past several years, on the hillsides where there was once bare, sandy earth and the blue-black glare of tarpaulin, there are now nurseries and gardens. Across the camps, more than 159,000 refugees are engaged in homestead gardening. Space is severely limited, and not all use agroecology techniques. Some farmers rely on chemical sprays and paddy fields to make ends meet.

But among them, there are traditional food gardens and permaculture designs that avoid synthetic pesticides entirely, relying instead on intercropping, a mix of trees and organic soil management.

Knowledge that crossed the border

Mongabay sat with Roshid Ahamed Bin inside Camp 27. He remembers the farmland in Rakhine state, Myanmar, before 2017.

Despite the confinement of the camp, Ahamed Bin has found a way to reconnect with the life he left behind. Like many Rohingya refugees here, he was a farmer in Myanmar. Now, he is among a growing number of refugees using agroforestry to restore the camp’s degraded landscape and feed their families.

“Our land may be far away, but the farming passion of our ancestors remains part of our lives,” he told Mongabay.

Back in Myanmar, farming was not just a livelihood for his family, but a way of life rooted in the land. His family grew rice, vegetables, and fruit, using layered intercropping and agroforestry. They planted local varieties of banana, papaya, and mango trees directly beside their vegetable gardens to maximize space and provide shade. They removed insects by hand, added animal manure and composted leaves to keep the soil alive, and saved seeds from healthy crops.

Several U.N. agencies and NGOs are providing support to these efforts and they actively integrate Rohingya traditional knowledge into their programs. The UNHCR SuLMER project has rehabilitated the Shoa Ma’r Jhiri stream, stabilized slopes, and introduced kitchen gardens, relying on community input to decide what to plant. CARE’s training in ‘sack and vertical gardening’ builds on the Rohingya tradition of maximizing tiny spaces. Similarly, when FAO and WFP distribute seeds, they rely on the refugees’ traditional knowledge of seed-saving and intercropping. Together, these programs have engaged tens of thousands of refugees.

“They have skills in planting, fertilizer, pest control, harvesting, timing,” said Jahir Ahamed, a staffer at the UNHCR SuLMER prokect. “We use suitable practices in gardening activities.”

Because families like his fled so quickly, they didn’t bring their own seeds from Myanmar and rely on those from distributed. They grow many leafy vegetables and gourds, like amaranth and Indian spinach.

Mabia Khatun, 38, from Camp 17, recalls her own farm practices. “We saved seeds from healthy plants,” she said. A practice, they still engage in with seeds provided by NGOs. “Sometimes we exchanged seeds with neighbors. Our elders taught us to care for plants and protect the land.”

According to FAO and UNHCR reports, the restoration involves a mix of fast-growing tree species for quick ground cover and slower native species for long-term slope stability. On the ground, this looks like multi-layered intercropping.

This method is highly strategic for the camp’s harsh environment. By stacking plants of different heights together, families can grow food in tiny spaces while the deep roots hold the sandy soil in place.…

item.title: In Republic of Congo, residents and a scientist take on a fight against lead pollution
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed account of a local environmental issue with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

- Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire in the Republic of Congo, filed a civil claim in October 2026, seeking compensation and medical care after years of suspected lead exposure allegedly linked to the Metssa Congo battery recycling plant.

- Blood tests conducted in 2023 with support from Amnesty International found lead levels in the blood samples of residents, including children, far above the WHO’s reference level.

- In 2026, residents worked with Columbia University researcher Alexander Van Geen to test soil around the former plant: Of 49 samples, 41% exceeded the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s threshold for safe levels for residential soil where children play.

- Although the plant closed in 2024, residents say no cleanup has taken place and researchers say that the contamination is serious but geographically limited.

Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, have filed a civil claim before the city’s High Court in relation to pollution allegedly caused by a foundry.

“We want tests, but also compensation for damages and losses,” Cyrille Traoré Ndembi, a plaintiff and president of the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective, which represents people living in the working-class neighborhood, told Mongabay on the phone.

The civil case, filed in October, is the latest in a series of actions taken against Metssa Congo, a foundry that opened in the neighborhood in 2013.The facility recycled, among other things, car batteries, extracting lead and turning it into lead bars for export. The plant is part of the Metssa Group, an industrial metals trading company based in the United Arab Emirates.

The battery recycling process can pose serious health risks. According to the WHO, lead can be released in the form of fumes, particles and dust at every stage of the process, from draining and dismantling to smelting and refining. Environmental contamination from recycling can be substantial, exposing workers and nearby communities to significant levels of lead, the health agency says on its website.

According to Traore Ndembi, residents of Vindoulou soon experienced this reality first-hand, complaining about toxic fumes coming from the plant. In 2019, they decided to register their discontent over pollution.

“We wrote to the public authorities, to the departmental director of health,” Traoré Ndembi said. “We also wrote to the local environmental authorities but they said there was no pollution. The health authorities in the Kouilou department then carried out medical tests like chest X-rays to prove that the area was not polluted. Their findings said we were not sick, that there was nothing wrong. So we decided to take matters into our own hands.”

To provide scientific evidence to support their complaint, in 2023 the communities, with the help of NGO Amnesty International, conducted blood tests on a small group of residents, including both adults and children. The results were unequivocal: The people tested had blood lead levels far above the threshold recommended by the WHO, namely 5 micrograms per deciliter (µg/dL) or one-tenth of a liter. While there is no known level of safe exposure to lead, the health agency recommends taking action when levels cross this threshold. In some cases, the levels detected were 10 times higher.

The situation was alarming, according to the human rights organization, and the findings proved decisive for the communities. The residents’ collective won its first legal battle: The administrative court of Pointe-Noire ordered the company to suspend its operations and the government instructed the operator to fund site decontamination and medical care.

‘I can’t keep [the children] locked indoors’

Yet, two years later, Traoré Ndembi, who still lives in Vindoulou with his wife and children, remains worried.

“The authorities are not telling us anything,” he said. “It is true that the plant has closed, but nothing has changed on the ground since then. Nothing has been cleaned up. We are still living in an area that has been polluted for years.”

“Closing the plant is not enough. The medical test results confirmed that we had been poisoned by lead, so we need to receive medical care and treatment! And the plant must clean up and decontaminate the site,” he said. “Because what guarantees that, even though it has stopped operating, it is no longer polluting? I don’t feel at ease when my children play outside, but I can’t keep them locked indoors either.”

Alexander Van Geen, a research professor specialized in environmental contaminants and member of the Earth Institute faculty at Columbia University, told Mongabay in a phone interview for a previous article about possible contamination from the Metssa plant that he had been shocked by the blood test results obtained by Amnesty International. “I have to admit that when I first saw the data, I thought, ‘This can’t be possible.’,” he said. “I thought that at levels this high, children would be dying or suffering from terrible tremors. I was horrified.”

According to the WHO, exposure to lead is highly toxic and can cause lead poisoning, a serious condition that affects the brain, liver, kidneys and bones. The U.N. agency estimates that lead exposure caused more than 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2021, mainly through cardiovascular effects. Aware of the scale of the problem, Van Geen told Mongabay in early 2026 that “something needs to be done.”

A new round of testing

His words were followed by action. After Mongabay published its article, he contacted Cyrille Traoré Ndembi and the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective to carry out another round of tests, this time on the soil.

“It was important to me that the affected communities carry out their own measurements,” he said after the new round of tests. “I thought that if blood lead levels were high, the lead had to be coming from somewhere. So, we began looking at the soil.”…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-27 15:19 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: International Jaguar Day: Big cats hold on at the edges of their range
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Informative piece on the status of jaguars with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

International Jaguar Day has been marked every Nov. 29 since 2018, to raise awareness of the threats faced by the Americas’ biggest cats and the efforts to protect them.

Jaguars (Panthera onca) were once found across some 19 million square kilometers (7.3 million square miles), from what is today the southwestern U.S. to central Argentina.

But their range has shrunk by more than half, and today spans about 9 million km² (3.5 million mi²). Most jaguars live in a stronghold ranging from the Amazon Rainforest and stretching into the Pantanal wetlands, the Chaco dry forest and the Llanos grasslands of Colombia and Venezuela.

However, recent sightings and reports from outside these core areas highlight that many jaguars are still holding on at the edges of their historical territory.

For example, in Brazil’s eastern Atlantic Forest and dry Caatinga, fewer than 250 adult jaguars survive, and researchers have begun banking their genes in an effort to save them through cloning.

At the northern edge of the species’ range, a male nicknamed Cinco showed up on camera footage in southern Arizona state in late 2025, becoming the fifth jaguar recorded there in 15 years.

Meanwhile, in Honduras’s Sierra del Merendón, a mountain range in the country’s northwest, camera traps recorded a young male at an altitude of about 2,200 meters (7,200 feet) for the first time in a decade.

“The fact that they’re able to travel through these high elevation areas also shows how resilient they are,” Allison Devlin, who directs the jaguar program at the wildcat conservation NGO Panthera, told Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman.

The Merendón mountains form a corridor between Honduras and Guatemala, allowing wildlife to move between the two countries.

“It reaffirms that there are dispersed populations in the northwestern part of the country,” said Marcio Martinez, a coordinator at Honduras’s National Institute of Forest Conservation.

Also in Honduras, authorities raided the home of a businessman in Olancho, in the east, and seized a female jaguar estimated to be about a year old, along with a capuchin monkey, two parrots and a python. The jaguar is thought to have been captured in the Mosquitia forests, a stronghold for the species.

The young cat now lives at a rehabilitation center run by the Honduran armed forces and may be returned to a protected area if considered fit enough.

Banner image: This female jaguar, kept as a pet by a businessman, was seized as part of a two-week-long operation. Image courtesy of the ICF Wildlife Department.
