item.title: Aerial photos show recovery of Florida Bay, US, as restoration sends Everglades water
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Illustrative story of environmental restoration with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

- Freshwater flows into Florida Bay, significantly reduced by decades of Everglades drainage, are slowly increasing under the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan.

- Helicopter surveys by avian ecologist Mark Ian Cook document returning wading birds, wintering waterfowl, American flamingos and threatened American crocodiles.

- Wading bird nesting reached a record high in 2018 but has since declined, while a severe 2025–2026 drought underscored the birds’ sensitivity to water fluctuations.

From a low-flying helicopter above the coastal Everglades in southern Florida, U.S., Mark Ian Cook looks down at dense mangrove forests and silty shallows rarely seen by others. Below him, bottlenose dolphins trap mullet in rings of mud, nurse sharks mate in sheltered waters and flamingos forage on remote mudflats.

Cook, an avian ecologist who heads the South Florida Water Management District’s Everglades Research Group, tracks how wading birds respond to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP), a decades-long federal-state effort to return freshwater to the southern Everglades and Florida Bay. He conducts a flying survey about every two weeks during the birds’ breeding season, photographing nesting colonies through a small flap in the helicopter door.

Some colonies hold tens of thousands of nests, too many to count by eye, so photos are the most reliable way to tally them, he told Mongabay in a video call. His best frames also help persuade water managers. “My information was so much more effective when I had an image rather than just data or a boring old graph with counts on it,” he said. Cook said he has two advantages when capturing his images: an ecologist’s sense of where and when to find unusual animal behavior and wildlife events, and regular flights over thousands of square miles of remote subtropical wilderness.

His photos play with shape, color and texture, like a flock of lesser scaup (Aythya affinis) that briefly formed a pyramid on a coastal lake after returning in large numbers. Striking images hold a viewer’s attention longer, he said, and “while they’re trying to figure out what they’re looking at, they are more likely to soak in my conservation message.” In those moments, Cook sees nature as the artist and his job as “simply to recognize the art and frame it appropriately.”

Wading birds such as storks, ibises, spoonbills and herons respond quickly to water levels, making them good indicators of restoration. Historically, summer rains caused Lake Okeechobee, approximately 182 kilometers (113 miles) away, to overflow, sending a shallow, slow-moving sheet of water south across the Everglades — the so-called River of Grass — to Florida Bay. Here it mixed with seawater to create the brackish conditions the estuary’s fish, crocodiles and birds depend on.

In the 1930s and early 1940s, the region supported more than 200,000 nests, most along the coast, Cook said. Canals, levees and roads then significantly reduced the freshwater reaching Florida Bay and coastal nesting collapsed.

“When inches of water can make a huge difference in such a flat landscape, that just really affected everything,” Cook said.

Reversing that damage is CERP’s main objective. Authorized by the U.S. Congress in 2000, it is the largest environmental restoration program in the South Florida region, addressing the quantity, quality, timing and distribution of water, with healthy wading bird populations a central goal. The most recent report to Congress projects it will take about 50 years at a cost of $26.9 billion in 2023 dollars, equivalent to roughly $29.8 billion in 2026.

When Hurricane Irma dumped heavy rain across South Florida in 2017, enough freshwater flowed through the Everglades to reach the coast. South Florida recorded 138,834 wading bird nests in 2018, the most since system-wide surveys began in 1995 according to the South Florida Wading Bird Report, which Cook edits. Nests topped 100,000 again in 2021.

“The response was just amazing,” Cook said. “The wading birds came back in really high numbers.”

Other species are rebounding too. American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus) populations are increasing, as are waterfowl numbers. In 2024, tens of thousands of waterfowl, including blue-winged teal (Spatula discors) and lesser scaup, returned to the area’s coastal lakes in concentrations not seen in roughly 80 years. American flamingos, hunted out of Florida more than a century ago, are back as wintering birds. They haven’t nested yet, but “even if they don’t nest, that doesn’t mean that they’re not native,” Cook said.

But progress has been uneven. After exceptional nesting seasons in 2018 and 2021, wading bird nesting has declined for several consecutive years. In 2025, drought contributed to the lowest nesting levels recorded in roughly 30 years in Everglades National Park, according to a recent wading bird report. Rising seas have also cut Florida Bay’s roseate spoonbill (Platalea ajaja) nests from about 400 in 2012 to 157 in 2022, even as the birds have established new nesting colonies farther north in Florida.

Storage remains a bottleneck: Without room to hold Lake Okeechobee’s excess water, managers release much of it to nearby coastal estuaries. The Everglades Agricultural Area Reservoir, built to store that water and send it south, is due to be completed in 2029.

Even so, new bridges along the Tamiami Trail, a highway and levee system that for decades blocked water from flowing south into Everglades National Park, are making a difference. About 10 times more water flowed beneath the road from January through July 2026 than in the same months of 2015, despite a harsher drought, according to the Everglades Foundation. That water moves through the park toward the coast, helping keep Florida Bay’s salinity low enough to avoid a repeat of the 2015 seagrass die-off.

“I like wet years, because that’s when we have very productive wildlife years,” Cook said.…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-27 14:04 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: ‘Vote for trees’: Taiwan community pins hope on ‘Forest Grandma’ to save beloved woods
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Engaging story on community activism with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

- In Kaohsiung’s Ciaotou district, a community is fighting an urban development project that threatens a 154-hectare (380-acre) woodland surrounding the former Ciaotou Sugar Refinery.

- After failing to find politicians to support their fight, they turned to an 83-year-old former factory worker to defend the Ciaotou Woodland, which provides habitat for local wildlife and helps protect the area from flooding.

- Chiang Huang-nu, nicknamed Forest Grandma, is running as an independent candidate in Taiwan’s local elections, with a campaign slogan: “Vote for trees, not for political parties.”

- The push for the development is tied to the growth of the semiconductor industry in southern Taiwan, with the project set to convert a large swath of land around the historic factory into commercial and residential zones for high-tech businesses and their workers.

KAOHSIUNG, Taiwan — At dawn, just as the birds begin to sing, Chiang Huang-nu usually puts on her traditional straw hat and walks through the wooded grounds of a former sugar factory in Ciaotou district in southwest Taiwan. Along the way, the 83-year-old might greet around 30 other regular strollers, most of them retirees.

Chiang has taken these morning walks among the greenery since she was a child. For the past several months, the walk has involved chatting with fellow community members about the community’s fight against the government’s plan to redevelop the area and demolish their beloved wood.

For decades, Chiang and fellow residents have spent their mornings in the Ciaotou Woodland, a 154-hectare (380-acre) urban forest surrounding the historic Ciaotou Sugar Refinery. Located in the eponymous district, north of Kaohsiung city center in southwestern Taiwan, the woodland is home to 100,000 trees, according to local environmentalists, and a habitat for local wildlife.

“Some of the trees were planted during the Japanese colonial period,” which lasted from 1895 to 1945, Chiang told Mongabay. “They are more than 100 years old. They protect us from the heat in summer.”

For the past year, however, residents can only walk in the nearby park. The woodland has been fenced off and made inaccessible to the public, following a government order. Its trees are under threat from the urban redevelopment project.

On a November morning, three elderly men in their 70s were sitting on plastic chairs in the middle of the park, sheltered from the sun by the trees. “I would rather see this place preserved, but what can we do against the government’s decisions?” said one 77-year-old man.

His two companions nodded in agreement.

Faced with such powerlessness, residents have found a glimmer of hope and a figure of resistance in Chiang.

The octogenarian, nicknamed “Forest Grandma” for her passion for protecting the woodland, is running in Taiwan’s local elections on Nov. 28. She is contesting a city council seat in Kaohsiung, the island’s third most populous city. Her only manifesto policy is to protect the wood. Her slogan is “Vote for trees, not parties.”

“Of course I’m going to vote for her,” a 70-year-old resident, who only gave her surname, Tsai, told Mongabay. “If you destroy this forest, what will we have left? We won’t have anywhere to go for a walk.”

Like Chiang, other morning residents on the morning walk come from working-class families. Either they themselves, their parents, or both were employed by the factory, which began operating in 1902. After the sugar refinery ceased operations in 1999, the surrounding area was transformed into a vast woodland.

For around 15 years, the old woodland became a place for many residents from Ciaotou and nearby districts to walk in the mornings or to hike or cycle on weekends.

Forest Grandma has no formal education and is illiterate. She does not speak Mandarin, the official language in Taiwan, and communicates only in Taiwanese Hokkien, the language spoken by descendants of early immigrants from China’s Fujian province who moved to Taiwan centuries ago.

Born into a poor farming family in 1943, during the Japanese colonial rule, she was given a Japanese name, Tamako. Her current name, Huang-nu, was registered after the Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan in 1949, following a civil war in mainland China.

For Chiang Huang-nu, who worked at the Ciaotou Sugar Refinery for years, her political involvement did not stem from an electoral ambition but from a long-standing attachment to a place she has known since her youth. “Destroying this forest means destroying my entire life,” she said.

The idea for her candidacy came from her son, Chiang Yao-hsien, also known as Jungle Chiang. The 68-year-old is a heritage and environmental activist. In 2001, two years after the Ciaotou Sugar Refinery was shut down, he turned the complex into an artists’ village, where his mother volunteers to work as a sweeper.

“My mother is popular in the area,” Chiang Yao-hsien told Mongabay. “Her background as a former factory worker speaks to an entire generation. I knew she could bring people together around our cause. So I encouraged her to run.”

Large-scale urban forest

In 2007, APEC nations made a regional commitment to increase forest cover by 20 million hectares (50 million acres) by 2020. Taiwan pledged to contribute to this goal by increasing its reforested areas by 11,550 hectares (28,540 acres). As part of the commitment, a woodland was planted near Tienpao River in Ciaotou between 2010 and 2012.

Environmentalists praise the woodland as a rare example of a large-scale urban forest in Kaohsiung.

“These trees are not even 20 years old, and today, while we continue to take part in APEC meetings, the authorities are considering destroying this forest for a real estate and land development project,” said Chuang Chieh-jen, chairperson of the Forest City Association, Taiwan (FCAT).…

Why it is here: original recipe with clear instructions and cultural context

Traditionally, a Gibson is a savory twist on a martini, substituting a cocktail onion for the olive. My version, which incorporates the very easy homemade Pickled Celery, has the same clean, briny qualities as the classic but with a touch of complexity from the pickling spices and a bright, leafy flavor. I like to stir my Gibson with a handful of celery leaves to amp up that fresh flavor, but if your celery is leafless, or if you’re making this for a big group, feel free to exclude that ingredient.

From Victorian celery vases to midcentury relish trays, celery has been part of hosting parties in the United States for many generations. At gatherings hosted by my grandma Dorothy in western New York in the ’90s, I remember big stalks of celery resting in pitchers of salt water in the middle of every table, acting as both a palate-cleansing snack and a centerpiece. Similarly, this recipe for pickled celery can function as a garnish (consider skewering it onto a cocktail pick with a cornichon and a cherry tomato for a Bloody Mary), part of a canapé, or just as a snack on its own.

Recipe information

- Total Time 10 minutes (plus 8 hours for pickling)

- Yield Makes 1

Preparation

- Pickled Celery Step 1 In a small saucepan over low heat, combine ½ cup [120 ml] distilled vinegar, 1 tsp. kosher salt, 1 tsp. sugar, 2 garlic cloves, 1 tsp. black peppercorns, 1 clove, and ¼ tsp. coriander seeds with ½ cup [120 ml] water. Cook for about 5 minutes, until the sugar and salt are dissolved. Place 4 celery stalks (about 200 g), cut into 1½" [4 cm] lengths, in a heatproof bowl, and pour the hot brine over it. Using a cocktail spoon, stir vigorously for 30 seconds, or until the outside of the glass feels extremely cold. Step 4 Strain into the chilled glass, garnish with 1 piece Pickled Celery on a cocktail pick, and serve.

item.title: Herby Cottage Cheese Scones
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique recipe with detailed description and culinary technique

These garden-inspired scones are a hit year round, but extra special in the spring and early summer when fragrant herbs grow rampant. I typically hydrate scones with cream or buttermilk, but in this case I use cottage cheese, giving the scones a sort of 1970s vintage feel. Cottage cheese is made by curdling milk with an acid, like vinegar or lemon juice, which separates the curds from the whey. The curds are then drained, rinsed to remove excess acidity, and sometimes mixed with cream. It may seem unusual to stir this retro breakfast staple into your scone dough, but it creates a tender, flavorful crumb that stays moist long after baking.

This is the kind of recipe that necessitates a mild-tasting flour such as Sonora wheat, ensuring nothing takes away from the delicate herbs. In addition to Sonora or other soft wheat flour, I use refined all-purpose flour and fine yellow cornmeal. You’ll find yourself mincing herbs to add to the mix. Make sure to use a sharp chef’s knife that won’t bruise the herby bits; this helps them retain their flavor and aroma. Roasting the scallions softens and caramelizes them a bit. I also add lemon zest and cracked black pepper. Both play a supporting role, never overpowering the herbs. To finish, garnish with a few flakes of crunchy salt, such as Maldon.

Smeared with butter, cream cheese, or even more cottage cheese, these scones are a dreamy addition to a weekend breakfast or afternoon tea. They also pair perfectly with smoked salmon or egg salad. For an elegant appetizer, they can be baked into smaller versions of themselves (see the variation that follows).

Variation: Cocktail Scones

To make cocktail scones, divide the dough into 3 equal portions and pat each down into a disk about 4" (10 cm) in diameter and ¾" (2 cm) thick. Cut each disk into 8 wedges. Finish as directed in the main recipe. You’ll end up with 24 mini scones. Bake on two baking sheets for 12 minutes, then rotate the sheets and switch their positions in the oven. Bake for another 10–12 minutes, until golden.

Recipe information

- Total Time 45 minutes

- Yield Makes 10

Preparation

- Step 1 Place an oven rack in the middle position and preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Step 2 Place 6 scallions on a rimmed baking sheet and drizzle with 1 Tbsp. olive oil. Roast until tender, 6–8 minutes. When the bulb part of a scallion can be easily pierced with a paring knife, the scallions are ready. Let them cool completely. Trim the roots and tops, leaving all the white part and 2" (5 cm) of the green part, and chop them roughly. Step 3 Increase the oven temperature to 400°F (205°C). Step 4 Combine ⅔ cup (85 g) whole-grain all-purpose wheat flour, ⅔ cup (90 g) all-purpose flour, ½ cup (65 g) fine cornmeal, 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. kosher salt in a mixing bowl. Add ½ cup (112 g/1 stick/4 oz.) cold unsalted butter, cut into ½" (1.25 cm) cubes, and toss to combine. Quickly cut the butter cubes into the dry ingredients by pinching the butter with your fingertips—imagine you’re snapping your fingers—until the mixture resembles a coarse meal with butter pieces the size of cornflakes. Add the scallions, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh dill, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh chives, 1 tsp. finely grated lemon zest, and ¼ tsp. freshly cracked black pepper and toss to combine. Step 5 Using your hands, make a well in the center of the mixture. Whisk 1¼ cups (295 ml) 4% cottage cheese with 1 large egg and a dash of hot sauce and pour into the well. Toss gently with both hands (as if tossing a salad) until a rough dough is formed. Step 6 To shape the scones, transfer the dough to a lightly floured surface. Pat it down into a disk about 6" (15 cm) in diameter and 1" (2.5 cm) thick. Using a large chef’s knife, slice into 10 equal wedges (as you would a cake or a pie). Step 7 Transfer each individual scone to the prepared baking sheet, placing them at least 2" (5 cm) apart. Brush with 1 large beaten egg, then season with a sprinkle of coarse sea salt and black pepper. Bake for 10 minutes, then rotate the baking sheet and bake for another 10–12 minutes, until the edges of the scones are golden. These are delicious while still warm, but you can also serve them at room temperature.

item.title: Breville Oracle Jet Review: This Beginner-Friendly Espresso Machine Is $200 Off Right Now
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: product review with personal experience and technical details

I’ve had quite a few dreams and aspirations in my adult life thus far. One of them was owning an espresso machine. As someone who would typically choose a cappuccino over a cup of drip coffee, the idea of waking up every morning and enjoying the perfect mug of milky espresso from the comfort of my own home seemed like the pinnacle of luxury.

Besides the obvious barriers to entry of price and counter space, one of the main reasons I waited so long to make my dream a reality was that, well, I was intimidated. The world of coffee—and espresso in particular—is one that intrigues me, but I’m admittedly no expert. And while the science nerd in me feels somewhat compelled to spend time delving deep into grind size and ratios and extraction times, the reality is I’ve always felt daunted at the prospect of actually doing so—and wary of investing in a machine that would be so complicated to use, I’d end up forgoing it anyway. At the same time, I shied away from the idea of fully automatic machines that operate at the push of a button, because the wannabe barista in me wants to feel like I’m doing something as I make my morning cup. That, and I’ve never found the espresso those kinds of machines make to be all that good.

That’s why, when I got wind a couple years ago that Breville was launching a new top of the line, not-quite automatic espresso machine that promised to guide me through all of the processes I was intimidated by, I was immediately intrigued. The machine in question? The Oracle Jet, the latest (at the time of its launch) in Breville’s Oracle line after 2017’s Oracle Touch. The Jet shares many of the same features that made contributor Carina Finn fall in love with the Oracle Touch when she tested it—namely, an easy-to-use touchscreen display with a multitude of drink programs, automatic grinding, dosing, and tamping, and an automatic milk frother. But the newer machine has several key improvements that make it an even better pick for home espresso drinkers—and it's $200 off for Black Friday right now. After years of testing, I can say quite confidently that there is no other machine I’d rather own.

How does the Breville Oracle Jet work?

The Oracle Jet is about as close to a super-automatic machine as you can get without actually being super-automatic. That is to say, you still have to complete a few steps along the way to your latte.

After unboxing my machine on its arrival, I was delighted to find that there was no need to flip through a physical manual. The entire setup process was explained (very clearly, I’ll add) via the touchscreen display, and the steps were laid out in a logical order, which I really appreciated.

After the initial set up, the display guided me through making my first drink and calibrating the grind size for the beans I had on hand. I had to make several rounds of espresso to get the ideal grind size (which the machine suggests based on extraction speed). As someone with no espresso machine experience but who likes to know why and how things work, I found this process fun and helpful, a great jumping off point in my own espresso journey.

Within 30 minutes of receiving my machine in the mail, I had set it all up and made a pretty damn good cappuccino—far better than the $6 ones I get from my local coffee shop, that’s for sure. To make a coffee drink, you’ll start by selecting from a catalogue of options (12+ at the time of writing) and inserting the portafilter under the grinder chute. Press the grind icon to begin the grinding process, after which it will automatically be tamped down. Then you’ll move the portafilter over to the group head, twist it into place, and press the brew icon to start the extraction process. The display will count the extraction time for you, and even suggest adjusting the grind size for next time if it notices the extraction taking too long or too short. If you’re making a milk-based drink, the last step is to add your milk of choice to the included stainless steel pitcher, place it under the steam wand, and press the milk frothing icon. The wand will steam the milk to whatever temperature and foam level you’ve selected (and according to which type of milk you used, be it animal or plant-based). After you’ve removed the pitcher, you’ll wipe down the wand and lower it back into place, where it’ll shoot out hot water to purge any remaining milk from the system.

What I love about the Breville Oracle Jet

I won’t bury the lede here: I’m a big fan of this machine. It’s revolutionized my at-home coffee routine, and after owning it for several months, I can’t imagine my life without it at this point. But now you know my stance, I’ll get into some specifics as to what makes this machine so great.

Whether you’re a beginner espresso maker or just tight on time (or both, like me), nothing beats the convenience of a machine that does the hard work of grinding, tamping, and temperature-setting for you. But if the idea of tinkering around with those things is appealing to you, the Oracle Jet offers (some) capability to do so as well. The built-in Baratza burr grinder has 45 grind settings that are easily tweaked by turning a knob on the left side of the machine, or via the touchscreen display, where you can also adjust the temperature at which your drinks are brewed. While there are some 12+ preset programs for drinks ranging from flat whites to cold brew (more on that later), you can also customize your own drink settings and save them to the system.

Everything about the Oracle Jet feels well thought out and intuitive. I’m not just talking about the actual brewing process here, either: There are a number of little design choices that go a long way in making the user experience more enjoyable, like a lever at the base of the machine that lets you lock it in place or unlock wheels if you need to move it around. I also appreciate that there’s a way to fill the water tank from the front of the machine, without needing to remove the whole tank.…

Source: Bon Appétit | Published: 2026-11-27 19:51 UTC | Difficulty: 41/100

item.title: The Coffee Mug I Rave About to Strangers Is on Sale for Black Friday
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: product review with personal experience and design details

The Fellow Move Mug is currently on sale for Black Friday. You can now get it for 20% off, bringing the price down to $24 for the 12 oz and $28 for the 16 oz.

I wouldn't call myself a minimalist by any means, but I am not someone who buys a lot of kitchen gadgets or rushes to snag the latest seasonal cup. But ever since I picked up my first Fellow Carter Move Mug five years ago, I’ve happily repurchased it several times.

This sleek little mug, designed by the coffee nerds at Fellow, keeps your brew hot (or cold) without sacrificing flavor. I use it so often that I’ve sung its praises to a coffee shop owner in Washington, a bed-and-breakfast proprietor in Maine, and countless other strangers.

I love this mug more than I can express—so much, in fact, that I reached out to Fellow founder, Jake Miller, to chat about it. He launched the brand 13 years ago with the goal of delivering great design to coffee brewing, but customers kept asking for an exceptional way to drink their coffee on the go. So a company founded by and for coffee obsessives made the ultimate companion container.

The Carter Move Mug is designed with a superior drinking experience in mind. The body of the mug tapers into a thin drinking lip that Miller said was inspired by a wine glass. When you take a sip, you’re touching metal and not paint, and the lip is protected when the mug is closed.

At the time, other to-go cups were designed with a small opening in the lid and completely missed out on the aromatics. “It was a pretty opinionated design choice, but we wanted people to experience the incredible smells of coffee,” he explained. “Once the lid is off, you have this really great drinking experience.” While the lip of the mug is metal, the inside of the mug is ceramic-coated, so it doesn’t impart any taste to the coffee. According to Miller, “that allows for a more pure expression of the coffee.”

When I tell people about the Carter Mug, I like to joke that it’s almost too good at its job. Hot drinks stay very hot for hours, and I regularly find ice in the mug a full day after I first made my chilled version. I once left a mug of hot coffee in a car during a blizzard, and after almost a day, the coffee was still pleasant to drink. Miller said this effective temperature control is from two things: the distance between the two walls and how much vacuum insulation the mug has. Also, Fellow designed the lid to be gasket-tight so there’s minimal heat loss.

The Move Mug on the Move

One of my favorite features of the Move Mug is the splash guard that clicks into the vessel and prevents big spills while you’re drinking in motion. (As a person prone to mess, this is very helpful.) This element, along with some other accessories, was born out of feedback based on how customers use their mugs, including a straw for cold coffee, a cup holder-friendly size, and the option for a slide top lid. “Everything we do is customer-driven,” Miller noted.

Maybe not important to how your coffee tastes — but important to aesthetics — the Move Mug is sleek and sophisticated, which means it’s suitable for most situations. There’s a nice range of colors, and it looks great in my hand on my commute and on my desk in the office. It’s truly the perfect accessory.

Why it is here: comprehensive historical context, detailed reporting

‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry

As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Pre-order your copy on Bookshop.

item.title: Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: in-depth analysis of historical and cultural manipulation

All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

item.title: Batima Zaurbekova’s Textiles Meld Traditional Kazakh Techniques with Modernist Influences, Defying Easy Categorization
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique artist profile with cultural significance

How does an artist sustain five decades of artistic production while remaining faithful to her cultural heritage? For Batima Zaurbekova, one of Kazakhstan’s most respected artists, the answer seems to be an unrelenting commitment to her craft. “You can’t be lazy,” the 80-year-old artist told me during a recent conversation.

That maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Her largest exhibition to date, it features the textiles she is known for as well as drawings and paintings. Curated by Alina Fedorovich, a curator at the Museum of Moscow, the exhibition traces a career in which tapestry becomes both a repository of cultural memory and a vehicle for artistic reinvention.

Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization. Her tapestries hold seemingly disparate influences, transforming traditional motifs into a distinct visual language. Ornamental Rug (1969), for example, revives motifs associated with horses, spiritual symbolism, and petroglyphs depicting mountain goats. Completed just after her graduation and the earliest work in the exhibition, Ornamental Rug provides a recognizable reference to the country’s landscape via the distinctive horns of the wild argali, a local mountain goat, while distilling these forms into rhythmic, stylized arrangements. The work’s title foregrounds the relationship between ornament and abstraction, suggesting how decorative forms can become a vehicle for modernist experimentation.

Zaurbekova grew up in the mountainous Zhambyl region of Kazakhstan, where textile-making was part of everyday life. She remembers watching older women create syrmak, traditional felt rugs, and kurak-korpe, patchwork quilts meaning “stitched from scraps.” Neighbors gathered to work, sing, cook, and share food, embodying the Kazakh tradition of asar, in which a community joins forces to help a household undertake a task, be it making a carpet or building a home.

Textile-making was as much a social practice as a technical one, transmitting skills and cultural knowledge across generations. This collective spirit is evoked in In the Yurt (1985), a weaving in which a maternal figure presides over the dastarkhan, the table prepared for guests. The yurt, a traditional felt dwelling associated with Kazakh nomadic life, becomes a symbol of hospitality, family, and belonging. Its ornaments merge with the surrounding figures, establishing a visual language equally rooted in the formal and the domestic.

In her youth, Zaurbekova had alternative ambitions for herself. “I really loved music, so I wanted to become a musician,” she recalled. However, her seamstress mother encouraged her to pursue painting instead. She is equally accomplished in oil painting and tapestry, and occasionally the same image is translated in both mediums.

Nevertheless, music has remained central to Zaurbekova’s life and practice, in which her visual compositions are animated by repetition, variation, and rhythm—the basic structure of music. This way of working is best observed in one gallery showing three works, each titled Composition and made in 1980, 2019, and 2024. Their stained-glass aesthetic, contrasting color planes, and rhythmic linear forms evoke Henri Matisse’s celebrated “Jazz” series. Undulating figures and vegetal motifs merge within an ornamental field, dissolving the distinction between figure and ground.

“Threads of Heritage” is being exhibited in dialogue with the museum’s collection of Kazakh decorative and applied art. Traditional felt objects, carpets, and ornaments establish the historical context out which Zaurbekova’s work emerges, while the installation reinforces the relationship between inherited forms and contemporary expression. Here, custom-built walls reference the architecture of the Khoja Ahmed Yasawi Mausoleum, an important historical monument whose forms recur in the artist’s imagery, like the monumental Antiquity (1993). The display also evokes the balbal, ancient stone monuments that connect contemporary life with earlier cultures.

The exhibition’s largest gallery showcases Zaurbekova’s technical mastery and evolving visual language. Each tapestry offers a dazzling array of color that boggles the mind. How, exactly, does she coax such subtle gradations from a seemingly limited collection of threads? “Selecting the right colors is a big part of the work—and it takes me a long time,” Zaurbekova explained. During the Soviet period, artists often dyed threads by hand, painstakingly creating transitions from darker to lighter shades. Although commercially produced threads from Belarus expanded her palette in the 1990s, Zaurbekova has continued to experiment, combining those threads and ones she has dyed to create colors all her own. “Kazakhstan, our land, is very rich, and this is represented in the rich colors of my work,” she told me.

Zaurbekova’s textiles are woven over several weeks to multiple months, and the artist still works for up to 18 hours a day. The vertical threads form the foundation of a given work, she explained, while horizontal threads of different colors construct the image. Through subtle variations in their combinations, Zaurbekova achieves tonal effects that can make woven surfaces appear almost painted. She is also deft at making alasha, a traditional yet simple Kazakh carpet.…

item.title: Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale, Report Details Limited Damage to Bayeux Tapestry Following Transport to the British Museum, and More: Morning Links for November 27, 2026
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: news aggregation with a mix of interesting topics

Good Morning!

- Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale.

- In a report, France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum.

- A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for $1.97 million.

The Headlines

THE PRINCESS AND THE VENICE BIENNALE. Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s largest recurring art exhibition, which runs from April 8 to November 26, 2028, ARTnews reports. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority. She will be the first Arab curator of the Venice Biennale, and was selected upon the recommendation of its president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. In a statement, Al Qasimi said: “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to President Pietrangelo Buttafuoco and the board for their confidence and trust.”

DAMAGE REPORT. A report made public yesterday by France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, Le Figaro reports. While the overall state of the 950-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened before the voyage. The loan of the fragile tapestry was heavily criticized for risking damage to the artifact, but was ultimately made possible in part thanks to carefully controlled ground transport that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations. The artifact has since become the hottest museum show in London, attracting long lines and selling out tickets within minutes.

The Digest

A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for £1.5 million ($1.97 million), and it is among several rediscovered paintings in an exhibition titled Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, open until December 18. [The Art Newspaper]

Two illuminated manuscripts and three crosses from the 15th century were returned from the American collection of Robert McCarthy to Ethiopia, as part of a unique new partnership between the Ethiopian Heritage Authority (EHA), the Toledo Museum of Art (TMA) and McCarthy. [The Voice]

Veruschka, the German supermodel, who became an iconic muse to the fashion, arts and cultural world of the 1960s and 70s, has died at 87. [WWD]

Neil Simmons, a sculptor whose famous marble piece depicting Margaret Thatcher was decapitated by a protester, has died at 73. [The Times of London]

A rare “Breast Bowl,” or “jatte-téton,” that belonged to French Queen Marie Antoinette and was used in her royal “pleasure dairy,” hammered in Paris for $3.23 million with fees, beating its high estimate of $2.19 million. [ARTnews]

The Princess of Wales, spent time at the Hugo Burge Foundation in Berwickshire, which supports the arts in the UK, and she spoke about the healing qualities of art-making with painter Siobhan McLaughlin, who makes her own pigment and works with stone and earth. [Times of London]

The Kicker

KANALIZING. On Saturday, Kanal or Kanal-Centre Pompidou, Brussels’ nearly 10-acre “city-museum,” opens to the public, heralding the Belgian capital’s first major modern and contemporary art museum organized in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou. As ARTnews reported in September, the mega-project of free and ticketed spaces has been met with controversy over the course of its decade in the making, notably because of ongoing uncertainty about its financial survival, its cost, as well as its dependence on the Pompidou in Paris. Unless there is a political turnabout, Kanal’s publicly funded budget allocated by the Brussels-Capital Region is expected to drop from its current €28 million to €10 million by 2029, which is not enough to keep the project running, according to its leaders. This week, at a large press conference attended by ARTnews, Boris Dilliès, the minister-president of the Brussels region, was on the defensive about the initiative, he said he has faith, while admitting to heavy criticism. The story of Kanal’s rocky road to becoming reality has been widely reported in stories pegged to this week’s opening, but few have offered their thoughts on the 10 exhibitions debuting with it, and what it’s like to wander the vast halls of this new cultural phenomenon. ARTnews stayed on to more fully experience the myriad of shows open to previewing guests, which, over the course of two days, included artists and about 5,000 local schoolchildren. Watch this space to hear our take on Europe’s latest, highly ambitious cultural endeavor, including where it already shines, and where there is room – literally, a whole lot of space – for much more still to come.

item.title: German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: innovative approach to museum engagement

We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this month and running through February 21, 2027, the Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf, Germany, has set up weight machines, mats, treadmills, ellipticals, and all manner of gym equipment in its permanent exhibition galleries, so that visitors can work out beside the historic and contemporary artworks, reported the Times of London. Whether or not participants are able to take in the art hanging in front of them while bench pressing, is anyone’s guess, but the idea has its fans, some of whom show up to the museum appropriately dressed in workout clothes.

What artworks do these health-conscious visitors get to enjoy while sweating away? The program titled “Gym. Fit with Art” unfolds across 20 stations beside the museum’s collection of over 800 works, which span pieces by Peter Paul Rubens to Gerhard Richter. It was conceived as a tribute marking the centenary of the GeSoLei, which was the largest trade fair held during the Weimar Republic, which was also dedicated to health.

“We want to target people who might prefer going to the gym rather than a museum on weekends,” and this particularly includes younger audiences, said Alina Fuchte, who has led the project. To wit, “the museum is transforming its collection into an extraordinary fitness circuit,” states the museum website. “Instead of just strolling from painting to painting and admiring the art, visitors will soon be able to get active,” it adds. The endeavor is sponsored by TARGOBANK in cooperation with Technogym, which makes fitness equipment, according to the website.

“Anyone who would rather simply take in the art is equally welcome,” continues the website. This, however, begs the question of whether that simple act may be tough to do while standing beside someone jogging on a treadmill in front of large busts of Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, and his wife, Anna Maria Luisa de’Medici, per just a few examples of the works on view.

One visitor, Kai Heimes, 25, tells the Times of London, “It’s cool to work out in the collection,” and if it feels “awkward” for some, “I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he added.

However, another, Moritz Rossmanith, 40, admitted to being “a bit confused by it all.” Rossmanith was visiting from Rome, and thought it was “very strange to see kids holding thick barbells while there’s old Italian art on the wall.” Children are reportedly the biggest fans of the gym gear.

As for bringing water bottles to the museum-gym, given that many other museums sternly scold visitors for taking covert sips of water inside art galleries, that rule doesn’t seem to apply here.

“Coming here and realizing this is also a space for me, I can feel comfortable here, I can be free here, I can try new things—that, for me, is the first step,” said Fuchte.

Did we mention there is also a range of scheduled fitness classes at the museum? You can sign up here.

item.title: Final Report Details Minor, But Visible Damage to the Bayeux Tapestry Following Trip to the British Museum
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: technical report on the condition of a historical artifact

A final report released by France’s ministry of culture yesterday details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained some minor damage following its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, reports Le Figaro.

While the overall state of the nearly 1000-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, who co-authored the report, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened, prior to the voyage. News of an initial condition report about the tapestry showing some damage made headlines in September, but this is the first time a final copy has been seen by the media.

ARTnews has reached out to France’s Ministry of Culture for a copy of the report, which was not shared via press release or posted on its website, as is customary with public announcements.

In other details, translated from the French news story, experts reportedly observed that “a red wool thread in an embroidered area and another from the linen background cloth have undergone a slight progression.” Additionally, they spotted “slight folds and pockets,” as well as areas of tension in the embroidery and its linen support. For the latter, the tapestry’s horizontal display, in contrast with its previous vertical hang, should help fix the stretching issue. The report also warns of areas to watch closely, particularly on the tapestry’s return trip to France in July 2027. These include several more pronounced folds, areas of wear, and a broken thread.

The authors, who conducted their report in July and August, added that it’s not possible to know precisely when the changes occurred within the time span of the tapestry’s transfer from Bayeux to its current display in London. Additionally, they noted that this last check, including additional, highly detailed photographs of the artifact, is the most complete review of the tapestry to date. It was compared with two less thorough assessments made in 2020 and 2025.

“We now know the condition of the tapestry as never before, which will be useful later on,” said Delphine Christophe, general director of heritage in France, speaking to Le Figaro. She added that the overall assessment, despite the noted damage, proved “exceptional,” given the fragile tapestry’s roughly 230-foot length and 20-inch height.

The loan of the tapestry was heavily criticized in the months leading up to the handoff, due to risks of harming it. But after three failed attempts to secure a loan, it was ultimately made possible thanks to a carefully controlled ground transportation plan that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations, aided by the political will of French President Emmanuel Macron. The latter was intent on making a strong diplomatic statement of friendship with the UK. In exchange, France will receive the Sutton Hoo archaeological ship burial and the Lewis Chessmen set from the British Museum. However, as Le Monde’s Roxana Azimi pointed out, “the Sutton Hoo treasure does not resonate at all with the French public,” and the French people “are getting objects that are certainly valuable, but not very impressive.”

As for the Bayeux Tapestry, it is believed to have been made in Canterbury following the coronation of William the Conqueror as king of England in 1066. It tells his side of the Norman Conquest, which was one of the most pivotal moments in English history. Meanwhile, British Museum director Nicolas Cullinan responded frankly to Azimi’s point in Le Monde. “Yes,” he said. “It’s very hard to beat the Bayeux Tapestry.”

Why it is here: news about an artist's design for an award

Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy. The trophy has previously been designed by the likes of Damien Hirst, Zaha Hadid, Es Devlin and Anish Kapoor.

The trophy will be bestowed upon musicians nominated for the prestigious award ceremony taking place on February 27, 2027. Each trophy takes inspiration from the image of Britannia, a tall, elegant female figure that personifies Britain. For her design, Whiteread has inverted the statue, exposing its silver lining with punched holes throughout. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music,” said the artist in a statement. “I accepted the invitation to design next year’s Brit Award trophy, as I saw this as a natural extension of my work—to continue to celebrate and recognize British art and creativity, and to have an opportunity to apply my own perspective within such an iconic British cultural institution.”

Whiteread said she also agreed to design the statue in an effort to safeguard arts and culture, which she described as being “under very real threat.” “The Brits have celebrated musical creativity and artistry for decades now. We have some fantastically creative musicians who have produced music that lays their souls bare, provides hope in times of darkness, or speaks directly about a moment in time,” she added.

In designing the trophy, Whiteread joins a prestigious list of other artists who have given the statue new life: Dame Peter Blake, Tracey Emin, Vivienne Westwood and Yinka Ilori. In 1997, Whiteread became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale, and in 2001, she became the third artist to have her work placed on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square, which took the form of an inverted resin recreation of the plinth.

item.title: Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism “Abstraction with a Hard-On”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: artist interview with some technical jargon

I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.

“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie, the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade.

The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.

Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin.

Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I quickly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this?”

Representing Camp 2 are John Yau (The Brooklyn Rail, 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he said, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”

Dunham walked me to the “other studio,” a smaller room reserved for painting, where acrylic tubes lay neatly on a table in gradients, labels down. A canvas he had just finishedstood on sawhorses. It showed a man with long black hair down on all fours in a sculpture studio. The painting is called Looking for Something, and its protagonist’s pants are on the floor. His skin is white, and a woman, who is purple, kneels behind him, her head thrown back in a wail or moan. With her hand, she does something to the man’s ass that is not visible to us. In the foreground, another purple person, a Peeping Tom, watches them through a window. Nine of these most recent “Sculptor” paintings, from about Covid to now, were to go up at the Matthew Brown gallery in Manhattan in September as a sort of appetizer for the Miami show.

I asked where these recent purple/white folks come from. “They come from my work,” Dunham explained. “And I don’t mean that to be glib. They really do. So to even answer that question, I would have to go, ‘Before I was doing these paintings, I was doing these paintings, then these paintings,’” he continued, miming with his hands successive leaps into the past.

BORN THE FIFTH IN A line of Carrolls to a Connecticut poultry farmer who turned to real estate, Dunham went to Phillips Academy (Andover), class of 1967. The sculptor Mel Kendrick was his roommate. “Tip was doing Rapidograph drawings,” Kendrick recalled as we spoke by phone, using Dunham’s nickname. “Almost hippie drawings, very fine sketches.” (Of “Tip,” Dunham said, “It’s a WASP thing.”) Kendrick also recalls Dunham’s appetite for science fiction. (Face-down on his studio table, I spotted James L. Cambias’s Darkling Sea.) Dunham took darkroom classes. In the school’s literary magazine, his finely exposed photograph of a pouting and rotund lady in a playground swing illustrates a poem by Anthony Grafton, the historian-to-be. “Anything he did, he always had a touch,” Kendrick said. “Tip is very specific. And that’s something I don’t know if people know about his paintings, even now.”…

item.title: Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear, well-structured English with original reporting and concrete detail.

Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil

Brazilian firm Estúdio 41 has completed Guaratuba House, which features exterior screens and a structural system that “explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete“.

Located in the seaside community of Prainha, which sits within the city of Guaratuba in southern Brazil, the holiday home was designed for a family to serve as “a refuge between the mountains and the sea”.

“One of their main requirements was, therefore, a strong visual connection between the interior spaces and the surrounding natural landscape,” said Estúdio 41, an architectural firm based in Curitiba.

Rectangular in plan, the 375-square-metre house has two floors. It is wrapped in folding screens made of perforated melamine panels.

The screens filter natural light and reduce solar gain on glass surfaces. When opened up, they reveal views of the scenic landscape.

“At night, the transparency and geometric patterns of the house’s skin give it the appearance of a lantern within the landscape,” the team said.

To protect against flooding, as the coastal site has been affected by storm surges in the past, the building was lifted up 70 centimeters (2.3 feet).

It has a prefabricated concrete structural system that was assembled in only six hours, with the concrete structural elements left visible.

The system consists of six columns, four beams and 20 double-tee slabs, also known as “π” (pi)-shaped slabs. The latter are pre-stressed concrete panels with a cross-section that resembles the Greek letter π.

“The project explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete,” said the team.

“The conception of a very simple and easily executable construction system reflects a concern for the realities of the local workforce,” it contniued.

“The construction technique, the modular arrangement of the structural components, and the ribs of the double-tee floor slabs are all clearly legible.”

Rooms feature artful decor and a neutral colour palette. The ground level contains an open-plan kitchen, dining area and living room, along with service areas and a guest bedroom.

The communal area opens toward a garden, and beyond it, a sheltered barbecue terrace and a swimming pool.

“The social areas were conceived as one large veranda in direct contact with the beach sand, with views of both the sea and mountains,” the team said.

The upper level contains four bedrooms, including the primary suite, and a family room. A bridge passes over the garden below and connects to a concrete terrace with sweeping views of the sea.

Other projects by Estudio 41 include a small white house in Brazil with a roof garden, and a prefabricated, teal-coloured research station in Antarctica.

Project credits:

Architecture: Estúdio 41

Structural engineering: Da Rocha Engenharia, Greco Engenharia

Foundation engineering: Da Rocha Engenharia, Greco Engenharia

Electrical engineering, plumbing, air conditioning: PD Engenharia

Brise-soleil: Favegroup, Lamitech

Concrete: Da Rocha Engenharia, Greco Engenharia

Texas reveals proposal for US Space Academy in Houston

The Texas Space Commission has published a proposal for the newly created United States Space Academy. It would be located in Houston on a site alongside NASA‘s Johnson Space Center, which was formerly home to Mission Control.

Revealed earlier this week, the proposals show clusters of buildings arranged in a flower-like shape, with petals surrounded by water. The renders place the facility on a currently vacant site alongside the NASA facility.

The proposal was created as a response to a request for information from the American space agency, which is looking to find a permanent home for the academy.

It follows an executive order issued earlier this year by president Donald Trump that established a presidential commission to determine how the proposed NASA-led institution could be formed.

In the order, he stated that the United States Space Academy would be established with the aim of training the “next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters”.

The proposed academy would contain facilities for academic and more hands-on training.

It has received bipartisan support in Texas, with Republican senator Ted Cruz and Democrat senator-elect James Talarico issuing a joint statement in support of the bid.

“Texas has maintained a leading role in America’s human spaceflight program for decades, from training astronauts to directing missions at Johnson Space Center,” said the pair in the statement.

“The Lone Star State has developed an extensive space industry, infrastructure, and expertise. Texas is best suited to train the next generation of American space leaders and is the natural home for the U.S. Space Academy.”

According to the Texas Space Commission, the scheme was designed to align with NASA’s proposed timeline, which envisions groundbreaking commencing next year.

NASA recently announced plans for a permanent moon base, with a multi-phased plan culminating in “semi-permanent habitation models”.

Photography courtesy of Texas Space Commission

item.title: Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear description of a unique architectural project with useful vocabulary.

Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone

Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro.

Named Casa Los Cobos, the home is located in Xangri-Lá on Brazil’s southern coast, and was designed to make the most of panoramic views out over the sea from the rear of the site.

Set back from the road, a series of routes both through and around the home “reveal the landscape gradually,” including a path beneath a timber canopy and via a paved veranda screened by lush plants.

“The main opportunity was the merging of two adjoining lots into a single site that extends to the rear, where the landscape opens onto the water,” Ambidestro co-founder João Pedro Crescente told Dezeen.

The ground floor of Casa Los Cobos has been given over almost entirely to a single large living, dining and kitchen space, wrapped by service spaces and bathrooms.

Full-height sliding glass doors allow this space to be opened out onto a large sheltered terrace alongside a swimming pool, with a lawn that slopes down to a nearby waterway.

“The ground floor is free of partitions: living, dining and the entertaining kitchen are integrated and turned toward the greenery, accommodating everything from a weeknight dinner to a Saturday party,” Crescente told Dezeen.

“Between the living room and the water lie, in sequence, the veranda, the garden and the pool, which wraps around the house. The eye passes through these layers before reaching the backdrop,” he added.

Both the exterior and interior have been given contrasting finishes of rough Morelo stone and white plaster and paint, with the rear terrace framed by white-painted masonry.

This is complemented internally with bespoke carpentry in pale oak, including a floating timber bar supported by a concrete column that defines one edge of the living space.

“The intention was to use natural, local materials in light, warm tones repeated inside and out, making the transition between spaces almost imperceptible,” said Crescente.

“Moledo stone clads the facades and changes in appearance from morning to late afternoon. Other natural stones continue onto the floors and wet areas,” he added.

A skylit staircase leads up to the more compartmentalised first floor of the home, which contains six en-suite bedrooms, two of which open onto a balcony overlooking the sea.

To provide both shading and privacy from the road, sliding timber shutters can be pulled down over the full-height bedroom windows.

Other homes in Brazil recently featured on Dezeen include a home in São Paolo by Studio Arthur Casas featuring dramatic overhangs and cantilevers, and a low-lying dwelling by Sabella Arquitetura that is topped by a gridded timber roof.

Photography by Gabriel Konrath

item.title: Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging profile of an influential designer with useful vocabulary and context.

Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler’s pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

Next up in Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.

Goti has experienced a remarkable rise since presenting a furniture collection made from salvaged foam insulation during the 2023 edition of Milan design week.

Her conceptual, research-led work typically explores heritage, identity and craftsmanship, resulting in playful objects and spaces that reexamine the cultural codes embedded in design.

Goti was nominated as an emerging talent to watch by American designer Wearstler, who praised how Goti “approaches ornament with the precision of an engineer and the instincts of a sculptor”.

“That refusal to treat craft and technology as opposites is going to matter more over the next 20 years,” Wearstler added.

As well as a shared love of ornament and the decorative arts, Wearstler also picked up on how Goti’s practice is informed by her background in robotics and machine learning.

“It’s amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail,” Goti told Dezeen.

It’s amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail

Goti added that she was pleased to be recognised by a leading female designer, as her creative muses are mostly women and femininity plays a major role in her own practice.

“My work is very personal so of course there are a lot of references to being a woman,” she said, adding that she draws inspiration from well-known artists and designers such as Louise Bourgeois and Faye Toogood.

Goti spoke to Dezeen from Paris, where she currently lives with her partner, French filmmaker Vincent Staropoli, having recently relocated there from New York.

She was raised in Thessaloniki and received a diploma in architecture from the local AUTh university before completing a masters degree in Integrative Technologies and Architectural Design Research at Stuttgart’s Institute of Computational Design.

The move to New York came after accepting a research position at Pratt Institute, but during the Covid pandemic Goti realised that she missed making her own work, so began experimenting with found materials.

“I really didn’t know what I wanted to do,” she recalled. “But through my research at the university and the New York design community I realised there were other people working in a similar way, which encouraged me to stick with it.”

The initial collection was followed by projects made with glass, marble and, most recently, a series of furniture pieces featuring lacquered wooden surfaces that contrast with bell-like aluminium elements.

The outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’

Goti explained that her work usually starts with research into a specific technique or a material that interests her, before she then applies her findings to the design of an object.

She said she finds this approach creatively fulfilling as it offers endless opportunities, though as someone early in her career it means there is no identifiable style associated with her work.

“I don’t usually have a form or a shape in mind when I start,” she said. “So the outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’.”

“In the long term I hope people will recognise my work because of its research-led approach,” she continued. “We need to take more time to understand other artists’ work and not judge everything based on a few images on social media.”

Decoration and ornamentation are recurring elements within Goti’s oeuvre, although she doesn’t want to be labelled as a maximalist.

“My work is sometimes very ornamental and sometimes it’s more minimal,” she added. “So there’s a gradient and the outcome is really determined by the process.”

Like many contemporary designers, Goti does not produce all of her own work, instead utilising a network of expert artisans to help bring her whimsical and deeply personal creations to life.

“I’m a very collaborative person and I think we can create better outcomes when we put our minds together with other people,” she said.

“My architecture background really helped me develop this collaborative mindset and I think one of the key things you learn as you get older is to be selective about who you work with.”

I’m a very collaborative person and I think we can create better outcomes when we put our minds together with other people

The collection she developed with Marble Sachanas (top) exemplifies this collaborative approach, applying Goti’s visionary and playful style to an ancient material sourced from a quarry close to her home town.

Goti met the company’s representatives during 2025’s Milan design week and struck up a conversation that led to them returning this year to exhibit the outcomes as part of the Alcova event.

Projects such as the marble pieces and the furniture she developed for Mexican gallery Toro Manifesto fall into the category of collectible design, which Goti pointed out is a consequence of their artisanal production rather than a conscious decision to make high-end, limited-edition objects.

“Everything nowadays is so expensive to make,” she explained. “If you want to make something that’s well-crafted you have to pay for the materials, the shipping, the labour and that causes the price to be high – it’s not the designer’s fault.”

The armchair, coffee table and sideboard were shown at the Collectible design fair in New York, but Goti said she would also be interested in working on designs that could be licensed and produced by a brand.…

item.title: Hawkins\Brown's temporary housing for homeless families in London is a UK first
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed explanation of a significant architectural project with useful vocabulary.

Hawkins\Brown’s temporary housing for homeless families in London is a UK first

Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London, the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK.

Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.

Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.

Intending to set a benchmark for temporary family housing in the UK, Hawkins\Brown aimed to create a welcoming building that eases the stress of families facing homelessness.

“Many of the families who come here are fleeing hugely painful domestic situations,” said Hawkins\Brown partner Nick Gaskell.

“The Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre aims to make a traumatic period a little more bearable by providing a caring, calming and uplifting environment for as long as they need it.”

Designed to be in keeping with the neighbouring buildings, the exterior of the U-shaped building is lined with striped bands of orange-toned bricks and pops of pale green metal sheeting.

A secure, landscaped courtyard with play space at the centre of the building helps bring natural light into the surrounding flats.

Inside, the apartments were designed to offer higher-quality living arrangements than typical temporary housing, with tall windows, underfloor heating and open-plan kitchen, living and dining rooms.

Community and family support spaces on the ground floor of the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre include a reception, visitor breakout areas, children’s indoor play spaces, communal laundries and staff facilities.

Based on the studio’s research into dementia-friendly design, Hawkins\Brown used colour zoning, visual landmarks, accessible graphics and high-contrast colours in the centre, aiming to make the space easy to navigate for residents and visitors of all ages and abilities.

Elsewhere in London, architecture studio HTA Design recently unveiled what it says is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

In Ukraine, architecture studio Office for Future is working on plans to transform a school into temporary housing for families affected by the war in the country.

Photography by Fred Howarth
