item.title: The energy of thought
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, thought-provoking analysis, and cultural relevance

Listen to this essay

20 minute listen

Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.

So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.

A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.…

Source: Aeon | Published: 2026-11-27 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Fairuz in the morning and Umm Kulthum at night
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, personal narrative, and cultural insight

Chatter floats around me and smoke rises from the bonfire. It is a warm August night in the Philadelphia suburbs, and one of my friends slowly taps the darbuka under his arm. Then he sings Umm Kulthum’s ‘Alf Leila Wa Leila’ (‘A Thousand and One Nights’). One after another, we join in, singing along to what I once considered the epitome of old people’s music:

My love, my love,

The night and its sky, its stars and its moon, its moon and its awakening,

and you and me, my own love, my own life.

The next line comes to me instinctively. I’m singing in ecstasy, as my parents used to on our night rides. I laugh to myself as I watch my friends sway in their seats.

I’m back at my grandparents’ house in the Palestinian town of Beit Sahour. After playing in their yard until sunset, my cousins and I would gather on their bed, where Teta would turn down Umm Kulthum on the television to tell us the story of the Elderly Woman and her Cow while slicing apples. Now and then, I’d glance at the flickering black-and-white screen to see the audience clap, sway and cry out in a state of tarab, surrendering to what they called ‘her grandeur’. She would finish a stanza, and the audience would erupt in applause, calling out Azama ala azama, ya Sit! (‘Greatness upon greatness, oh lady!’), waiting for her to sing again.

They were out of their minds, I thought. Why such reverence for an Egyptian woman with dark sunglasses, a silk handkerchief draped over her hand, standing on a stage for hours accompanied by a full orchestra, repeating almost the same lyrics relentlessly?

Morning came and so did Fairuz. I woke up to my grandfather’s voice calling me. Eyes half-open, I put on my school uniform and ran down the stairs to my grandparents’ house, the scent of Arabic coffee rising from the stove. My Teta was in the backyard. She embraced me with her flour-dusted hands, then continued kneading the dough, humming along with the voice on the radio:

I write your name, my love, on the old poplar trees.

You write my name on the sand of the road.

Tomorrow winter will come on wounded stories,

your name shall remain, and my name shall be erased.

Fairuz, again. I expressed my dismay at the music choice, only to hear Teta’s monologue on the renowned Lebanese vocalist, the great ‘Bird of the East’, and the horrific possibility of a morning without her songs. I sighed and accepted my fate. I rolled my eyes and tapped my foot, taking a bite of Teta’s bread and waiting to be saved by my ride to school.

Naively, I had forgotten that my suffering would not end. It felt like an epidemic when Fairuz’s voice trailed from Teta’s radio to Amo Essam’s van. Oblivious to my frustration, with a cigarette between his teeth, he would sing along:

The people have asked me about you, my darling.

They’ve written letters and the wind took them.

It’s not easy for me to sing, my darling,

when for the first time, we are not together.

We left Beit Sahour when I was 15 for a ‘better life’, my father said – one where his kids’ futures would not be restricted by political turmoil and economic instability, but filled with security, opportunity and dignity that presumably awaited us in the West. So, in the summer of 2017, we packed our bags, gathering whatever crumbs of our life in Beit Sahour we could carry, and headed for the United States.

Philadelphia was beautiful – tall buildings and ancient architecture, enormous roads, and cheesesteak shops around every other corner. As we explored the suburbs for a place to settle, we drove past rows of identical houses with gable roofs, vast stretches of lawn and fast-food chains. Walmart was a sensational experience. It was our family’s picnic destination for the first few weekends in the US. I couldn’t believe there was a store with gardening tools, clothes, groceries and toys, all under one roof. There seemed to be infinite choices for everything – milk, bread and even eggs: cage-free, organic, conventional, and free-range. I had no clue what any of it meant. It was just eggs.

The mornings were quiet. I started eating a blueberry muffin on my way to school. I sat alone on the bus, where the speakers blasted country music. I had nothing to say to the bus driver. I searched for an English equivalent of Ya’tik Al Afiye. But my tongue was tied, and I settled for ‘Thank you.’

My ears searched for Arabic across campus. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me

Amid the white American student body, my frizzy hair, bushy brows and distinctive nose made me conspicuous. Although students invited me to join their table, I sometimes chose to eat lunch alone, especially when I had a za’tar mankoushe – flatbread with dried crushed thyme and olive oil. I dreaded explaining that, no, I was not having marijuana for lunch.

I was not necessarily left out – kids liked to sit with me and ask me about my life in Palestine – but I always felt like an exotic creature among them. I couldn’t follow their conversations and cultural references. Listening to Taylor Swift, watching American TV or wearing flannels with miniskirts never quite made me feel that I belonged. Back with my family, I would exhale a long breath of Arabic phrases, exhausted from a seven-hour shift of imitating an American accent.

In college, I gravitated toward Arabs wherever I found them – and I was determined to find them. My ears searched for Arabic across campus, and when I detected it, I was filled with such giddiness that I ran to introduce myself. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me. For the first time in my life, my closest friends were Jordanian, Lebanese, Syrian and Egyptian. We ate za’tar mankoushe together, argued over who made the best shawarma, laughed at the differences between our accents and traded stories about our homelands.…

Source: Psyche | Published: 2026-11-27 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: What happened to King Harold's children after the battle of Hastings?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, historical context, and cultural significance

What happened to King Harold's children after the battle of Hastings?

William the Conqueror had conquered and launched a new era in England under the Normans, but he had to keep an eye on the heirs of his fallen foe

The battle of Hastings was over: from the bloody fighting on 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, emerged as King of England while Harold Godwinson, after less than a year on the throne, was dead.

The Norman Conquest had begun, yet the family of the fallen king still posed a threat to William the Conqueror. Yes, three of Harold’s brothers also died that same year: Tostig had allied with Harald Hardrada and been killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge, while Gyrth and Leofwine perished alongside Harold at Hastings.

But in the early years of William’s reign Harold’s mother Gytha became a figurehead of rebellion in Exeter, and there were concerns that his seven children may one day seek to restore their line.

Who were Harold Godwinson’s children?

Harold Godwinson had five sons and two daughters. With his first wife, Edith Swanneck, he had three boys, Godwin, Edmund and Magnus, and two girls, Gunhild and Gytha. He had two more boys, Harold and Ulf, possibly with his second wife, Ealdgyth, although the lack of historical records means there remains confusion over who gave birth to Ulf.

What happened to Harold’s wives?

Details are scant, but it seems that Edith Swanneck – also called Edith the Fair or the Handfasted Queen as she may have been unofficially married to Harold – survived the immediate aftermath of the battle of Hastings. According to legend, it was she who identified Harold’s body on the battlefield.

Ealdgyth, or Edith of Mercia, was married to Harold in early 1066 as part of a political alliance. After Hastings, her brothers, the earls of Mercia and Northumberland, took her to Chester for safety. It was possibly there that she gave birth to Ulf.

What happened to Harold’s sons?

The eldest sons, Godwin and Edmund, were teenagers in 1066 and fled to Ireland, where they lived under the protection of Diarmait, King of Leinster. Twice, they launched a campaign to western England in the hopes of overthrowing the Norman regime.

In 1068, leading a force of Dublin Norse mercenaries, they failed in their initial aim of seizing Bristol before losing a decisive battle in Somerset. They found no support from their father’s former allies, who had made peace with William. The following years, they returned with a fleet of ships and headed for Exeter, but again failed.

Instead, Godwin and Edmund raided parts of Devon and Cornwall, then, with no hopes of success, they fled again, this time to the court of their relative, Sweyn II of Denmark.

It is possible that their younger brother Magnus accompanied them, but only clues remain in the historical sources. He may have died during Godwin and Edmund’s doomed campaigns, or became a monk in Sussex or a count in modern-day Poland.

Accounts suggest that Harold (junior) found his way to the court of Olaf III of Norway, the son of Harald Hardrada. Despite Harold Godwinson defeating and killing Hardrada, he spared Olaf’s life at Stamford Bridge, so Olaf welcomed the young Harold into his service. It appears that he participated in expeditions to the Orkneys, Hebrides, Isle of Man and Anglesey.

Ulf, however, had been immediately captured after Hastings and was imprisoned in Normandy until William’s death in 1087. By then, any thoughts of opposition had been stamped out: in fact, he became a knight of the new Duke of Normandy.

- Read more | How well did Harold Godwinson and William the Conqueror know each other prior to the battle of Hastings?

What happened to Harold’s daughters?

Gunhild was at a nunnery at Wilton Abbey in 1066 and remained in England. She married one of William’s inner circle, Alan the Red, possibly a strategic alliance to help Alan secure his lands, which had belonged to Gunhild’s mother. When he died shortly afterwards, she ended up with his brother, Alan the Black.

Gytha, meanwhile, escaped to Denmark and married Vladimir II Monomakh, ruler of Smolensk and Chernigov and the future Grand Prince of Kiev. They had several children together, with one of them becoming known as Harald; a small way of honouring Gytha’s father, since reclaiming the English crown was out of reach.

Authors

Jonny Wilkes is a former staff writer for BBC History Revealed, and he continues to write for both the magazine and HistoryExtra. He has BA in History from the University of York.

item.title: Listen to the Music of the Ancient World: From 40,000-Year-Old Flutes to Ancient Greek Songs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit its ruins. But nothing gets us quite as close to entering the consciousness of our distant forebears as hearing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In the new Archaeologist’s Notebook video above, Giselle Király gives us a tour through ancient musical history, explaining the instruments of those times that survive in one form or another today. That tour begins at a much earlier point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punctuating their struggle for survival with organized sound.

As evidence, Király points to the “tiny, exquisitely crafted flutes carved from animal bone and mammoth ivory” discovered on cave floors around Europe. Surprisingly, when played in replica form, these vulture- or swan-bone flutes actually sound somewhat Middle Eastern. But whatever the stylistic traits of the music their original players produced, that music had the potential to confer benefits beyond immediate pleasure: “It would’ve connected people, built cohesion within the community,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the living with some spiritual world.” Each of the other discovered or reconstructed instruments, like swingable “bullroarers,” bone rasps, and lithophones (of the kind previously featured here on Open Culture) would have played its own sonic part to that end.

Király also discusses the lavishly decorated Lyres of Ur, the world’s oldest surviving stringed instruments; a 3,500-year-old Egyptian long-necked lute with a guitar-like fingerboard; and a set of 65 Chinese bianzhong bells covering a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also important are the means of recording it, an ancient example of which Király cites in the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the oldest known complete musical notation. Centuries later, in the Greek-speaking world — and in the more monumental form of a marble stele — a man named Seikilos recorded an epitaph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this oldest completely preserved, fully playable musical composition exhort the listener: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients needed to hear this no less, perhaps, than we do.

item.title: 'A bit strange' - Leclerc seeking outlier to catch Mercedes in Qatar
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Charles Leclerc seeking outlier as Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull try to catch Mercedes at Qatar Grand Prix

Friday 27 November 2026 20:50, UK

Charles Leclerc believes an “outlier” has given Mercedes a “massive” advantage at the Qatar Grand Prix, after Kimi Antonelli and George Russell dominated Friday’s practice sessions.

Mercedes were nearly half a second quicker than the rest of the field at the Lusail International Circuit as Antonelli topped both sessions from Russell.

Their four-tenths advantage over closest challenger Lando Norris in second practice could have been even greater, with neither Antonelli nor Russell completing a full low-fuel lap on the soft tyres. It was an ominous sign for the rest of the field ahead of Saturday's qualifying, which gets under way at 6pm, with coverage live on Sky Sports F1 from 5.15pm.

- Qatar GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports

- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column

- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺

Mercedes' dominance was similar to their pace advantage earlier in the season but the second half of 2026 has largely been very close between F1's top four teams - Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren.

Ferrari were over one second behind Antonelli on a dismal Friday as Leclerc spun in second practice and Lewis Hamilton suffered an engine problem which brought his Ferrari to a halt.

"Honestly it's been a very difficult day. It's not that we didn't try on the softs, we couldn't improve our lap time on the mediums," said Leclerc.

"I lost the car and had some damage so we had to repair the car but that was the first lap of FP2 and I couldn't improve and even on the new soft later on I couldn't improve.

"A very, very difficult day. The feeling is just very difficult to get right. Not even on high fuel we were strong, so for now, it looks like a very difficult weekend but we are working hard to try and understand something.

"For some reason, Mercedes are so much faster than everybody expected, so the gaps are just a little bit strange, so there's something that's an outlier and we just need to find that."

Ferrari were not expected to be strong at the Lusail International Circuit due to the long flat out zones and high-speed corners but Leclerc suggested his team, along with McLaren and Red Bull were missing a trick that will give them more pace.

"I don't think we know yet what's the outlier. I think other teams probably didn't find that because Mercedes still have a massive advantage," he said.

"We are going to work towards that and analyse the data to understand what's going on."

Norris: Mercedes not even worth thinking about

McLaren were predicted to be very competitive in Qatar due to their strength in the high-speed corners but Norris and Piastri were never close to matching the pace of Mercedes.

On Saturday, McLaren are expected to put the new floor they ran in Las Vegas on the car but Norris does not think it will make a big enouch difference to catch Mercedes who are in "a different category".

"I don't know how much that will help around here compared to Vegas," said last year's world champion.

"But obviously tonight [Friday] we will see how much we can gain from that. It's not going to be the gap we need.

"We are probably seven tenths off the Mercedes a lap so it's not even worth thinking about them. But relative to the rest we seem to be in a good place. The fact we can have the new floor on tomorrow will add a little bit and a little bit is better than nothing. We seem in a relatively decent place."

Both Antonelli and Russell pointed out that Verstappen will always be a threat and the four-time world champion is coy about his chances of challenging the Mercedes in qualifying.

"A bit of a difficult day. The balance of the car is a bit too disconnected at the moment to go fast, so that's what we need to fix," said the Red Bull driver.

"The all-round balance is not there at the moment and is costing us quite a bit of lap time. We will keep trying and see how good we can get it."

"Mercedes look quite far ahead on the short run and long run. Let's see how much we can close the gap."

Update (Friday afternoon): With Iowa’s dominant win over Nebraska, the Hawkeyes are still alive for a spot in the Big Ten Championship Game.

Big Ten Championship Game scenarios and tiebreakers

Six teams have a shot at the Big Ten Championship Game: Here is what each team needs to get in

In addition, Iowa’s win has eliminated both USC and Ohio State from contention.

However, what two teams will play in that game is far from unsettled.

Entering Rivalry Week six — yes six — teams still have a chance to clinch one of the two spots in the Big Ten Championship Game. Those six teams (UCLA, Iowa, Oregon, USC, Ohio State, and Indiana) have much different paths to Indianapolis.

But they each have a path.

Here are the scenarios and tiebreakers you need to know ahead of the weekend.

Big Ten Standings

First, here is how those six teams stack up in the standings:

1. UCLA (10-1 overall, 7-1 in conference)

2. Indiana (9-2 overall, 6-2 in conference)

3. Iowa (9-2 overall, 6-2 in conference)

4. Oregon (8-3 overall, 6-2 in conference)

5. USC (8-3 overall, 5-3 in conference)

6. Ohio State (7-4 overall, 5-3 in conference)

Yes, all six of these teams could get into the title game.

How UCLA clinches a Big Ten berth

UCLA has the easiest path to a spot in the Big Ten Championship Game.

With a win over USC on Saturday afternoon, the Bruins are in.

However, UCLA can back into the Big Ten Championship Game a few different ways:

Got it?

Good, because we are just getting started. And remember, this was the team with the easiest path.

How Oregon clinches a Big Ten berth

- A win against Washington AND an Indiana win against Purdue, OR

We will catch our breath next, moving to the team with the toughest road to Indianapolis.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Phil Taylor says he is quitting competitive darts for good as he and Adrian Lewis are knocked out of MODUS Super Series

Phil Taylor retired from professional darts in 2018; he came out of retirement for this week's MODUS Super Series International Pairs, teaming up with friend Adrian Lewis; the Pair finished second-bottom in group C and were knocked out of the event

Friday 27 November 2026 20:51, UK

Phil Taylor says he is quitting competitive darts for good and has no plans to come out of retirement again.

The 16-time world champion was lured back to the oche for this year's MODUS Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth alongside his long-time friend Adrian Lewis.

The English duo lost all five of their matches on Thursday but rebounded on Friday, winning three and losing two matches, to finish second-bottom in the Group C standings.

- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results, schedule

- Luke Littler faces nightmare route at World Championship

- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract

Taylor, 67, retired from the competitive circuit in 2018, five years after winning his final world crown, and when asked if he would make another comeback, the 14-time PDC World Championship winner told Pluto TV: "[This is] proper retirement."

A heartwarming moment unfolded after Taylor and Lewis were beaten 4-3 in their final group match against Scotland, as each of the other nations arrived to give Taylor a guard of honour, as he walked away from the oche.

"I mean I'm 67, I get my pension next February," Taylor said, when asked if this would be his last competitive appearance. "I'm a pensioner now, officially!"

"I'll still do personal appearances, more having a chat with people, talking about my career, that kind of thing."

Taylor and Lewis, who teamed up to win four World Cup of Darts titles between 2012 and 2016, finished Thursday at the bottom of Group C. Friday started poorly for the Englishmen, losing to Denmark's Ivan Springborg-Poulsen and Andreas Toft Jørgensen 4-2.

Speaking on his retirement U-turn this week, Taylor said: "I was dreading it to be honest with you because I know I wasn't playing like I can do, but now I've been here and it's all over, I've loved it."

The pair hit back on Friday with a 4-3 win against Germany, then beat Switzerland and Sweden, both 4-2.

The Englishmen would tie Scotland at three legs apiece in his final competitive match, before Taylor missed a checkout for 48 for victory, in what would have been a fairy-tale finish.

"Looking back now, it's like it never happened," Taylor said, reflecting on his glittering career.

"I've said to other people who have been on stage and retired: 'How do you feel now?'

"'It's like you've never been there'. It's ever so weird. And you come up on YouTube and you just go: "No, I know. I know I was there, but I can't remember it."

"It's very, very strange because, mentally-wise, you move on. That was your former life and now my life is different."

Instead of flying around the world competing, Taylor says retirement has allowed him to spend more time with his grandchildren.

"I've got 11 grandchildren," Taylor said. "So I spend a lot of time with them now.

"[I do] things I've never done before. Go to bed when I want; I go to bed early. For me, 9pm would be like, I'd be asleep two hours before 9pm, and it's great.

"I love getting up early as well. We can do all the chores. We can go shopping and get everything done, and it isn't even 11am. It's great!

"People say I'm the GOAT [Greatest of All Time]-I'm an old goat now!"

item.title: Campagnolo Super Record X review: Gucci gravel gearing
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Standing on the opposite side of the world, looking in, Campagnolo had seemingly had a rough few years. A lot was riding on the iconic Italian manufacturer’s new groupset lineup, consisting of 1x and 2x variations of Super Record designed to span road and gravel, each with 13 speeds in the back, wireless shifting, and hydraulic braking. Since then, Campagnolo has brought those options down a pricing tier to Record, has earned a decent amount of praise, and has taken on some outside investment.

This review looks at Super Record X (SR X), Campagnolo’s top-tier, partly Italian-made, and eye-wateringly-priced 1x-specific gravel groupset. It’s arguably the only groupset that directly competes with SRAM’s flagship RED XPLR E1, especially given that Shimano doesn’t yet have a top-tier gravel-focused option.

For those keen on a different version of the groupset, Super Record X shares plenty of tech with Campagnolo’s other 13-speed wireless options. The wholly revised shifters are shared across all Wireless 13 groups, and same goes for the brakes. Shift quality, the battery system, and general servicing are all the same, too. And all that stuff is equally applicable to the more affordable Record range.

Before we uncork this European-made groupset review, it’s worth noting that I arrived at testing Campagnolo’s latest flagship offering with scepticism. While it may be brutal to admit, I haven’t been excited to own or recommend Campagnolo components since 11-speed was considered innovative, and even then, I thought they’d made some missteps compared to the legendary 10-speed generation.

Along the way, Campagnolo not only managed to underwhelm me, but they also had products that straight up upset me. There were three generations of problematic EPS (Campagnolo’s earlier electronic shifting) that at times felt like owning a modern Alfa Romeo with the electronics on the fritz. Meanwhile, many liked Campagnolo’s entry into gravel with its Ekar 13-speed mechanical shifting, including some people whose opinions I trusted. I thought I was going crazy for thinking the ergonomics and shift quality were disappointing. So I arrived at this test thinking that if I like this stuff and it works without fault, then I damn better shout about it. So:

This stuff is good!

Highs: A high-end product throughout, where the quality is felt in the shift buttons, aesthetics, and ownership. Comfortable hoods with multiple shift options. 10-48T gear range option likely to find favour with many. Record version feels and functions the same, and is priced directly against GRX Di2 and Force XPLR.

Lows: Thumb lever placed a little too rearward for intuitive thumb levering. Shifter shape not optimised for small hands. A labyrinth of instruction manuals. Spares availability more scarce than the two S’s in many parts of the world. Price is comparatively high in the USA. Brakes feel great, but power lags behind the competition. Shortest crank length is 165 mm.

Price: Complete Super Record X groupset from €3,497 / US$4,475 / AU$5,519. Record X from €2,200 / US$2,678 / AU$3,789.

The basic rundown

Campagnolo may have upset many of its loyalists by deleting the thumb shifter in its first wireless groupset (WRL), but a short two years later, they rectified that with Super Record Wireless 13. That new shifter, shared amongst all new Super Record options, brought back one of Campagnolo’s more unique features, albeit with a modern twist.

This fully revised shifter offers a paddle behind the brake lever, a rethought “thumb” paddle on the inner side of the hood (also reachable with a wrapped-around finger), and a third button on the upper inside of the hood to be configured for shifting or accessory control. The whole hood shape has been reworked, with a flatter rear profile that doesn’t feel out of place against the latest from Shimano or SRAM, while the front section retains a signature hook.

With the introduction of SR X comes a 1x-specific left-only lever option that removes the buttons and electronic guts. This saves 20 grams and some money for those who only want to operate the gears from the right shifter. I opted for the regular left shifter, which gave plenty of options for shifting customisation, including the option to operate it SRAM-style (left hand sends the derailleur one way, right hand goes back the other way).

Wirelessly synced to those shifters are reworked derailleurs. There’s a range of 2x and 1x options, and Super Record X (SR X) has its own 1x-specific version. Where SRAM’s XPLR E1 requires a UDH-compatible frame to fit the unique Full Mount derailleur, Campagnolo has kept it traditional, mounting to whatever derailleur hanger your frame has. That SR X derailleur is reinforced for off-road use and offers a longer cage for pairing with Campagnolo’s 9-42T or 10-48T cassettes. A sprung clutch-type mechanism, the same as Ekar, provides increased chain control (although, as I’ll get to, not as much as others).

Powering the derailleur is a new removable and rechargeable battery. Packing 450 mAh, it’s bigger in capacity and physical size than SRAM’s 300 mAh unit. Campagnolo quotes 750 km of riding from a single charge, but keep in mind that nobody’s use case is identical. Charging can be done with the battery on or off the bike, using yet another proprietary USB-C magnetic charge cable (included with the battery).

First introduced with Ekar, the 13-speed cassettes continue to require Campagnolo’s own N3W freehub design, which is effectively a chopped version of its earlier freehub that allows the fitment of smaller 9T or 10T cogs. It’s a freehub design that’s well catered for by Campagnolo, sibling brand Fulcrum, DT Swiss, and quite a few other premium hub and wheel options.…

Source: Escape Collective | Published: 2026-11-27 20:07 UTC

item.title: Mercedes set pace in eventful Qatar second practice
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Mercedes set pace in eventful Qatar second practice

World champion Kimi Antonelli set the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix.

Italian Antonelli was 0.127 seconds quicker than Russell on the medium tyre, as neither driver set a time on the soft compound because of two red flags that punctuated the session.

Lewis Hamilton also came to halt after his Ferrari lost power, with a virtual safety car deployed so the marshals could come to the seven-time world champion's aid.

The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri plus Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the top five at the Lusail International Circuit, with the trio setting soft-tyre times that were more than four tenths adrift of the two Mercedes.

The first red flag was to clear gravel off the track after an incident for Ferrari's Charles Leclerc early on, while the other was to recover the Alpine of Pierre Gasly following a high-speed spin.

Frenchman Gasly hit a marker board before beaching himself after taking too much kerb at Turn 14 in the middle of the qualifying simulation runs.

The interruptions led to the second hour being extended by 13 minutes to allow drivers more time on track in the representative conditions.

"It was a productive day," said Antonelli. "We tried a lot of things on the car between FP1 and FP2, but in FP2, it seemed like we did a step back with the car.

"But it was very interesting to see how the car behaved after those changes. It's not easy."

Antonelli, who secured his maiden title in Mexico City earlier this month, was also fastest in the opening session on the mediums. Mercedes did fit the 20-year-old with the soft tyre in the first hour, but he failed to set a lap time on them.

He said he feels it will be close between himself and Russell for the race victory, but added: "You can never write off Max [Verstappen] and the others."

Norris, meanwhile, said Mercedes "were in a different category" to McLaren, highlighting the Silver Arrows "were quicker in every single corner by miles".

The 2025 world champion added: "We seem in a relatively decent position, similar on pace with Red Bull, and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I'd say it's OK."

Four-time title winner Verstappen said it had been a "difficult day" following his issues with heavy steering towards the end of the session.

"The balance of the car is probably too disconnected at the moment to go fast," he added. "It's costing us quite a bit of lap time."

1 of 5

Hamilton also had a moment with Verstappen that was noted by the race control. The Briton was on a flying lap when he got too close to the Dutchman, who was on a long run.

Verstappen said Hamilton had moved under braking, but the stewards decided no further investigation was needed.

The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was sixth on the timesheets, with Leclerc leading Hamilton in seventh and eighth, 1.3 seconds away from Antonelli's time.

The two Racing Bulls of British rookie Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson were ninth and 10th.

Leclerc had to head back into the garage after spinning and going through the gravel when Lawson was just ahead of him at Turn Nine.

The Monegasque driver said the car did not feel right, and the Italian team spent a chunk of time repairing the damage to the floor. After the session he said he lost control after going a little bit early on the throttle.

Ferrari arrived in Qatar after another on-track incident between Leclerc and Hamilton, this time in Las Vegas. The pair made contact and Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, with Hamilton saying on Thursday the team were facing "very, very challenging times".

Leclerc thinks this weekend could potentially be another struggle for the Italian team, who can secure second in the constructors' championship if they can retain at least a 44-point lead over third-placed Red Bull.

"A very, very difficult day. Not even on high fuel were we strong," said Leclerc.

"We are working hard but for some reason, Mercedes is so much faster than I think everyone expected. So the gaps are just a little bit strange."

Drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at the Lusail circuit, meaning teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix on Sunday, which starts at 16:00 GMT.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed, 16-corner track. Laps to the grid, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

Hamilton was told by his engineer in first practice tyre degradation was "much higher than expected" after highlighting his own issues.

Qatar and next week's finale in Abu Dhabi are going ahead as planned despite the ongoing conflict between the United States/Israel and Iran.

- Published1 hour ago

Source: BBC Sport | Published: 2026-11-27 19:50 UTC

item.title: Wales aim to finish historic campaign with Japan win
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Wales aim to finish historic campaign with Japan win

It is not the traditional ending to a Wales rugby autumn campaign.

After the euphoria and then disappointment of two epic international weekends in Cardiff, Wales face the prospect of finishing a November series in south west London with a fixture against Japan.

It sounds unusual because the conclusion of the inaugural Nations Championship is exactly that.

The concept of a finals weekend in one venue with six games over three days is laudable, but trying to get Welsh fans excited about defeating Japan to finish ninth rather than 10th in a 12-team tournament at a neutral ground is a tough sell, especially when you compare it to what happened in Cardiff two weeks ago.

This autumn will always be remembered as the campaign where Wales shocked the rugby world by beating New Zealand for the first time since 1953.

Either side of that momentous day, there has been a lacklustre 28-21 defeat of Japan and a narrow 29-26 loss against Australia in a game Wales could and maybe should have won.

Those exciting occasions in Cardiff will now be followed by a trip to Twickenham to take on Eddie Jones' Japan. It takes some getting used to.

Wales v Japan

Nations Championship

Saturday, 28 November (13:10 GMT)

Allianz Stadium, Twickenham

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra 2 on BBC Sounds

Wales face double-header dilemma

It will be a strange experience with Wales facing Japan on a Saturday afternoon before England play New Zealand for third place.

Is it a double-header or will Wales be providing the curtain-raiser to the main event?

Whichever way you view the occasion, Wales head coach Steve Tandy knows his side will have to provide their own atmosphere with a sparse crowd present for Friday afternoon's match between Italy and Fiji before Ireland took on Australia in the evening.

"We've spoken about it all week," said Tandy.

"There's also a 40-minute bus trip which is not normal either because we usually stay closer.

"We have also spoken about it being an early kick-off.

"There might be people walking in while the game is going on, the crowd might fill up as the game goes on, so there's all these little things to consider.â

Tandy says the squad know Twickenham will not match the intensity of Cardiff's Principality Stadium during the past couple of weeks.

"It is a different type of atmosphere for us after three massive games at home and being unbelievably well supported," said Tandy.

"We've got to adapt a different sort of mindset and create that energy on the field for ourselves."

- Jenkins ready to resume Wales captaincy role

- A world-class winger - Louis Rees-Zammit 2.0

Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere table of the inaugural Nations Championship to face Japan, who finished in the same position in the southern standings.

It will be the fifth time in 16 months the two sides have faced each other, with Wales winning three out of the four games.

So opposing coaches Tandy and Jones will again lock horns.

"I am looking forward to seeing him once more but it is probably a little bit too much," said Tandy, who saw his side labour to an 28-21 win over Japan three weeks ago.

Since that result, Japan have suffered a 78-15 hammering by England and a 67-5 drubbing by Scotland.

"We can't be fooled by the scoreboards, Japan have still got the core of their forward pack and line-out pressure," said Tandy.

"We're going to have to produce one of our best performances of the tournament to make sure we finish the campaign the way we want to."

Japan are down to their bare bones after a hard programme they are not used to, but Jones remains bullish.

"It should be good, a great occasion," said Jones.

"Wales don't like coming to Twickenham and for us, it's a great experience, so we will give it a red-hot crack."

Fighting words, but this is a chance for Wales to produce the type of commanding performance and victory that has been missing against this opposition.

Wales' three victories in the past four games against Japan have been by nine, seven and one point.

Given Tandy's selection this week and Japan's exertions in recent weeks, a commanding win should be on the agenda to match Scotland and Englandâs exploits against the Brave Blossoms.

Source: BBC Sport | Published: 2026-11-27 19:35 UTC

Leonardo’s UK Loss Shows the Cost of Renting Hotels

Rising wages and payroll taxes are squeezing Leonardo Hotels' UK business, but the bigger problem is the rent on its hotels, according to accounts filed with Companies House, the UK company register.

On paper, the drop is steep. The hotel chain swung to a £55.6 million ($74 million) pre-tax loss in 2025 from a £50.1 million ($67 million) profit. But the 2024 profit included an £89.8 million ($119 million) one-off gain from revaluing its leases. Without it, 2024 would have shown a loss of about £40 million ($53 million), so the loss widened by about £16 million ($21 million) rather than appearing from nowhere.

The filing shows revenue at Leonardo Hotel Management (UK) Ltd was steady, rising 1.3% to £350.1 million ($466 million), with no new hotels opened. Gross profit fell 12% to £37.6 million ($50 million), and the gross margin slipped to 10.7% from 12.4%. Staff costs rose 6% to £102.5 million ($136 million), and employer social security costs rose 34%.

Welcome to “What’s in My Bag,” a new series where TPG staffers open their carry-ons, personal items and dopp kits to share the travel essentials they never leave home without.

- Bag of choice: Lululemon New Crew Backpack Large 30L, $128

What’s in my bag

As a travel expert who’s constantly on the go, I will say some of my favorite things that you’ll find in my bag revolve around staying organized and being comfortable — I always know where my essentials are. At this stage of my life, I’m willing to splurge a bit on handcrafted or well-made products that last. Quality is nonnegotiable.

Prada Re-Nylon and Saffiano leather travel pouch

This travel pouch is so chic, but definitely a splurge. It’s made with Saffiano leather and Re-Nylon, an innovative fabric that’s produced from recycled plastic recovered from the ocean. You can find it at Saks Fifth Avenue. I love it for keeping everything I might need on the go organized — with two top zipper pockets and one each on the front and back, I never run out of room.

Buy: Prada Re-Nylon and Saffiano leather travel pouch, $1,120

Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones

These Bose noise-canceling headphones are comfortable and seamlessly connect via Bluetooth. Plus, they are stylish and have great sound quality. The surround sound is awesome.

Rode wireless microphones

As a content creator, I needed a good lav microphone with an iPhone receiver for when I’m out and about. The Rode wireless mic is super easy to use, holds a charge all day and slips right into my travel pouch.

Healthy snacks

My go-to quick snack is Quest protein peanut butter cups — indulgent yet packed with protein. I keep Grüns gummies in my bag for a healthy mix of essential vitamins and prebiotics. They keep me feeling energized and are more than just a multivitamin — they’re made with whole fruits and veggies too.

Aspinal of London wallet

Extra iPhone

I have a second phone for travel that’s connected to the T-Mobile network as a backup, and, depending on your service plan, T-Mobile also offers free Wi-Fi on U.S. airlines. I keep my main phone on Verizon, but you never want to be stuck without a phone when abroad.

item.title: Opinion: Behind the Teacher Recruitment and Retention Problem Is a Crisis of Mattering
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis with useful vocabulary and context.

Behind the Teacher Recruitment and Retention Problem Is a Crisis of Mattering

Wallace: As families and communities depend on educators to help children thrive, they must also make sure those educators feel valued and supported

Across the country, schools struggle to recruit and retain talented teachers. These challenges are often described as a staffing problem. But new Gallup research points to a deeper issue: Too many educators question whether they matter to the communities they serve.

Mattering is the fundamental human need to feel valued and to have an opportunity to contribute to others. When people feel like they matter, they thrive. When they don’t, they struggle. The new study, the first nationwide survey to focus on educator mattering, reveals what that struggle looks like in the classroom: Among educators who lack a sense of mattering, 68% are frequently burned out, and fewer than half plan to remain in the profession long-term.

Over eight years of researching my book, Mattering: The Secret to a Life of Deep Connection and Purpose, I’ve spoken with hundreds of educators around the country who feel passionate about their work and students but unappreciated and underinvested-in as people.

Of 1,952 K-12 classroom teachers, teaching assistants, substitutes and paraprofessionals surveyed, only 35% said they matter a great deal at their school. Just 1 in 5 said someone at their school invests a great deal in their growth and development.

Only 25% of respondents said they received appreciation from supervisors weekly or more often, and two-thirds said they always or often give more to their school community than they get back. Among those who always experienced that imbalance, 57% reported feeling burned out always or very often.

Overall, 1 in 4 educators said they were likely to leave their job within a year.

Gallup researchers interpreted these sobering findings through a framework of mattering that I developed, called SAID. It consists of four components: significance (do people know me as a person?); appreciation (do people notice and value my contributions?); invested in (is someone supporting my growth and well-being?); and depended on (do others rely on me in sustainable ways?).

Feeling appreciation had the strongest link to educators’ sense of mattering, with recognition from supervisors outweighing that of students or parents. Among the four SAID dimensions, feeling invested had the strongest relationship with educators’ likelihood of quitting within the next year.

Teachers know they are needed. But that is only part of what it means to matter. This echoes what researchers call the passion tax — the expectation that people will accept extra work, low pay or little support because they love what they do. Devotion to your students shouldn’t mean ignoring your own needs and limits.

This isn’t just an issue for schools: Parents have a stake in the mattering crisis, too. As is commonly noted, educators’ working conditions become students’ learning conditions. In other words, caring for teachers is also a way to care for children.

Mattering is not a slogan. It’s built from the accumulation of everyday signals educators receive from colleagues, supervisors, students and parents, and it erodes when those signals go missing. The survey findings offer a lens and a shared language for understanding where educators’ experiences are falling short and where schools might focus their attention. Here are some steps schools and parents can take to bridge the mattering gap:

- Schools can make appreciation a regular part of staff meetings and supervisor check-ins by recognizing both the contribution and the person, by saying, for example: “You have a gift for helping students see their own potential.”

- Schools can also invest in educators’ growth by asking what they need to succeed and then following through. This can include providing dedicated time for mentoring and collaboration, offering professional development teachers actually want and giving them a voice in decisions that affect their classrooms.

- Parents can ask themselves: How often do teachers hear from us when something goes wrong, compared with when we appreciate something they’ve done? Even a short, positive message — “Because of your enthusiasm and patience, my son loves math again” — can connect educators to their impact.

These practices belong alongside adequate pay, full staffing and manageable workloads as choices that communicate just how much educators matter.

The mattering gap is a wake-up call. School and parents can start addressing it today. Just as families and communities depend on educators to help children thrive, all of us need to make sure those educators feel valued and supported so they will, too.

Source: The 74 | Published: 2026-11-27 11:30 UTC | Difficulty: 62/100

item.title: New Mexico Education Advocates, Lawmakers Oppose Federal Education Tax Credit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Clear reporting with concrete details and useful vocabulary.

New Mexico Education Advocates, Lawmakers Oppose Federal Education Tax Credit

State House Education Committee Chair Romero says federal program undermines state’s work on student equity.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

New Mexico education advocates, teachers union representatives and a state lawmaker on Tuesday held a news conference to decry the state’s participation in a controversial federal education tax credit.

The Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, established in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act enacted last year, allows eligible taxpayers to receive a federal tax credit of up to $1,700 annually for charitable contributions to qualified nonprofit “scholarship granting organizations.” Those organizations then award scholarships to eligible K-12 students in public and non-public schools to cover qualified educational expenses. States can opt in to the program, which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Earlier this month, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced that New Mexico would become the 32nd state to participate, saying in a statement that at a “time of diminishing federal investment in education, New Mexico must take advantage of every dollar we can to bolster public education and continue our state’s upward trajectory in literacy and student achievement.”

During Tuesday’s news conference, Bethany Jarrell, president of the National Education Association New Mexico, said the tax credit “may be packaged as an opportunity for families, but let’s be clear, this is a voucher scheme.” She added that while the New Mexico Constitution “establishes a responsibility” to provide education for all children, the scholarship organizations are “private” and “do not have the constitutional responsibility to educate every child.”

That constitutional right to education for all students was at the heart of the state’s landmark Yazzie/Martinez equity case, in which the court ruled that the state did not provide equitable education support to at-risk students such as English language learners, Native American students, students from low-income families and students with disabilities.

“New Mexico must not import a policy that risks deepening educational inequities while leaving public schools with greater responsibility and fewer resources,” Yazzie/Martinez reform advocate Loretta Trujillo, executive director of Transform Education NM, said on Tuesday.

Michael Coleman, Lujan Grisham’s communications director, told Source NM in an emailed statement that the governor “would have preferred more direct federal investment in public education in lieu of this tax credit — full stop.” He added that the tax credit is open to public school students and that the governor “is doing everything she can to make sure they benefit from it.”

Lujan Grisham “had to choose whether to opt-in and allow donations to flow to public and private school students in New Mexico or opt-out and allow donors in New Mexico and elsewhere who claim the tax credit to send their money to other states,” Coleman continued. “Given those limited choices, Governor Lujan Grisham decided to keep that money in New Mexico where it belongs.”

Several state lawmakers also denounced the governor’s decision.

At the news conference, Sen. Linda Lopez (D-Albuquerque) said she was “very disappointed” Lujan Grisham had opted in to the tax credit, saying the “voucher program is a backdoor entry to remove money from our public schools.” She said that the Legislature has stood against “anything that is associated with vouchers,” and added that “as we move forward under a new governor, I will stand with my colleagues to say no, we will not.”

In a recent phone call with Source NM, Rep. Andrés Romero (D-Albuquerque), chair of the House Education Committee, said that the governor’s decision undermines the Legislature’s work when it comes to Yazzie/Martinez students.

“These voucher programs in the states that have had them disproportionately gone to affluent families and students, and have benefited private school over public schools,” Romero said, calling claims that the program will fund things like after school programs “a hope and a wish.”

item.title: In the Shadow of the Afghanistan-Pakistan Border
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of a geopolitical issue with clear reporting and context

Fighting flared again along the Afghan-Pakistani border in early 2026. For weeks, Afghan villages near the frontier came under fire. By the time I arrived in June, the guns had been silent for a while. Families were slowly returning home and beginning to repair the damage. But the calm was fragile: neither side had laid down its weapons; they had only set them aside.

Sometimes They Shoot, and We Shoot Back

“There’s no particular reason for the fighting. Sometimes they shoot across the border, and we shoot back,” Ibrahim told me. He was the police commander of a border village in Kunar province. As we stood in the courtyard, he pointed toward the mountains separating Afghanistan from Pakistan.

Ibrahim had been fighting since childhood. He fought the Soviets, later the Americans, and now he faces the Pakistani army. I asked him which war had been the easiest. After a long pause, he said, “There’s no such thing as an easy war. They were all bad.”

The Durand Line, which marks the border between Afghanistan and Pakistan, was drawn in 1893 between British India and the Afghan emirate. Shaped by the interests of distant great powers, it cut through Pashtun communities, leaving people of the same ethnic group on opposite sides. The border dispute remains a source of tension, but it only partly explains the renewed fighting in early 2026.

Another major source of friction is the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), the Pakistani Taliban movement. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban leadership in Kabul of allowing TTP militants to find refuge in Afghanistan and carry out attacks against Pakistan. Pakistan says its cross-border military operations are aimed at armed groups. Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers deny supporting the TTP and regard the strikes as violations of Afghan sovereignty. In early 2026, tensions once again erupted into heavy fighting, with artillery attacks along the border and Pakistani airstrikes on targets inside Afghanistan.

The civilian toll extended far beyond the villages of Kunar. According to the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), cross-border fighting killed 56 civilians and injured another 129 in Afghanistan between February 26 and March 5, 2026. Women and children accounted for 55 percent of the casualties.

When I visited in June, I wanted to see how people in the border villages were living in the aftermath of the attacks. Once I had secured the necessary permits, I made my way into Kunar, the border province battered by the fighting, to report from the ground.

The Last Checkpoint

It took me nearly a full day to travel from Kabul toward the Pakistani border. I changed cars several times along the way, keeping my cameras carefully hidden. Dressed in local Afghan clothing, I was often mistaken for a local at checkpoints, where guards usually waved us through. But just before Kunar, a soldier stopped my car. He pointed at me, visibly agitated, then ordered me out of the vehicle. I couldn’t understand what they were saying, but the way he studied my papers and shook his head told me something was wrong.

My interpreter later told me the soldier had mistaken me for a member of the local Hazara minority because of my Asian features, which may have made him even more suspicious. He thought my ministry-issued permit was fake and refused to believe I was a foreign national. When the papers failed to convince him, my interpreter took a more pragmatic approach and finally got us out of trouble. He pulled up a photo on his phone of the Taliban official who had issued the permit, then told the guard that if he refused to let us pass, he would tell the official exactly how we had been treated. The soldier promptly waved us away.

The Kunar Valley

Once inside Kunar, I checked in with the Taliban authorities in town. They offered to clear the way for me to the border. The next day, I bounced along a rough dirt road beside the Kunar River in a Toyota pickup repurposed for military use. Checkpoints grew more frequent as we approached the frontier. With a Taliban official riding with me and several armed men in the truck bed, we were mostly waved through.

We stopped at a camp of white UNICEF tents along the road, where children were playing soccer. When we got out of the car, the children gathered around us. We met Farid, who, along with others, cared for and taught the children at the camp. He told us that roughly 300 children had taken shelter there after fleeing the fighting. He said families living on the Pakistani side were not safe either: as the conflict intensified, Pakistani authorities had harassed residents in some villages, forcing them from their homes and across the border into Afghanistan.

A double fence several meters high ran along the mountain ridges, marking the border. It was covered in so much barbed wire that one look was enough to put anyone off even trying to approach it. As we passed a bombed-out building, I asked the soldiers whether someone might shoot at us from the other side. They shrugged. No one had fired in weeks, they said, and if someone did start shooting, we would definitely notice.

We continued to Barikot, a small Afghan village right along the border. Almost every wall bore marks of the fighting. On the main street, we met Mohamed, dressed in a white coat. He was the only doctor in the area. He welcomed us outside the war-torn hospital. Shrapnel had punched fist-sized holes in the hospital’s iron gate, leaving much of the courtyard visible through them. Explosions had ripped entire window frames out of the wards, cracked walls, and scattered equipment everywhere. The patients had been evacuated before the attacks, but Mohamed had stayed. He told us he had work to do there, even when shells were falling. He could not leave the villagers without medical care.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-27 20:15 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Millions lose access to benefits and pensions services after 'cyber incident'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant cyber incident with personal stories

Millions lose access to benefits and pensions services after 'cyber incident'

Millions of people have been left without access to online benefits and pensions services after the government said its system had been hit by a "cyber incident".

Downing Street has not ruled out an attempted hack but said there was "currently no evidence" personal data had been lost, adding an investigation was ongoing.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it took the digital services down as a "precaution", and assured claimants regular benefit and pension payments would be paid.

But a number of benefits recipients say money they rely on has still not come through - and they fear being penalised for not being able to fill in an online journal that proves they are looking for jobs.

The UK's former Chief Technology Officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the incident was an attack.

"They've taken down some of the citizen-facing services which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door," he said.

Single Cardiff mother-of-four Samantha Reah told the BBC the technological disruption meant she was missing Â£1,600: "I rely on the payment today - it's my payday.

"I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop. I'm panicking - it's going to be a long and stressful weekend."

Georgina Howarth, 30, from Plymouth, said she had to ask her mother for money to help buy food after not receiving her universal credit payment.

"I've been on the phone to them [DWP staff] every hour since 8am. They said they can't even get on the system."

Claimants are also unable to fill in an online journal which shows the DWP they have been applying for jobs, a condition of their benefits.

Gemma Barnes from St Neots in Cambridgeshire told the BBC she was worried her payments could be cut as a result.

She said she has been trying to access the universal credit website "all of today and since last night as well" but she has not been able to get through to the site.

"With it being so close to Christmas I need [that money] at the moment," she said., explaining she has to often rely on items in the reduced food section to make ends meet.

The DWP says regular payments are not affected and if customers have any issues with their payments, they should call on their benefit phoneline. They say they will not be sanctioned over missing journal entries during the incident.

There are also problems with Healthy Start, an NHS scheme for women who are pregnant or have young children to help them buy milk or fruit.

A spokesperson told the BBC the online application service was unavailable but there was no interruption to payments.

- What we know about Department for Work and Pensions 'cyber incident'

As of around 12:00 GMT on Friday, the online systems for pensions, universal credit and Pip applications, as well as the "Tell Us Once'" system to inform government when someone has died, could not be accessed.

It was not clear when the government expected services to be up and running again.

A DWP spokesperson said: "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption."

A statement continued: "As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links."

Tech disruption to major service around the world have hit the headlines repeatedly in recent months.

There was a major outage of Microsoft services, the grounding of all US flights, problems at the US National Security Agency, and disruption at major American banks.

The causes of these incidents have varied. Many were linked to upgrades going wrong but experts have also mentioned factors including outdated IT systems and the use of AI to potentially exploit tech vulnerabilities.

While the nature of the DWP incident is unclear, officials could not rule out the involvement of a "malicious actor", but added there was "no evidence" that other government departments had been targeted in this way.

The DWP outage follows warnings that AI technology could fuel attacks on UK digital infrastructure.

Earlier this month a National Cyber Security Centre report urged organisations to strengthen their defences against hackers as the technology becomes more complex and capable.

Its CEO Richard Horne said there was a "real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents".

Last month the government carried out inspections on several websites after a flaw was identified in a programming language used around the world.

The PHP security flaw prompted a global race for organisations to identify whether they were impacted and fix it before it could be exploited.

UK government websites have been impacted by other cyber incidents in recent years.

In April 2025, the government reported that cyber attackers had breached the Legal Aid Agency's online services.

It said the group responsible accessed a "significant amount" of personal data going back decades, including contact details of people who had applied for legal aid.

The agency took some services offline while responding to the incident.

item.title: Ex-council leader jailed for fraud and tax evasion
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed account of a political scandal with legal and financial implications

Ex-council leader jailed for fraud and tax evasion

A former council leader accused of inventing a fake heritage society to scam a local authority out of thousands of pounds has been jailed for 27 months.

Jason Zadrozny set up the Ashfield Heritage Society before applying for council funding, which he then transferred into his personal account.

He claimed the cash was "to support heritage projects", but pocketed the money for himself. He was convicted of fraud and tax evasion on 21 September following a trial.

At Northampton Crown Court on Friday, the 46-year-old, of Stanton Hill, sobbed in the dock as Judge David Herbert KC told him he had "failed the electorate and harmed public confidence in the district council by your fraudulent conduct".

The six-week trial heard Ashfield District Council leader and county councillor Zadrozny - of the Ashfield Independents - set up the heritage society in 2018 before applying for funding from Nottinghamshire County Council.

This, the trial heard, included Â£7,500, requested three days after setting up a bank account for the society, which Zadrozny claimed was "to support heritage projects in Ashfield".

The council issued the funds and they were sent directly to Zadrozny, who deposited them in the account, before withdrawing them in cash in March.

Prosecutors alleged part of the money was used to buy a house with friends.

Jurors were also told Zadrozny was a landlord who did not pay tax on income from four of his properties, estimated in court to be "less than Â£15,000".

Zadrozny told the jury he did not keep the money for himself, and gave cash from the heritage society to Tony Brewer, a former Ashfield District Council chairman who died from Covid in 2020, to repair war memorials.

Zadrozny also helped set up a Classic Cinema Club for people who liked the Carry On films, which the court heard "was probably legitimate when he set it up" - although he later helped himself to its funds.

The court heard Â£5,000 was withdrawn in cash from the Ashfield Heritage Society account, while Â£1,200 was withdrawn from the cinema club.

Zadrozny denied the offences and told the trial the funds he had received were spent on the community.

The former council leader was found not guilty of three counts of fraud.

'A shameful day'

In mitigation, defence barrister Sam Robinson KC said up until 2015, Zadrozny was "a model citizen, in the way he has behaved in his public life but also in his personal life".

Robinson added: "He went off the rails from 2015 onwards. He blew his life spectacularly up.

"It's so easy to look at someone who has unravelled and think why on earth did he do any of this? That's the enigma we're dealing with."

He also said medical experts suggested mental health conditions could have caused "compromised judgement", and "can produce avoidance, indecision and impulsive behaviour".

However, in his sentencing remarks, the judge said Zadrozny had undertaken "dishonest conduct that took place over a number of years".

"I know that today is a shameful day for you," he said.

"When it became apparent that your offending would be uncovered, you sought to cover your tracks in an elaborate series of lies."

The judge said the sentence reflected the "gross abuse of trust", and how the "offending was conducted over a sustained period of time".

On 12 November, the district council confirmed that Zadrozny resigned as councillor for Larwood, adding there would be no by-election until the local elections in May.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) also decided to launch a rapid review of the local authority after MPs raised concerns about a decision to appoint Zadrozny to the council's planning committee in the wake of his conviction.

Ten councillors quit the Ashfield Independents as a result, with some forming a new group called the District Alliance.

An MHCLG spokesperson added: "We have powers to investigate and intervene where councils fail to meet their Best Value Duty, and we're conducting a best-value assessment on Ashfield District Council to ensure it's delivering for local people."

In a letter to Labour MP Michelle Welsh, local government minister Jim McMahon confirmed he had ordered a "rapid best-value assessment" to be carried out into the authority.

Following the sentencing, Theresa Hodgkinson, chief executive at Ashfield District Council said Zadrozny "no longer has an affiliation with the council".

"We do understand why recent events may have damaged confidence in the council and caused concern across our communities," she said.

"Residents are right to expect the highest standards from those elected to represent them, and from their council, and while recent events cannot be changed, we are focused on rebuilding confidence in our council and maintaining and enhancing services and investment into the district.

"Our residents should be reassured that our focus remains firmly on providing high-quality services, investing in our communities and achieving the best outcomes for local people."
