item.title: Tory candidates must sign pledge to scrap net-zero targets, says Badenoch
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains a political stance with clear reporting and contrasting opinions

Tory candidates must sign pledge to scrap net-zero targets, says Badenoch

All Conservative candidates will have to sign a pledge committing themselves to leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and scrapping net-zero emission targets ahead of the next election, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said.

Unveiling her "candidates covenant" at an event in the East Midlands, Badenoch said both policies were "necessary for a stronger economy and a stronger country".

The move could see some senior Conservatives blocked from standing for the party at the next general election.

Lord Barwell, a former Conservative minister and No 10 chief of staff, said: "After a summer in which the impacts of climate change were clearer than ever, this is bad policy."

He added: "Given the seats Conservative strategists say they are targeting, it is also bad politics."

Tobias Ellwood, a former Conservative MP and defence minister, told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5Live he had applied to stand as a candidate in the next election but had not passed what he described as "the purity test".

He criticised Badenoch's covenant, saying: "Can you imagine if... prior to the war, you had to sign up to [Neville] Chamberlain's 'peace in our time' speech, you know, [Winston] Churchill wouldn't have been allowed to stand."

"I mean, there must be times where you can have different views and different views within a party are actually helpful," he added.

Addressing party activists in Newark, Badenoch said: "The government that cleans up Andy Burnham's mess is going to have to make some very difficult decisions... it is not going to be for the faint-hearted.

"I need everyone who stands as a Conservative candidate at the next election to know what they are standing for - I don't want to hear complaining from MPs that they didn't know what we were going to do."

The covenant also states that candidates must support staying out of the EU, reducing the size of the state and changing the welfare system.

Sir Mark Spencer, a chief whip in the last Conservative government, became the first to sign the new pledge.

He lost his seat in the 2024 election, but is now standing in Newark, where he hopes to unseat the Conservative-turned-Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick.

A Labour spokesperson said: "Kemi Badenoch is living in an alternate reality. She says the Tories have changed but the truth is they're the same old Tories."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Kemi Badenoch tells us the Conservative Party has changed - it's hard to believe when she's surrounded by so many Remainers and her party is selecting lots of failed ex-Tory MPs who got kicked out at the last election."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "The Conservatives pretend they care about winning back support from millions of former Conservative voters, yet Kemi Badenoch is now asking her candidates to sign the 'Farage pact'.

"They are taking people for fools."

- Net zero by 2050 'impossible' for UK, says Badenoch

- UK will leave ECHR if Tories win election, Badenoch says

- Shapps blocked from standing again for the Conservatives

Both the commitments to leave the ECHR and repeal net-zero targets represent a shift from previous Conservative governments.

The net-zero target was originally legislated for by the Theresa May-led Conservative government in 2019. The party's 2024 manifesto said it was proud of its record on reducing emissions and remained "committed to delivering net-zero by 2050".

In the run-up to the election, then Prime Minister, and Conservative leader, Rishi Sunak resisted demands from some in his party to commit to leaving the ECHR.

Since becoming leader, Badenoch has argued that the net-zero target - which commits the UK to reducing its net greenhouse gas emissions to almost zero by 2050 - couldn't be achieved "without a serious drop in our living standards or by bankrupting us".

Last year, she also announced that, if elected, her party would take the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights, the treaty that guarantees certain human rights such as the right to privacy, protection against torture and a right to a family life.

Badenoch said the convention prevented the UK from being able to secure its borders and deport foreign criminals.

Over the past year, the Labour government, along with other European countries have agreed to negotiate a new approach to the convention with the aim of making it easier to deport people.

item.title: Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed reporting on a government decision with significant implications

Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid

Puerto Rico Supreme Court allows governor to fire company that runs the island's troubled power grid

LUMA Energy took over the electric grid five years ago. The court's ruling nullifies its contract, and gives the government a year to find a new operator.

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

Puerto Rico's supreme court has ruled the island's governor can kick out the private company that's been running its troubled power grid for five years. The decision could have huge consequences for electric service in Puerto Rico. Here is NPR's Adrian Florido.

ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: After Hurricane Maria flattened Puerto Rico's already rickety power grid in 2017, the island's government privatized it. It gave a company called LUMA Energy, based in Canada and Texas, a 15-year deal to take over the power lines, promising that LUMA would rebuild the grid stronger and improve the notoriously unreliable service. LUMA took over in 2021. But things have not gone as planned.

Blackouts are still a constant fact of life. LUMA has come in for harsh criticism from customers and officials. Last year, Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez-Colon filed suit to nullify LUMA's contract. Yesterday, the Puerto Rican Supreme Court ruled in her favor that LUMA must go.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

JENNIFFER GONZALEZ-COLON: Today is a day of celebration on the island.

FLORIDO: This is the governor speaking after the ruling. She said LUMA has not lived up to its promises.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GONZALEZ-COLON: More outages on the island, more shutdowns on the island. They have not fulfilled the requirements of the contract.

FLORIDO: In fact, the island's supreme court ruled on procedural grounds, saying officials had not followed local requirements when approving agreements with the company. The court gave the local government a year to put a new operator in place. The governor said the work to find a new private company will start immediately.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GONZALEZ-COLON: It's going to be a good transition. We're going to make it in a year. And I hope that all companies that are interested in participating in this process will fulfill and follow the process of law. And we're going to be opening that process for public bid.

FLORIDO: The court gave LUMA Energy 10 days to request a reconsideration of its ruling. In a statement, LUMA said it is considering its legal options. The company has long argued that the grid it took over was in awful shape and that it is not fully to blame for the blackouts. A new operator will need approval from both the local government and a federal oversight board that Congress put in place 10 years ago to get Puerto Rico out of bankruptcy. In a statement, that board criticized the governor for ending LUMA' s contract without having a new company ready to go. It said it's worried about the continuity of service on the island. In her remarks yesterday, the governor said she has a plan in place and will reveal it soon.

Adrian Florido, NPR News.

item.title: Ahead of Taiwan’s Local Elections, China’s Interference Looms Large
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Analysis of political interference with clear context and examples

Taiwan is scheduled to hold local elections, also called the “nine-in-one” elections, on Saturday, November 28. Voters will select city mayors and county magistrates throughout all of Taiwan’s 22 cities and counties. Campaigns focus on local issues, such as housing, welfare, transport, and the environment, rather than Taiwan’s contentious ties with China.

Beijing, nevertheless, has become the elephant in the room due to the increasing threat posed by its attempts to interfere in Taiwan’s elections.

China’s attempts to subvert Taiwan’s local elections and control the island’s domestic politics are not new. Beijing’s strategy to undermine Taiwan’s November elections relies on both intimidation and inducements – delegitimizing Taiwan’s national government by framing its governance as “unstable,” holding military exercises around Taiwan to manipulate public perception, offering campaign financing for candidates supporting unification with China, and subsidizing airfare for Taiwanese businesspeople based in China to return to Taiwan to vote for pro-China candidates.

But Chinese Communist Party (CCP) interference activities in Taiwan’s local elections have become more complex as technology advances. Ahead of the November 28 vote, Taiwanese officials flagged nearly 2,700 China-linked accounts to Meta as part of an information warfare campaign orchestrated by the CCP to sow distrust, discourage voting, and incite public anger against the governing party, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). These accounts initially posed as ordinary Taiwanese users sharing snippets of daily life to gain trust, before shifting tactics to launch political attacks and urge voters to “abstain from voting.”

Beijing’s advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and AI-generated deepfakes make “methods of infiltration increasingly sophisticated,” warned Shen Yu-chung, deputy head of Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council (MAC). AI has now become a tool for election manipulation, making it “easier to produce misleading content” and conduct influence operations.

Shen said investigations into China’s election interference show that China has utilized AI to operate “massive facial recognition systems,” which could help Beijing collect data on Taiwanese people’s daily lives. This data, specifically facial images, could be combined with AI-generated content to dodge detection systems used by social media platforms to identify and remove fake accounts. Experts have warned that, by gathering detailed personal background information, the CCP could precisely target specific individuals, such as those with ties to the military or those who lean toward a particular party, for the dissemination of disinformation and the execution of cognitive warfare operations.

The CCP’s online infiltration tactics have been steadily changing. Online operations have gradually shifted from the use of crude, fraudulent identities that can be easily detected to the cultivation of accounts that appear to have legitimate personas. When these personas infiltrate online communities, the artificially generated “buzz” can be mistaken for real public sentiment. This can sway how people think about political issues.

For instance, the deliberate spread of messages like “voting is pointless” or “all candidates are the same” can discourage the electorate’s eagerness to participate. Such tactics will eventually erode public trust in the government and democratic institutions, thus diminishing the credibility of Taiwan’s democratic electoral system.

AI-generated social media campaigns rely primarily on non-political content, such as food, animals, celebrities, or sexually suggestive “clickbait” videos, while interspersing these with political messages that are pro-China or support unification. This technique of using messages anchored in “unrelated, celebrity-focused feeds” but aimed at political purposes was also observed during the U.S. midterm elections.

Certain fake accounts directly attack Taiwan’s ruling party, accusing it of corruption and belittling its governance. Others pose as DPP supporters, “liking” and sharing content from pro-China accounts that otherwise struggle to gain traction, thereby helping to amplify Beijing’s messaging.

To establish credibility, the CCP has also co-opted prominent public figures and influencers to adopt a nuanced strategy of “minor criticism, major backing” – offering minor, superficial critiques of China while advancing narratives that align with CCP policies and interests.

Beyond social media posts, Beijing also hires private investigators and uses public “wanted” lists as a form of cognitive warfare. The China & Taiwan Update, co-published by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and the American Enterprise Institute (AEI), revealed that officials from the Shanghai Public Security Bureau recruited a Taiwanese private investigator to surveil two prominent Taiwanese YouTubers and political commentators, “Ba Jiong” (八炯, Wen Tzu-yu) and “Min Nan Lang” (閩南狼, Chen Po-yuan) – both famous for exposing CCP United Front (the CCP department tasked with advancing Chinese influence abroad) tactics targeting Taiwan – while also gathering their personal information.

Furthermore, by subjecting individuals – such as Puma Shen, the DPP’s mayoral candidate for Taipei, online influencers, pro-Taiwan figures, and military personnel – to public “wanted” lists, doxxing, and surveillance, Chinese authorities and affiliated entities have conducted cognitive warfare in Taiwan. This campaign aims to instill a sense of defeatism among the public, fostering the perception that Beijing can infiltrate Taipei and monitor or punish opponents at any time. This “punishment and intimidation” tactic allows Beijing to “create a chilling effect in Taiwan, making voters afraid to openly support particular candidates or parties.”…

item.title: Government to limit costly legal claims aimed at silencing whistleblowers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains a legal change with implications for whistleblowers and public interest reporting

Government to limit costly legal claims aimed at silencing whistleblowers

The government has pledged to change the law to stop abuse victims, whistleblowers and journalists being silenced by spurious legal actions or threats.

Strategic litigation against public participation, known as Slapps, are often brought by wealthy individuals or companies to stifle scrutiny and suppress matters of public interest.

Existing protections only apply to Slapps linked to economic crime, but the government is now supporting a bill tabled by Conservative MP Sir John Whittingdale to extend protections to all forms of public interest reporting.

Labour's Courts Minister Sarah Sackman said the "justice system should never be a weapon of intimidation".

Speaking in the House of Commons, Sackman said: "The government, working with [Sir John], is determined to stop the wealthy, the powerful using the threat of costly legal proceedings to silence people.

"We are pleased to support the bill and to help ensure that those who expose wrongdoing hold the powerful to account and those who speak out in the public interest are protected."

Opening the debate on his bill, Sir John cited ex-Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed as someone who used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse of young female employees".

The MP for Maldon said: "That resulted in 27 years in which the information was never publicised."

Hundreds of women have accused Al Fayed of rape, sexual assault and trafficking, after a BBC documentary first publicly detailed the allegations in 2024.

Conservative MP Alicia Kearns said Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, "turned a culture of abuse and silence into the norm" for women working at Harrods.

The luxury store has previously said it "apologises unreservedly for the sexual abuse inflicted upon survivors by Fayed", and set up a compensation scheme for his victims.

Another example raised by Sir John was journalist Catherine Belton, the author of Putin's People, who faced five legal claims brought by Russian oligarchs and firms.

Sir John also referenced Eliot Higgins, the founder of investigative website Bellingcat, telling MPs he was sued by Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2021 for his tweets suggesting the Russian mercenary leader was associated with the Wagner Group.

He said: "Prigozhin was already sanctioned in this country because of his association yet nevertheless that case was allowed to proceed."

Measures in Sir John's bill include allowing judges to dismiss abusive claims before they go to trial and to protect defendants from exorbitant legal costs.

The UK Anti-Slaap Coalition said last week it "strongly" supports the bill making progress in Parliament although it voiced concerns over its current wording.

It noted there is an "almost impossibly high threshold" to make use of the early dismissal mechanism and offered to work with Sir John and others to refine the bill.

The National Union of Journalists voiced similar concerns, adding the protections must be "truly accessible and robust".

Sir John acknowledged there are concerns over "hurdles" in the proposed legislation which "could act as a deterrent", adding he expects further talks with the minister.

The Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No.2) Bill was debated in the House of Commons on Friday and was given an unopposed second reading, which means MPs endorsed the main principles of it.

It will undergo further scrutiny in the Commons at a later date. It will need to be approved by MPs and peers in the House of Lords to become law.

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

item.title: Reform's Joe Martin threatens legal challenge after being banned from speaking in Senedd
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Reports on a political ban with legal implications and free speech concerns

Reform's Joe Martin threatens legal challenge after being banned from speaking in Senedd

A Reform UK politician banned from speaking in the Senedd after referring to the "replacement" of white people in the UK says he will seek legal action to overturn the decision.

Joe Martin said elected representatives should be able to "speak up for the people who elected them" and raise "difficult subjects".

Reform ended a two-week boycott of most Senedd proceedings on Tuesday in response to the ban, and failed in a bid to remove the parliament's presiding officer.

The Free Speech Union (FSU) campaign group said Huw Irranca-Davies' ruling breached European law, and has sent a pre-action letter challenging it.

The Senedd Commission, which runs the parliament, declined to comment.

On Thursday night, Martin, who represents the Caerdydd Penarth constituency, called the ruling an "unprecedented attack on free speech".

Martin accused what he called a "uniparty" in Cardiff Bay of trying to silence Reform and protect a "cosy consensus".

"That is why I have taken legal action to defend the right to free speech in Wales," he said.

"Every elected representative should have the right to speak up for the people who elected them, without being silenced simply for raising difficult subjects."

FSU said it had sent a pre-action letter to the Senedd Commission, calling for the decision to be reversed, and said it argued that Irranca-Davies "misused his powers".

It also said the decision to prevent Martin from speaking and an order for him to apologise breached Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, external, which is the right to freedom of expression.

The ban was handed to Martin earlier this month, after he had asked a minister for a "statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place" in the UK.

"Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years' time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country," he said.

Irranca-Davies had described Martin's words as "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive", but stressed that members could "raise legitimate policy matters" on immigration.

Martin's focus "on race and ethnicity was clearly discriminatory, offensive and detracted from the dignity of the Senedd", Irranca-Davies previously said.

He said Martin would not be called to speak in the Senedd chamber until he had received "clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises".

In June, Plaid Cymru had accused Martin of dangerous rhetoric for claiming attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were inevitable.

The next day Senedd members walked out during a speech where Martin joked that Welsh students were unable to read and Indian nurses were taking Welsh jobs.

He was later accused by the presiding officer of making offensive remarks in a debate about the Welsh Gender Service.

item.title: Autoimmunity and the Stories Women Tell About Illness
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

For many women, being good has always meant being useful. Their sense of worth becomes tied to anticipating everyone else’s needs, taking responsibility for problems that aren’t theirs, and making sure no one is disappointed. Their own needs fall to the bottom of the list. Over time, it can become difficult to remember what it feels like to put themselves first.

What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

Sara Hirsh Bordo spent 15 years as a documentary filmmaker telling women’s stories before she began examining her own. Her experiences with serious illness led her to question the rules she’d been living by, and the result is her first book, Autoimmunity and the Good Girls. She calls herself a “recovering good girl.”

When we spoke, she kept returning to one question: What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

The Fear Beneath the Shoulds

We all know the vocabulary. I should do more. I should be available. I should be able to manage all of it. Bordo thinks the shoulds are not where this starts.

“I don’t think the ‘shoulds’ come first. I think the fears come first,” Bordo says.

She describes the questions that can arise when we begin challenging expectations we’ve lived with for years: What will my family think? Will I disappoint someone? What happens if I become someone new—and what if I don’t like that person?

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” Bordo says.

For Bordo, recognizing those fears meant reconsidering the rules she’d built her life around. She began questioning the expectations she’d inherited and making room for new ways of thinking about herself and her relationships.

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” she says.

She also recognizes how deeply these fears can be passed down through generations. They’re not just her own, she explains, but part of the expectations she saw reflected in her mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.

She said this the morning after a Zoom conversation with a book club of about 17 women of color, where the conversation about permission brought several of them to tears. The discussion prompted reflection on expectations and beliefs that some women had carried for decades.

The Stories We Inherit

Bordo’s question started with a pattern. The women around her who had been diagnosed with chronic or autoimmune conditions were all eldest or only daughters, herself included. At first, she assumed it was connected to birth order. So she and what she calls her “crack team of volunteers” started calling the CDC and the NIH. They found research about birth order and health in general, but nothing on autoimmune disease specifically.

She then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters.

She then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters. A few of the others wrote her personal notes describing how they’d taken on significant responsibility for others, despite not being the eldest or only daughter.

The survey was not a scientific study and had no comparison group, so the findings cannot establish a connection between birth order and autoimmune disease. But the notes stayed with her, because they pointed past birth order to something she describes as “heightened responsibility too soon.”

These observations also led Bordo to think differently about the relationship between personal experiences and physical health.

“Our body doesn’t just speak science, it speaks story,” Bordo says.

A doctor she names as Dr. Carmona then introduced her to epigenetics, the study of how changes in gene activity can occur without altering the underlying DNA sequence. She used it to map experiences from different chapters of her life against what her body might have been doing at the time. She is clear that this is her own framework and not a medical explanation. But it gave her a way to think about the body’s immune response in autoimmune disease, and about permission as the story we tell about who we’re allowed to be.

Permission, she told me, “is just the ground floor.”

To describe what it feels like when fear loosens, she reaches for a heist movie. She means it as a picture of how the change felt; she doesn’t claim it explains how autoimmune disease starts or ends.

“I feel like that level of fear and the power of fear is holding the space for freedom. And when freedom lives more than fear does, I think that’s when we are jackknifed into an immune system that actually starts almost unlocking itself. And then it’s like an Ocean’s Eleven scene. They’re opening the safe, and it’s like the inner workings of the safe, and the wheels are spinning, and then the doors are opening, and then that’s the image that I feel is happening in a body. You actually become sovereign enough, and brave enough, and self-permitted enough to choose for yourself first, and other people second. That’s the shift.”

I told her that last line made me think of someone I know. She’s smart, she knows what she wants, and she keeps handing the decision back to the good girl. The story about what she should do wins out over her own happiness more often than not. I can watch it from the outside, going in circles.

What It Looks Like at 4 A.M.

Bordo shared an example from earlier that morning. Her best friend’s mother was dying, with perhaps 48 hours left, and Bordo was due to fly out very early the next day. She had been on the road for 12 straight days and had a Reiki appointment booked for 3:30 that afternoon.…

item.title: Know Nothing: Finding Openness in Uncertainty
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English with useful vocabulary

Know Nothing: Finding Openness in Uncertainty

By Leo Babauta

The world is overwhelmed by rapid change, economic stress, wild weather, animosity towards our neighbors, and unprecedented levels of uncertainty.

All of us are feeling it in our own way. It’s a lot to deal with.

In the midst of this uproarious uncertainty, each of us reaches for our protection mechanisms: the ways we’ve learned to gain some sense of control in the uncontrollable.

Those protection mechanisms are familiar:

- We judge others, and turn to blame and lashing out, instead of finding empathy and compassion

- We avoid, hide, procrastinate, and go to distractions and comforts, instead of facing the discomfort of change

- We drive ourselves to work harder and harder, until burnout comes

- We get stuck in perfectionism and indecision, instead of taking action or being vulnerable

- We harden in our opinions and judgments, rather than being curious

- We seek systems of control, optimizing, getting more tools, relying on AI for answers, instead of being open to possibility and discovery

I could go on, but I think you get the idea. We’re thrashing about wildly as we feel out of control.

I’ve found that it’s absolutely possible to find calm and even openness in the midst of this kind of uncertainty. Not easy, but possible.

The answer is in what I like to call the Know Nothing approach. Let’s take a look!

Needing to Know vs. Not Knowing

All of our protection mechanisms (look at the list above) are forms of needing to know, to be in control, … but we’re in a situation where we can’t know, and where we can’t control things.

We want to judge and blame, so we know who’s wrong. We avoid to stay away from the discomfort that we don’t know we can handle. We overwork and optimize and get stuck in perfectionism, trying to control things to turn out the right way. We harden into our opinions, as if we could create certainty this way.

This is all to avoid staying in the space of not knowing. But that’s where we are — we don’t know how things will turn out right now, and we don’t know what to do about that. We simply can’t know.

What if we didn’t need the solid ground of knowing and controlling?

Not knowing is letting go of our demand to be in control and certainty, and opening to the idea that we can survive in the uncertainty … and even find some spaciousness.

We can also discover the delight in the not knowing:

- The ability to be surprised and to discover

- The curiosity to learn when we let go of already knowing

- The thirst to really get to know our fellow human beings, rather than putting them in predetermined categories

- The deliciousness of play, which doesn’t need to be in control

Our deepest learning, love and intimacy, and joy are all possible in this place of not knowing.

How to Live, with the Not Knowing Approach

Living with this approach of not knowing isn’t about being passive or not planning anything. It’s about being open, curious, playful, and open to discovery.

What if we could plan, but hold the plans lightly with an attitude of adventure?

What if we could be in a moment without needing to get anywhere, but instead just be present and savor the experience?

What if we could be with another person, without needing to categorize them first, letting go of any judgments we might have so that we can sit with them and get to know them?

What if we could let down our armor, and be vulnerable?

Each day, we could say, “I don’t know what today may bring. May I be open to it.”

We could walk through the day with a rough agenda, but also be willing to be present with someone in need who isn’t on the agenda, or to explore and play when the opportunity arises.

We could take on our tasks with an attitude of wanting to learn, rather than needing to get through it or get it right.

We could let go of expectations, and be open to finding out.

How to Practice

The main thing is to notice when you’re reaching for your armor. Notice if you’re judging, blaming, avoiding, shutting down, rushing, trying to get it perfect or right.

The best way to notice is to recognize what it feels like in your body: you’ll feel tightness and possibly anxiousness. You’ll feel like you’re bracing against danger.

When you notice that, you can try relaxing your body physically with some breathing and relaxing of your tighter muscles. And then relax yourself mentally as well: into not knowing, softening, opening, curiosity.

You might also have a mantra, like, “I don’t know” or “I know nothing.”

When you say this, drop your story of what you think or how you think it’ll go, or what you know about someone else. And then just see. Be open.

When you’re reaching for answers (like an AI tool, or other tech tools) … there’s nothing wrong with that, but could you take a breath and ask a question instead? And then go for a walk, and let yourself wonder and explore.

I’d like to leave you with a Zen koan (from the Book of Equanimity), which goes, “Not knowing is most intimate.”

In this sense, not knowing isn’t a problem, but the opportunity to be fully present with this moment, without a fixed idea of who we are or who we should be, or what the world should be.

I invite you to practice with this not knowing for the next week, and see what “I don’t know” could yield for you.

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-11-27 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: “An Air of Magic”: Scandi, Shaker, and Snug Lodgings in Bovina, New York
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting topic, but less depth and learning value

Have you, like us, pored over the handwritten menus and Shaker-style dining room of Bovina Farm & Fermentory and wanted to book a trip to upstate New York?

“The world of hauling laundry baskets, bed making, sneaking treats onto pillows, and rising with the sun to bake bread for breakfast is one which certainly suits us,” Elizabeth wrote to us a few weeks back. With the addition of a new-build guest cottage, a redone bedroom evocatively called the Pasture Room, and two lodgings above the restaurant, those who come to Bovina for home-brewed beer and a candlelit communal meal can tuck in afterwards in linen sheets and bed down by the heat of a wood stove.

By way of background: “We began building the main house and brewery barn in 2019 with the help of a local barn builder and my father,” Elizabeth writes. “We took about two years to reach ‘completion’—completion in quotes because things are constant works in progress around here.” The two welcomed dinner guests downstairs (read more about the restaurant here) and stayed, meanwhile, in the empty apartment upstairs. “Jake and I lived there for a while with no furniture. I remember sitting on a quilt on the floor with our new puppy and reading through old cookbooks weeks before our opening. We were radiating with anticipation and truly couldn’t care less that we were living in a construction zone.”

Fast forward a few years, and the couple has finally finished the lodgings they envisioned. “We wanted the inn spaces to match the simple, airy interiors of the dining room in the farmhouse, but with some extra warmth and comfort layered in. We stuck with the basic staples you might find in an old farmhouse or tavern: striped bedding, wrought-iron candlesticks, wooden stools that serve as bedside tables. There is minimal art or flourish in our spaces, as we like the views down the valley over the cow pasture or out toward the sheep paddock or into the woods and ferns to do the talking.”

Today, Elizabeth takes us on her rounds about the inn. Join for a tour:

Photography by Sarah Elliott, courtesy of Bovina Farm & Fermentory.

The Cottage

“Jake and I built The Cottage from the ground up, mostly just the two of us, but pulling in many friends and my father along the way,” Elizabeth says. “We built out the foundation in the winter of 2023—it was a particularly mild December and January.

“Even as a build site, The Cottage had an air of magic all around it—it was hard to pull ourselves away up the hill to get back to the restaurant sometimes. Before we started, this plot of land was densely wooded and thick with ferns and brambles that made a nearly impenetrable forest floor. It hadn’t been touched by human hands for maybe 70 years, and the beauty of that was obviously striking. We gently took down trees, leaving as many as we could, and watching this plot of land carefully transform under our nose has been magic all on its own.”

The green interiors were inspired by the land the cottage sits on, “its own secluded patch of woods ” studded with cherry trees. “The exterior, the interior walls, the cabinetry, and the bed nook curtains are all varying shades of green: Farrow and Ball Bone, Farrow and Ball Vert de Terre, DeVol Wikes Green, and a green blue linen gingham, respectively.

“The wood floors and butcher block countertops are cherry. Our neighbors recently restored their old farmhouse using cherry trees that they cut and milled from their own mountain, and we realized how integral cherry was to our area’s original homes and furniture. The depth and warmth of the dark, toasty cherry immediately welcomes you in and makes you feel held in a space. I think cherry is due for a comeback in interior design, but really we chose it simply to match the trees and materials that have been used in our region for hundreds of years. I’d say that’s the trick to nailing interiors: using natural materials that are found in your region. (Take it with a grain of salt coming from someone with no design background.) Like in the restaurant: What grows together goes together.”

“Whenever we’re about to embark on a new build, even for an outbuilding like a new chicken coop or woodshed, we head to The Shaker Village in Hancock,” says Elizabeth.” Every time, we see a new bit of architectural ingenuity or innovation that inspires us and reminds us to stay grounded in design that is beautiful due mostly to its hardworking functionality.”

There are pieces by small makers and friends, too: The pendant above the kitchen table is by “local friend Camille Callahan, who also makes sconce versions, candlesticks, and other objects.”

The Bedroom

The Maison

More details made by artists and friends, according to Elizabeth: “We asked Kelli Cain, local ceramics artist and owner of Luck Dragon arts supply store in the neighboring town of Delhi, to make our coffee mugs for the inn. The hand-dipped beeswax tapers placed around the guesthouse and restaurant come from family-owned Green Tree Home Candle in nearby Treadwell, NY. Maura O’Connor, artist and longtime family friend, drew up the detailed property map that is placed in each inn room and Stephanie Hare of Share Studios in Downeast Maine supplies the handmade papers that Elizabeth scribbles dinner menus on each week. The list goes on—we are so lucky!”

“The sun rises, we slip out of bed and into the arms of a warm oven loaded with dutch ovens filled with baking bread. We work quietly, hoping to wake our guests only with the smells of coffee and rye sourdough wafting their way through the floor vents. The morning gives way to breakfast and farm chores, and then to garden tasks, housekeeping, or whatever jobs are beckoning us that day. Fires are tended to;…
